items.title: Agentic search doesn't find pages, it assembles answers
items.summary: Ryan sits down with Jeff Wang, co-founder at EXA, to talk about the huge scale required to support trillions of agentic searches, the technical complexities of building custom embeddings and performant vector databases from scratch, and the need to dedupe the massive amounts of redundant content on the web to deliver high-trust answers.

items.title: Microsoft struggles to get M365 services back online after widespread outage
items.summary: If you’re struggling to send or receive emails, you’re not alone. Microsoft has been unable to fully restore Microsoft 365 more than 13 hours after an Exchange Online failure took down Outlook and spread to Teams, SharePoint, Copilot and parts of the company’s security tooling, and it said overnight that its latest fixes were “not taking as expected.” The outage began at 16:17 UTC on Nov. 12, according to Microsoft’s service health dashboard . “Users may be unable to access their mailbox using Outlook on the web, Outlook desktop (MAPI), Exchange ActiveSync (EAS), or REST-based connections, and email delivery may be delayed,” Microsoft wrote in the dashboard. Users in the Americas could not reach their mailboxes through Outlook on the web, desktop Outlook, mobile clients, or the REST API. Within two hours, Microsoft said users in any region could be affected. It opened a wider incident covering Teams, SharePoint Online, Copilot, Defender XDR, Intune, Power BI, and several Purview services. Downdetector logged more than 130,000 Outlook problem reports at the peak. In its latest service-health updates for incident MO1550821 , Microsoft said it had observed a surge in calls from routing services to backend servers as it applied mitigation measures. The company said traffic rebalancing had contributed to the increased volume and that it was scaling virtual machines to add capacity and reduce the load. “As we’ve applied our current ongoing mitigation actions, we’ve observed a surge in outbound call volume from our routing services to our backend servers,” Microsoft said in the update. It added: “We’re continuing to observe heightened volume due to traffic rebalancing actions that we have taken throughout this event.” Server failures behind the disruption Microsoft initially investigated elevated infrastructure load and the possibility that a recent change had contributed to the incident. It later said the problem was not being driven by an overall increase in traffic. “We’ve determined that the elevated load isn’t driven by an overall increase in traffic, but by a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, which is shifting load onto the remaining infrastructure,” the company said in its Exchange Online incident update . In a subsequent update, Microsoft identified a process responsible for establishing secure connections as a source of the problem. “Our investigation has found that a process on the affected servers responsible for establishing secure connections becomes overwhelmed, causing the servers to stop processing requests,” the company said. Microsoft said it was preparing a configuration change to address the behaviour and testing it on a subset of servers before wider deployment. It was also reverting a recent network configuration change that correlated with the start of the disruption, while restarting affected infrastructure and monitoring server stability. The recovery process has involved restricting some traffic and gradually reintroducing connections as Microsoft checks whether servers can remain stable under load. The company also reported that some servers became unresponsive again after traffic was restored, requiring further analysis and mitigation. Impact extends beyond email Microsoft’s incident notification said the impact varied by service and feature, depending in part on whether they relied on Exchange Online. The company said users might be unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes through Outlook on the web, Outlook desktop, Exchange ActiveSync, or REST-based connections, and that email delivery might be delayed. It said Teams’ core messaging and online meetings remained largely functional, but Exchange-dependent features such as calendar access and meeting scheduling could fail. Microsoft also said that direct access to files stored in SharePoint Online remained functional, while features dependent on Exchange Online could be affected. For Microsoft 365 Copilot, users might be unable to load Copilot Chat or receive responses, and Copilot experiences might be unable to access work data such as email, calendars, and files. The notification also identified potential impacts to Defender for Office 365 Safe Links, which might be unable to verify URLs clicked in Outlook and Teams, and to some Defender XDR portal pages. Other reported impacts included selected Intune device enrolment and compliance scenarios and Purview functions such as data loss prevention, automatic labelling and communication compliance. Enterprise concentration risk The incident has renewed attention on the operational dependencies created when organisations consolidate email, collaboration and security functions within a single cloud ecosystem. “Enterprises have priced Microsoft 365 as a licence and never as a single point of failure,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research. Gogia said that when mail, meetings and security functions such as Safe Links depend on the same service estate, an infrastructure disruption can affect several business functions at once. “The answer is not a second suite. It is a rehearsed fallback for the few things that cannot stop: an out-of-band channel for incident command, mail continuity for critical roles, and a written decision on whether each security control fails open or closed,” he said. For security teams, the distinction between a service being unavailable and a dependent security function being impaired is important. Microsoft’s notification about Safe Links, for example, points to a specific URL-verification impact rather than the loss of all Defender for Office 365 capabilities. Gogia also said enterprise customers would want a detailed account of the incident, including a timeline showing when Microsoft identified the different causes and how it validated the recovery measures. Microsoft has continued to publish updates through its Microsoft 365 service status portal. The company has not yet published a final post-incident root-cause report. The article originally appeared on CIO .

items.title: Codex Never Crashed. It Just Quietly Did Nothing.
items.summary: Codex Never Crashed. It Just Quietly Did Nothing. From the agentpolicy v0.1.0 release: a local-first, Cedar-based policy decision point for AI agents (decide allow, deny, ask, rate-limit, or redact for every agent action, with shipped rule packs). Now on PyPI . This story is journal Group 21 of the v0.1.0 field test report . AI disclosure: this article was drafted and edited with AI assistance. The field test, the defects, the fixes, and every number are real and linked below. Three bugs stood between me and a live Codex CLI integration. Not one of them printed an error. Every one of them let my harness sit there looking finished while producing nothing. This is the kind of debugging session that makes you stop trusting a quiet process. Trap one: the API you assumed still exists I wired Codex CLI against my local model server the way I had wired everything else: chat completions, the endpoint every OpenAI-compatible server speaks. Codex refused at startup: wire_api = "chat" is no longer supported . The CLI dropped chat completions entirely. The only transport it accepts now is the OpenAI Responses API. The lesson is not "read the changelog," although yes. The lesson is that my local server, oMLX, happened to serve /v1/responses natively, and I only found that out with a curl probe instead of an assumption. One probe, a real resp_* body, HTTP 200. The entire integration unblocked with zero translation layers. Vendor APIs drift. Probe the transport fresh for every CLI-to-endpoint pairing, every CLI version. Yesterday's working config is today's silent startup rejection. Trap two: the stdin hang codex exec , run headless from a test script, printed "Reading additional input from stdin..." and then sat there. No error. No timeout. No exit. My harness, which was watching the process and its output, looked "busy." The run produced zero evidence and appeared, from a process list, to be working. The cause: codex exec reads stdin, and in a harness stdin is whatever the parent left connected, which is never a closing TTY. The fix is two characters of shell: . Close stdin by default in every headless invocation. This one deserves a rule of its own: any headless CLI that consumes stdin will hang your harness quietly. An unattended process with a blocked read is the most patient bug in the world. It will wait forever, and your CI will show a spinner. Trap three: the 404s that blamed the server With transport sorted and stdin closed, every model call returned 404. Uniform, instant 404s. I spent a while on the server side, checking routes, because 404 says "server problem," right? Codex appends /responses to the provider base_url I configured. My proxy URL was http://127.0.0.1:PORT , so Codex called /responses . The server serves /v1/responses . The fix: base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:PORT/v1" . Off by one suffix, every call dead, server completely healthy the whole time. Paths are config. Config is a test surface. A uniform 404 across every request is almost never "the server is broken." It is "the client is asking somewhere else." The honest scoping problem There was a fourth decision, not a bug, a design call. Claude Code has a pausable per-call approval hook. I could wire the policy engine directly into the ask-a-human loop and test it live. Codex, headless, does not. Its governance surface is the sandbox and the config file: --sandbox read-only , provider config, executed commands. I could have forced parity and written a fake approval flow. Instead the case tests what the surface actually guarantees. Allow means the command executed, a real cat that printed real output. Deny means the destructive command was blocked, the target directory stayed intact with its keep.txt , and the agent replanned. Plus a parity check: the same three commands decided by the engine before execution, with an audit file showing allow , escalate , deny matching the in-process engine exactly. A harness test should assert what the surface guarantees and say so out loud. Stretching a different harness's shape over a vendor surface produces tests that pass and prove nothing. The final wiring, for the record Codex CLI 0.135.0 against the box-local model, no OpenAI key. A stdlib logging proxy ( t1_proxy.py ) between the CLI and the model server captured 4 request and 4 response pairs, sanitized, all 2xx. The parity audit trail has 3 decisions. The allow executed, the deny held and replanned, and the whole thing reproduces from the committed config ( t1_codex.sh , codex-home/config.toml in the case's evidence directory). What worked Probing before wiring. The Responses API question was settled with one curl before any config existed. Capturing LLM traffic as a hard requirement. Every pair on disk or the case fails. That rule is the only reason "looked busy, did nothing" runs got caught at all. Testing the pieces standalone before composing them: policy through evaluate first, then the proxy with curl, then the CLI through the proxy. Each failure lived in exactly one layer. What did not work Trusting that chat completions would still be the transport. It was not, and finding out cost me a full debug cycle. Leaving stdin connected. Obvious in hindsight, invisible in the process list. Reading 404 as "server broken" before reading it as "client asking in the wrong place." More detail and evidence The full Codex story: field test report, journal Group 21 (FT-T1-CODEX), plus Field Notes 12 for the write-up version of the same traps. The harness, in the repo: t1_codex.sh (config, parity triple, sandbox triple) · t1_proxy.py (the /responses -aware capture proxy) · t1_policy.yaml (the shared Tier-1 policy). The captured evidence: field-test/v0.1.0/results/s18-tier1/cases/FT-T1-CODEX/ in the repo (live transcripts, audit trail, 4 LLM pairs, provider config). The plan row that scoped the case honestly: FIELD_TEST_PLAN.md , the FT-T1-CODEX row and the Tier-1 R-map. The product: agentpolicy , pip install agentsec-agentpolicy , PyPI 0.1.0 , docs reference (adapters, authzen, surfaces), part of the agentic-suite agent-security stack. What is the most patient bug you have shipped in a harness? The one that produced no output, no error, and no exit, just quiet nothing. I want to know I am not alone.
items.summary_html:
Codex Never Crashed. It Just Quietly Did Nothing.

From the agentpolicy v0.1.0 release: a local-first, Cedar-based policy decision point for AI agents (decide allow, deny, ask, rate-limit, or redact for every agent action, with shipped rule packs). Now on PyPI. This story is journal Group 21 of the v0.1.0 field test report.

AI disclosure: this article was drafted and edited with AI assistance. The field test, the defects, the fixes, and every number are real and linked below.

Three bugs stood between me and a live Codex CLI integration. Not one of them printed an error. Every one of them let my harness sit there looking finished while producing nothing. This is the kind of debugging session that makes you stop trusting a quiet process.

Trap one: the API you assumed still exists

I wired Codex CLI against my local model server the way I had wired everything else: chat completions, the endpoint every OpenAI-compatible server speaks. Codex refused at startup: wire_api = "chat" is no longer supported. The CLI dropped chat completions entirely. The only transport it accepts now is the OpenAI Responses API.

The lesson is not "read the changelog," although yes. The lesson is that my local server, oMLX, happened to serve /v1/responses natively, and I only found that out with a curl probe instead of an assumption. One probe, a real resp_* body, HTTP 200. The entire integration unblocked with zero translation layers.

Vendor APIs drift. Probe the transport fresh for every CLI-to-endpoint pairing, every CLI version. Yesterday's working config is today's silent startup rejection.

Trap two: the stdin hang

codex exec, run headless from a test script, printed "Reading additional input from stdin..." and then sat there. No error. No timeout. No exit. My harness, which was watching the process and its output, looked "busy." The run produced zero evidence and appeared, from a process list, to be working.

The cause: codex exec reads stdin, and in a harness stdin is whatever the parent left connected, which is never a closing TTY. The fix is two characters of shell: . Close stdin by default in every headless invocation.

This one deserves a rule of its own: any headless CLI that consumes stdin will hang your harness quietly. An unattended process with a blocked read is the most patient bug in the world. It will wait forever, and your CI will show a spinner.

Trap three: the 404s that blamed the server

With transport sorted and stdin closed, every model call returned 404. Uniform, instant 404s. I spent a while on the server side, checking routes, because 404 says "server problem," right?

Codex appends /responses to the provider base_url I configured. My proxy URL was http://127.0.0.1:PORT, so Codex called /responses. The server serves /v1/responses. The fix: base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:PORT/v1". Off by one suffix, every call dead, server completely healthy the whole time.

Paths are config. Config is a test surface. A uniform 404 across every request is almost never "the server is broken." It is "the client is asking somewhere else."

The honest scoping problem

There was a fourth decision, not a bug, a design call. Claude Code has a pausable per-call approval hook. I could wire the policy engine directly into the ask-a-human loop and test it live. Codex, headless, does not. Its governance surface is the sandbox and the config file: --sandbox read-only, provider config, executed commands.

I could have forced parity and written a fake approval flow. Instead the case tests what the surface actually guarantees. Allow means the command executed, a real cat that printed real output. Deny means the destructive command was blocked, the target directory stayed intact with its keep.txt, and the agent replanned. Plus a parity check: the same three commands decided by the engine before execution, with an audit file showing allow, escalate, deny matching the in-process engine exactly.

A harness test should assert what the surface guarantees and say so out loud. Stretching a different harness's shape over a vendor surface produces tests that pass and prove nothing.

The final wiring, for the record

Codex CLI 0.135.0 against the box-local model, no OpenAI key. A stdlib logging proxy (t1_proxy.py) between the CLI and the model server captured 4 request and 4 response pairs, sanitized, all 2xx. The parity audit trail has 3 decisions. The allow executed, the deny held and replanned, and the whole thing reproduces from the committed config (t1_codex.sh, codex-home/config.toml in the case's evidence directory).

What worked
  • Probing before wiring. The Responses API question was settled with one curl before any config existed.
  • Capturing LLM traffic as a hard requirement. Every pair on disk or the case fails. That rule is the only reason "looked busy, did nothing" runs got caught at all.
  • Testing the pieces standalone before composing them: policy through evaluate first, then the proxy with curl, then the CLI through the proxy. Each failure lived in exactly one layer.
What did not work
  • Trusting that chat completions would still be the transport. It was not, and finding out cost me a full debug cycle.
  • Leaving stdin connected. Obvious in hindsight, invisible in the process list.
  • Reading 404 as "server broken" before reading it as "client asking in the wrong place."
More detail and evidence
  • The full Codex story: field test report, journal Group 21 (FT-T1-CODEX), plus Field Notes 12 for the write-up version of the same traps.
  • The harness, in the repo: t1_codex.sh (config, parity triple, sandbox triple) · t1_proxy.py (the /responses-aware capture proxy) · t1_policy.yaml (the shared Tier-1 policy).
  • The captured evidence: field-test/v0.1.0/results/s18-tier1/cases/FT-T1-CODEX/ in the repo (live transcripts, audit trail, 4 LLM pairs, provider config).
  • The plan row that scoped the case honestly: FIELD_TEST_PLAN.md, the FT-T1-CODEX row and the Tier-1 R-map.
  • The product: agentpolicy, pip install agentsec-agentpolicy, PyPI 0.1.0, docs reference (adapters, authzen, surfaces), part of the agentic-suite agent-security stack.

What is the most patient bug you have shipped in a harness? The one that produced no output, no error, and no exit, just quiet nothing. I want to know I am not alone.

items.title: Adding LocalBusiness Schema to a Next.js App Router Site Without Breaking Anything
items.summary: If you build websites for plumbers, dentists, law firms or any other local service business, structured data is one of the cheapest technical wins you can ship. A few lines of JSON-LD tell search engines exactly who the business is, where it operates, when it is open and how to reach it. Done well, it supports rich results and helps Google connect the website to the business behind it. Done badly, it gets ignored or flagged in Search Console. This post walks through a clean, maintainable way to add LocalBusiness schema to a Next.js App Router project. We will keep the business data in one typed file, render JSON-LD on the server, generate per-page schema for service and location pages, and validate everything before it goes live. Why structured data matters for local sites Search engines are good at reading pages, but they still guess. Is that phone number in the footer the main line or a fax? Is the address a storefront or a mailing address? Which city does the business actually serve? Schema markup removes that guesswork by describing the business in a format machines read without interpretation. For local service businesses, the useful pieces are usually: Business name, logo and main URL Phone number and contact options Address, or service area if the business has no public storefront Opening hours Links to official profiles (the sameAs property) The services the business offers If you want the non-technical background on what each property means and which ones matter most, the CodeHunterz guide on schema markup for a local business covers it in plain language. Here we focus on the implementation. Step 1: Keep business data in one typed source The most common schema bug is drift. The phone number in the header changes, but the JSON-LD still shows the old one. Fix that by storing business details in a single file and reading from it everywhere: header, footer, contact page and schema. // lib/business.ts export type OpeningHours = { days : string [ ] ; opens : string ; closes : string ; } ; export const business = { name : "Example Plumbing Co" , url : "https://www.example.com" , logo : "https://www.example.com/logo.png" , phone : "+1-555-010-0000" , email : "hello@example.com" , priceRange : "$$" , serviceAreas : [ "Austin" , "Round Rock" , "Cedar Park" ] , hours : [ { days : [ "Monday" , "Tuesday" , "Wednesday" , "Thursday" , "Friday" ] , opens : "08:00" , closes : "18:00" } , { days : [ "Saturday" ] , opens : "09:00" , closes : "14:00" } , ] as OpeningHours [ ] , sameAs : [ "https://www.facebook.com/exampleplumbing" , "https://www.yelp.com/biz/example-plumbing" , ] , } ; The values above are placeholders. In a real project they come from the client, and they must match the Google Business Profile exactly. Mismatched names or phone numbers between the site and the profile are a classic local SEO problem, and schema will not fix that for you. Step 2: Build the JSON-LD object with a helper Instead of hand writing JSON in a component, build it with a function. That keeps it testable and lets you reuse parts for other schema types. // lib/schema.ts import { business } from "./business" ; export function localBusinessSchema ( ) { return { "@context" : "https://schema.org" , "@type" : "Plumber" , "@id" : `${business.url}/#business` , name : business . name , url : business . url , logo : business . logo , image : business . logo , telephone : business . phone , email : business . email , priceRange : business . priceRange , areaServed : business . serviceAreas . map ( ( city ) => ( { "@type" : "City" , name : city , } ) ) , openingHoursSpecification : business . hours . map ( ( h ) => ( { "@type" : "OpeningHoursSpecification" , dayOfWeek : h . days , opens : h . opens , closes : h . closes , } ) ) , sameAs : business . sameAs , } ; } A few details worth calling out: Use the most specific type you can. Plumber , Dentist , Attorney , HVACBusiness and many others are subtypes of LocalBusiness . A specific type gives search engines more context than the generic parent. Give the entity a stable @id . Using something like https://www.example.com/#business lets other schema blocks on other pages reference the same business instead of declaring a new one each time. Service area businesses can skip the street address. If the client works from home and does not serve customers at that location, leave address out or include only the city and region, and rely on areaServed . Publishing a home address that the business keeps hidden on its Google profile creates a conflict. Step 3: Render JSON-LD on the server In the App Router, the simplest approach is a small server component that outputs a script tag. No client JavaScript is needed, and the markup is in the initial HTML that crawlers fetch. // components/JsonLd.tsx type Props = { data : Record < string , unknown > } ; export function JsonLd ( { data } : Props ) { return ( < script type = "application/ld+json" dangerouslySetInnerHTML = { { __html : JSON . stringify ( data ) . replace ( / g , "\\u003c" ) , } } /> ) ; } The replace call escapes any < characters so that a stray string in your data cannot close the script tag early. It is a small safety habit that matters when content comes from a CMS. Now add it to the root layout so the business entity appears on every page: // app/layout.tsx import { JsonLd } from "@/components/JsonLd" ; import { localBusinessSchema } from "@/lib/schema" ; export default function RootLayout ( { children } : { children : React . ReactNode } ) { return ( < html lang = "en" > < body > < JsonLd data = { localBusinessSchema ( ) } /> { children } body > html > ) ; } Some teams prefer to place the main business schema only on the homepage and contact page. Either works. What matters is that the data is consistent and that you do not declare conflicting versions of the same business on different pages. Step 4: Add Service schema to service pages Most local sites have pages like "Drain Cleaning" or "Water Heater Repair". Each of these can carry a Service block that points back to the business through its @id . // lib/schema.ts (continued) export function serviceSchema ( opts : { name : string ; description : string ; path : string ; } ) { return { "@context" : "https://schema.org" , "@type" : "Service" , name : opts . name , description : opts . description , url : `${business.url}${opts.path}` , provider : { "@id" : `${business.url}/#business` } , areaServed : business . serviceAreas . map ( ( city ) => ( { "@type" : "City" , name : city , } ) ) , } ; } Then use it in a dynamic route: // app/services/[slug]/page.tsx import { JsonLd } from "@/components/JsonLd" ; import { serviceSchema } from "@/lib/schema" ; import { getService } from "@/lib/services" ; export default async function ServicePage ( { params , } : { params : Promise < { slug : string } > ; } ) { const { slug } = await params ; const service = await getService ( slug ) ; return ( < main > < JsonLd data = { serviceSchema ( { name : service . title , description : service . summary , path : `/services/${slug}` , } ) } /> < h1 > { service . title } h1 > { /* page content */ } main > ) ; } Because the description comes from the same content that renders on the page, the schema always matches what visitors see. That alignment is important. Structured data that describes content not visible on the page goes against Google's guidelines. Step 5: Breadcrumbs for deeper pages Location and service pages often sit two or three levels deep. A BreadcrumbList helps search engines understand the hierarchy and can show a cleaner path in results. export function breadcrumbSchema ( items : { name : string ; path : string } [ ] ) { return { "@context" : "https://schema.org" , "@type" : "BreadcrumbList" , itemListElement : items . map ( ( item , i ) => ( { "@type" : "ListItem" , position : i + 1 , name : item . name , item : `${business.url}${item.path}` , } ) ) , } ; } You can pass an array of schema objects to a single JsonLd component, or render one component per object. Both are valid. I usually render separate tags because it keeps each block easy to inspect in the browser. Step 6: Things to avoid A few patterns cause more trouble than they are worth: Self-serving review markup. Adding aggregateRating to your own LocalBusiness schema with reviews you collected yourself is not eligible for review rich results. Leave ratings out unless you have a clear, guideline-compliant reason to include them. Inventing data. Do not add hours, prices or service areas the business has not confirmed. Schema should mirror reality. Client-side injection only. If you add schema with a useEffect hook, it may still be picked up, but you are adding a rendering dependency for no benefit. Server rendering is simpler and more reliable. Duplicate entities from plugins. If the project mixes Next.js with a headless CMS or third-party widget that injects its own schema, check the final HTML. Two different LocalBusiness blocks with different names or phone numbers send mixed signals. Step 7: Validate before and after deploy Never ship schema blind. A quick validation routine: Run the page through the Schema Markup Validator at validator.schema.org to catch syntax and type errors. Use Google's Rich Results Test to see which rich result types the page is eligible for. View the page source in production and confirm the script tag is present in the server HTML, not only after hydration. After deploy, watch the Enhancements and structured data reports in Google Search Console for warnings over the following weeks. You can also add a simple test that parses your schema helpers and checks required fields, so a missing phone number fails CI instead of silently shipping. // __tests__/schema.test.ts import { localBusinessSchema } from "@/lib/schema" ; test ( "local business schema has required fields" , ( ) => { const s = localBusinessSchema ( ) ; expect ( s . name ) . toBeTruthy ( ) ; expect ( s . telephone ) . toMatch ( /^ \ + 1 / ) ; expect ( s . url . startsWith ( "https://" ) ) . toBe ( true ) ; } ) ; If you also want a quick look at how a live site handles status codes, HTTPS and meta tags, the free website tools on CodeHunterz are handy for spot checks before handing a project over. Where schema fits in the bigger picture Structured data is a supporting signal, not a ranking shortcut. It works best on a site that is already fast, crawlable and clear about what the business does and where. For local businesses, that also means a well maintained Google Business Profile, consistent citations and real reviews earned from real customers. Schema simply makes sure the technical layer tells the same story as everything else. For developers, the takeaway is to treat schema like any other part of the codebase: one source of truth, typed helpers, server rendering, tests and validation. That is how we approach it in our own Next.js development work, and it makes handoffs and later edits painless. If you are building for local clients and want to understand the marketing side that sits on top of this technical foundation, the CodeHunterz page on local SEO services explains how the pieces fit together from the business owner's point of view. Happy shipping. CodeHunterz Team
items.summary_html:
If you build websites for plumbers, dentists, law firms or any other local service business, structured data is one of the cheapest technical wins you can ship. A few lines of JSON-LD tell search engines exactly who the business is, where it operates, when it is open and how to reach it. Done well, it supports rich results and helps Google connect the website to the business behind it. Done badly, it gets ignored or flagged in Search Console.

This post walks through a clean, maintainable way to add LocalBusiness schema to a Next.js App Router project. We will keep the business data in one typed file, render JSON-LD on the server, generate per-page schema for service and location pages, and validate everything before it goes live.

Why structured data matters for local sites

Search engines are good at reading pages, but they still guess. Is that phone number in the footer the main line or a fax? Is the address a storefront or a mailing address? Which city does the business actually serve? Schema markup removes that guesswork by describing the business in a format machines read without interpretation.

For local service businesses, the useful pieces are usually:

  • Business name, logo and main URL
  • Phone number and contact options
  • Address, or service area if the business has no public storefront
  • Opening hours
  • Links to official profiles (the sameAs property)
  • The services the business offers

If you want the non-technical background on what each property means and which ones matter most, the CodeHunterz guide on schema markup for a local business covers it in plain language. Here we focus on the implementation.

Step 1: Keep business data in one typed source

The most common schema bug is drift. The phone number in the header changes, but the JSON-LD still shows the old one. Fix that by storing business details in a single file and reading from it everywhere: header, footer, contact page and schema.

// lib/business.ts
export type OpeningHours = {
  days: string[];
  opens: string;
  closes: string;
};

export const business = {
  name: "Example Plumbing Co",
  url: "https://www.example.com",
  logo: "https://www.example.com/logo.png",
  phone: "+1-555-010-0000",
  email: "hello@example.com",
  priceRange: "$$",
  serviceAreas: ["Austin", "Round Rock", "Cedar Park"],
  hours: [
    { days: ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday"], opens: "08:00", closes: "18:00" },
    { days: ["Saturday"], opens: "09:00", closes: "14:00" },
  ] as OpeningHours[],
  sameAs: [
    "https://www.facebook.com/exampleplumbing",
    "https://www.yelp.com/biz/example-plumbing",
  ],
};

The values above are placeholders. In a real project they come from the client, and they must match the Google Business Profile exactly. Mismatched names or phone numbers between the site and the profile are a classic local SEO problem, and schema will not fix that for you.

Step 2: Build the JSON-LD object with a helper

Instead of hand writing JSON in a component, build it with a function. That keeps it testable and lets you reuse parts for other schema types.

// lib/schema.ts
import { business } from "./business";

export function localBusinessSchema() {
  return {
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "Plumber",
    "@id": `${business.url}/#business`,
    name: business.name,
    url: business.url,
    logo: business.logo,
    image: business.logo,
    telephone: business.phone,
    email: business.email,
    priceRange: business.priceRange,
    areaServed: business.serviceAreas.map((city) => ({
      "@type": "City",
      name: city,
    })),
    openingHoursSpecification: business.hours.map((h) => ({
      "@type": "OpeningHoursSpecification",
      dayOfWeek: h.days,
      opens: h.opens,
      closes: h.closes,
    })),
    sameAs: business.sameAs,
  };
}

A few details worth calling out:

Use the most specific type you can. Plumber, Dentist, Attorney, HVACBusiness and many others are subtypes of LocalBusiness. A specific type gives search engines more context than the generic parent.

Give the entity a stable @id. Using something like https://www.example.com/#business lets other schema blocks on other pages reference the same business instead of declaring a new one each time.

Service area businesses can skip the street address. If the client works from home and does not serve customers at that location, leave address out or include only the city and region, and rely on areaServed. Publishing a home address that the business keeps hidden on its Google profile creates a conflict.

Step 3: Render JSON-LD on the server

In the App Router, the simplest approach is a small server component that outputs a script tag. No client JavaScript is needed, and the markup is in the initial HTML that crawlers fetch.

// components/JsonLd.tsx
type Props = { data: Record<string, unknown> };

export function JsonLd({ data }: Props) {
  return (
    <script
      type="application/ld+json"
      dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{
        __html: JSON.stringify(data).replace(/g, "\\u003c"),
      }}
    />
  );
}

The replace call escapes any < characters so that a stray string in your data cannot close the script tag early. It is a small safety habit that matters when content comes from a CMS.

Now add it to the root layout so the business entity appears on every page:

// app/layout.tsx
import { JsonLd } from "@/components/JsonLd";
import { localBusinessSchema } from "@/lib/schema";

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <JsonLd data={localBusinessSchema()} />
        {children}
      body>
    html>
  );
}

Some teams prefer to place the main business schema only on the homepage and contact page. Either works. What matters is that the data is consistent and that you do not declare conflicting versions of the same business on different pages.

Step 4: Add Service schema to service pages

Most local sites have pages like "Drain Cleaning" or "Water Heater Repair". Each of these can carry a Service block that points back to the business through its @id.

// lib/schema.ts (continued)
export function serviceSchema(opts: {
  name: string;
  description: string;
  path: string;
}) {
  return {
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "Service",
    name: opts.name,
    description: opts.description,
    url: `${business.url}${opts.path}`,
    provider: { "@id": `${business.url}/#business` },
    areaServed: business.serviceAreas.map((city) => ({
      "@type": "City",
      name: city,
    })),
  };
}

Then use it in a dynamic route:

// app/services/[slug]/page.tsx
import { JsonLd } from "@/components/JsonLd";
import { serviceSchema } from "@/lib/schema";
import { getService } from "@/lib/services";

export default async function ServicePage({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug: string }>;
}) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  const service = await getService(slug);

  return (
    <main>
      <JsonLd
        data={serviceSchema({
          name: service.title,
          description: service.summary,
          path: `/services/${slug}`,
        })}
      />
      <h1>{service.title}h1>
      {/* page content */}
    main>
  );
}

Because the description comes from the same content that renders on the page, the schema always matches what visitors see. That alignment is important. Structured data that describes content not visible on the page goes against Google's guidelines.

Step 5: Breadcrumbs for deeper pages

Location and service pages often sit two or three levels deep. A BreadcrumbList helps search engines understand the hierarchy and can show a cleaner path in results.

export function breadcrumbSchema(items: { name: string; path: string }[]) {
  return {
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "BreadcrumbList",
    itemListElement: items.map((item, i) => ({
      "@type": "ListItem",
      position: i + 1,
      name: item.name,
      item: `${business.url}${item.path}`,
    })),
  };
}

You can pass an array of schema objects to a single JsonLd component, or render one component per object. Both are valid. I usually render separate tags because it keeps each block easy to inspect in the browser.

Step 6: Things to avoid

A few patterns cause more trouble than they are worth:

Self-serving review markup. Adding aggregateRating to your own LocalBusiness schema with reviews you collected yourself is not eligible for review rich results. Leave ratings out unless you have a clear, guideline-compliant reason to include them.

Inventing data. Do not add hours, prices or service areas the business has not confirmed. Schema should mirror reality.

Client-side injection only. If you add schema with a useEffect hook, it may still be picked up, but you are adding a rendering dependency for no benefit. Server rendering is simpler and more reliable.

Duplicate entities from plugins. If the project mixes Next.js with a headless CMS or third-party widget that injects its own schema, check the final HTML. Two different LocalBusiness blocks with different names or phone numbers send mixed signals.

Step 7: Validate before and after deploy

Never ship schema blind. A quick validation routine:

  1. Run the page through the Schema Markup Validator at validator.schema.org to catch syntax and type errors.
  2. Use Google's Rich Results Test to see which rich result types the page is eligible for.
  3. View the page source in production and confirm the script tag is present in the server HTML, not only after hydration.
  4. After deploy, watch the Enhancements and structured data reports in Google Search Console for warnings over the following weeks.

You can also add a simple test that parses your schema helpers and checks required fields, so a missing phone number fails CI instead of silently shipping.

// __tests__/schema.test.ts
import { localBusinessSchema } from "@/lib/schema";

test("local business schema has required fields", () => {
  const s = localBusinessSchema();
  expect(s.name).toBeTruthy();
  expect(s.telephone).toMatch(/^\+1/);
  expect(s.url.startsWith("https://")).toBe(true);
});

If you also want a quick look at how a live site handles status codes, HTTPS and meta tags, the free website tools on CodeHunterz are handy for spot checks before handing a project over.

Where schema fits in the bigger picture

Structured data is a supporting signal, not a ranking shortcut. It works best on a site that is already fast, crawlable and clear about what the business does and where. For local businesses, that also means a well maintained Google Business Profile, consistent citations and real reviews earned from real customers. Schema simply makes sure the technical layer tells the same story as everything else.

For developers, the takeaway is to treat schema like any other part of the codebase: one source of truth, typed helpers, server rendering, tests and validation. That is how we approach it in our own Next.js development work, and it makes handoffs and later edits painless.

If you are building for local clients and want to understand the marketing side that sits on top of this technical foundation, the CodeHunterz page on local SEO services explains how the pieces fit together from the business owner's point of view.

Happy shipping.

items.title: Evolving JuiceFS Enterprise Edition for Exabyte-Scale AI Storage
items.summary: As AI workloads scale from petabytes to exabytes, storage systems face challenges that go far beyond capacity. File counts can reach hundreds of billions, client connections can grow from thousands to hundreds of thousands or even millions, and training throughput continues to increase. At the same time, data reclamation, cross-cloud access, multi-tenant isolation, and daily operations all become more demanding. These challenges put pressure on four key areas of the storage architecture: the metadata engine, data lifecycle management, the data path, and the client and control planes. The previous article explored how Horizon Robotics, an autonomous driving technology company, uses JuiceFS Community Edition at exabyte scale. This article focuses on JuiceFS Enterprise Edition and how these four areas have evolved to meet the demands of exabyte-scale data, hundreds of billions of files, and millions of clients. Metadata engine: from single-node performance to horizontal scaling across hundreds of billions of files Metadata challenges at the scale of hundreds of billions of files When a file system manages hundreds of billions of files, metadata access faces three major challenges: Hotspots : During peak training periods, a small number of heavily accessed directories and frequent metadata operations can turn a single metadata node into a bottleneck. Increased latency : Path resolution, attribute lookups, and file opens all require metadata access. Any additional round trip can directly slow down training jobs. Scale-related overhead : Large directories, such as those in the trash, can contain tens of billions of entries. Global information, including mount configurations and capacity data, is also queried repeatedly. To address these challenges, JuiceFS Enterprise Edition has evolved its metadata engine with a custom-built metadata service. The service distributes hotspots, reduces access latency, and supports horizontal scaling. Metadata engine design: in-memory, lock-free, and multi-zone The Enterprise Edition metadata engine combines an in-memory architecture, single-threaded lock-free processing, and Raft. All core data structures are processed by a single thread. This design ensures atomicity by default and avoids latency spikes caused by lock contention between threads. Keeping metadata in memory eliminates the need to access disks for metadata requests, keeping per-request processing latency in the hundreds of microseconds. Raft handles replication across nodes and automatic failover. A single metadata process can manage approximately 300 million files with 30 GiB of memory. However, an in-memory design also means that memory consumption directly affects hardware costs. At the scale of hundreds of billions of files, even a small difference in per-file memory usage can translate into substantial resource overhead. JuiceFS Enterprise Edition uses several techniques to reduce memory consumption, including memory pools, manual memory management, serialization and compression of idle directories, and compact representations of small files. These optimizations have reduced average memory usage per file from nearly 600 bytes to approximately 100 bytes—about 27% of that of an HDFS NameNode and 3.7% of that of a CephFS MDS. System Memory per file Reference HDFS NameNode ~370 B Third-party technical blog CephFS MDS ~2,700 B Ceph cluster monitoring (32 GB RAM / 12 million files) Alluxio (heap memory mode) ~2,100 B Alluxio documentation (64 GB RAM / ~30 million files) JuiceFS Community Edition ~430 B Community Edition documentation JuiceFS Enterprise Edition ~100 B Production cluster monitoring (30 GB RAM / 300 million files) Higher memory efficiency allows the same hardware to manage more files. In other words, it significantly reduces the metadata infrastructure costs of managing hundreds of billions of files. Building on the capabilities of a single process, Enterprise Edition uses multiple metadata zones to scale horizontally. Each zone manages part of the file tree, while clients combine the zones into a single namespace. The design keeps subtrees complete whenever possible, so most operations stay within a single zone and require fewer distributed transactions. Cross-zone migration uses links and references, remaining transparent to POSIX paths. Extremely large directories can also be split into multiple virtual subdirectories, allowing finer-grained migration and preventing a single large directory from remaining a long-term burden on one zone. The high-order bits of each inode encode its zone information. Clients automatically discover the zone topology and connect to all zones. Adding a zone therefore requires no changes to application access patterns. For reliability, each zone consists of three instances: a service instance, a hot standby instance, and a cold standby instance. The service and hot standby instances use different memory compression strategies. Snapshots and change logs are continuously persisted to disk and can also be backed up to a remote location (see the Trash, background tasks, and audit backups section). Version evolution and scale validation Starting with v5.2, Enterprise Edition focused on improving multi-zone stability and reducing metadata memory consumption, bringing file management into the hundreds-of-billions range. In production, a single cluster now manages more than 50 billion files while keeping metadata access latency at the millisecond level. In v5.3, the maximum number of zones increased to 1,024, allowing a single file system to support more than 500 billion files. The release also introduced automatic hotspot migration and supporting operations tools. Frequently accessed directories can be split into smaller units and migrated concurrently to distribute hotspots more quickly. Periodic self-checks detect and repair intermediate states that may remain after cross-zone migrations. In v5.4, the focus expanded from file count to client scale. Metadata nodes and network proxies can now be deployed together, and clients can connect to any node. Requests for other zones are forwarded internally by the cluster. Combined with connection reuse, this architecture supports up to a million client connections. In the last section, we’ll cover this design in more detail. Data lifecycle management: built-in deletion, recovery, and auditing Data lifecycle challenges when deleting petabytes of data Deleting petabytes of data requires more than reclaiming storage space promptly. The system must also support recovery from accidental deletion, deletion traceability, and audits for orphaned objects. Object storage can accumulate billions of objects awaiting reclamation. An accidental deletion can disrupt training jobs, while leftover objects must be continuously detected and accounted for. Trash, background tasks, and audit backups The trash is enabled by default in Enterprise Edition. Deleted files first move to the trash, where the retention period is configurable (typically seven days). During this period, users can restore files through the console or a restore command. Restoration only updates metadata; it does not copy the underlying data. Starting with v5.3, the trash in multi-zone environments records each file's original path to ensure that files are restored to the correct location. In v5.4, users can filter deleted files by time range and keywords. This makes it easier to find accidentally deleted files among large volumes of deletions. Storage reclamation is handled by a unified background tasks framework. Tasks such as chunk compaction, trash cleanup, and cross-cloud replication are scheduled by the metadata service and executed concurrently across clients throughout the cluster. This approach offers three main benefits: Scalable deletion: Deletion capacity scales with the number of clients. To speed up reclamation, simply add more mount points. Controllable execution: Deletion traffic can be limited by access token. Background tasks can be disabled for specific clients, while the metadata service centrally configures the execution windows for chunk compaction. Observable progress: Both chunk compaction and deletion tasks expose monitoring metrics. Auditing and disaster recovery are also built into the system. Change logs record every deletion operation and the session that initiated it. Combined with audit logs, they help answer the questions: who deleted what, and when? The console provides centralized configuration for metadata snapshots and change logs. By default, backups are sent to remote object storage every hour. Local backups are retained for two days, and a retention period of at least 30 days is recommended. On the object storage side, garbage collection and consistency-checking tools audit orphaned objects. In v5.4, both tools gained an external sorting mode that uses disk space instead of memory for sorting. This keeps memory consumption manageable when checking hundreds of millions of files. External sorting is intended for inspection and assessment only; it does not delete any objects. Data insights and dataset branching Deletion decisions require reliable data. The console's monitoring dashboard provides metrics such as the number of files in the trash, pending object chunks for deletion, and fragmented chunks. File searches filter results on the metadata side, supporting hot/cold data analysis and data aging assessments. Directory, user, and group quotas help enforce storage budgets across workloads. For dataset preparation, v5.4 supports cross-zone directory cloning. Cloning a directory containing 100 million files takes approximately 1 minute and 40 seconds, or about 1 million files per second. Data path: balancing performance and cost with caching and mirroring Accessing EB-scale data: throughput, storage costs, and cross-cloud access Training workloads require throughput at the terabyte-per-second level. Dataset loading involves large volumes of random reads, while training checkpoint writes involve sequential writes of large files. These workloads have different IOPS and write-throughput requirements. At the same time, storing all EB-scale data in a hot storage tier is not possible. Compute resources deployed across multiple clouds also need to access data from nearby locations whenever possible. Therefore, read performance, storage costs, and data locality must be addressed together. Multi-level caching and distributed cache groups Enterprise Edition turns shared caching across clients into a distributed caching solution. Multiple clients can form a cache group and share data blocks through consistent hashing. When a node fails, the system automatically removes it from the group. Cache misses fall back to object storage, so read operations can continue without interruption. Application clients can also be configured to use cache without serving cached data to other clients. This allows a dedicated cache cluster , made up of stable nodes, to serve frequently accessed training data. The read path is hierarchical. Data retrieved from a cache group is also retained in the local cache of the requesting client, so subsequent accesses do not need to traverse the network again. Enterprise Edition also provides a comprehensive set of tools for cache group operations and efficiency: Data warm-up to load data into the cache before workloads need it. Cache group backup to improve cache hit rates while group membership changes. Scale-out protection to let new nodes retrieve data from existing nodes on a cache miss, reducing requests to object storage. No-backfill-on-miss to protect hot data from being displaced by less frequently accessed data. Cache block compaction to reduce the number of files on large cache disks. Range-based warm-up to warm up specific byte ranges within files. The transport layer has also evolved through the introduction of the custom IORPC protocol in v5.2 and RDMA support starting with v5.3. The following benchmarks illustrate the performance improvements: v5.2: With 100 nodes equipped with 100 Gbps network interfaces, aggregate read bandwidth reached 1.2 TB/s. v5.3: With 160 Gbps network interfaces and 1 MB random reads, CPU utilization dropped to approximately one-third of that of the TCP-based approach. v5.4: In an environment with 400 Gbps client nodes and 800 Gbps cache nodes, a single client achieved 45 GB/s of read bandwidth, while a single cache node achieved 90 GB/s. Network interface utilization exceeded 90%, and random-read IOPS under high concurrency more than doubled. Cross-region mirroring and on-demand synchronization To bring data closer to compute resources, Enterprise Edition provides mirror file systems . A metadata replica is deployed in the mirror region and kept in sync with the source. Clients prioritize reads from local object storage. Writes follow a read/write separation model: write operations are committed to the source cluster to maintain consistency across regions. Starting with v5.3, read requests can fall back to the source cluster when the mirror is unavailable. In v5.4, mirroring gained on-demand data synchronization. Only metadata is continuously synchronized. Object data is fetched on demand when first accessed and then cached locally. This avoids synchronizing an entire dataset when only a small portion is needed. If the goal is to accelerate metadata reads alone, read-only metadata nodes can be deployed directly. Elastic capacity and onboarding existing data Object storage provides the underlying capacity. Storage can scale up or down on demand, and a single file system can manage multiple buckets across regions and providers while providing caching for all of them. Existing data in object storage can be onboarded transparently through the import feature. The process creates metadata entries without copying the underlying data. Starting with v5.2, data can be imported on demand when first accessed. Starting with v5.3, all imported objects can benefit from cache acceleration. Hot data is served by caches and mirrors, while cold data remains in object storage. This means that exabyte-scale capacity no longer needs to be provisioned based on peak demand. Clients and control plane: isolation, observability, and operations at a million connections Control plane challenges at the million-client scale Hundreds of thousands of clients connect through Kubernetes and CSI, the S3 Gateway, SDKs, and other interfaces. The number of active connections can reach one million. At this scale, any client could overwhelm a shared metadata cluster. Each client also generates hundreds of metrics, making direct collection impractical due to time-series cardinality. Multi-tenant environments require clear access controls and resource budgets. Upgrades must also minimize disruption to training workloads. Connection reuse: supporting a million clients In v5.4, Enterprise Edition expanded client connectivity to the million-client scale by introducing a network proxy layer. The proxy can be deployed together with metadata nodes or separately . Clients can connect to any metadata node. Requests for the local zone are handled directly, while cross-zone requests are forwarded internally. Multiple client sessions share physical connections between nodes. In stress tests, 10 internal proxy nodes handled one million client connections while requiring only about 400 physical backend connections to metadata service nodes. Session management was also optimized. The system uses index-based lookups instead of full scans, while paginated queries and sampled reporting keep the amount of session state under control. Expired sessions are cleaned up in batches. Multi-tenant isolation, observability, and operations In multi-tenant environments, Enterprise Edition uses access tokens to define client access boundaries. These controls include allowed IP ranges, read/write permissions, accessible subdirectories, and whether a client can participate in background tasks. In v5.4, Enterprise Edition extended the existing single-subdirectory restriction with a whitelist mechanism. This allows multiple top-level subdirectories to be configured for a client. Resource controls cover different types of traffic, including uploads, downloads, deletions, and background tasks. The system also supports session-level CPU quotas to prevent a single tenant from continuously consuming resources needed by the shared cluster. In v5.2, global rate-limit messages were consolidated to reduce the overhead of synchronizing rate-limit state. The client access layer supports multiple interfaces and client types, including POSIX through FUSE and CSI, the S3 Gateway, the Hadoop SDK, the Python SDK, and Windows clients. This flexibility accommodates different training and data-processing workflows. For observability, the console integrates Prometheus and Grafana. It provides metrics for file systems, client sessions, and cluster health, and can also integrate with existing monitoring and alerting systems. For daily operations, Enterprise Edition has supported centralized client upgrades and diagnostic information collection through the console since v5.2. The metadata service also supports rolling upgrades without service interruption. Conclusion From v5.2 to v5.4, the evolution of JuiceFS Enterprise Edition for large-scale environments has not been about adding isolated features. Instead, the goal has been to make the metadata engine, data lifecycle, data path, and client and control planes all scale together. Metadata: An in-memory engine, multi-zone architecture, and automatic balancing extend single-node capabilities to hundreds of billions of files and beyond. Data lifecycle: The trash, background tasks, auditing, and backups are integrated into a unified framework. Data path: Distributed caching, RDMA, mirroring, and data import bring hot data closer to compute resources while preserving the capacity elasticity of object storage. Clients and control plane: Connection reuse, access controls, rate limiting, and centralized observability support hundreds of thousands to millions of connections. These capabilities address common challenges that emerge as infrastructure scales. The goal is to let the file system handle more of the foundational work itself, reducing the need for platform teams to build and maintain additional systems around it. JuiceFS Enterprise Edition is already running in production environments at the exabyte scale, and its architecture continues to evolve. We hope these design choices offer useful insights to teams planning their AI data infrastructure. If you have any feedback on this article or ideas to share, we invite you to participate in the discussions on GitHub and join our community on Discord .

JuiceFS Enterprise Edition uses several techniques to reduce memory consumption, including memory pools, manual memory management, serialization and compression of idle directories, and compact representations of small files. These optimizations have reduced average memory usage per file from nearly 600 bytes to approximately 100 bytes—about 27% of that of an HDFS NameNode and 3.7% of that of a CephFS MDS.

System Memory per file Reference HDFS NameNode ~370 B Third-party technical blog CephFS MDS ~2,700 B Ceph cluster monitoring (32 GB RAM / 12 million files) Alluxio (heap memory mode) ~2,100 B Alluxio documentation (64 GB RAM / ~30 million files) JuiceFS Community Edition ~430 B Community Edition documentation JuiceFS Enterprise Edition ~100 B Production cluster monitoring (30 GB RAM / 300 million files)

Higher memory efficiency allows the same hardware to manage more files. In other words, it significantly reduces the metadata infrastructure costs of managing hundreds of billions of files.

Building on the capabilities of a single process, Enterprise Edition uses multiple metadata zones to scale horizontally. Each zone manages part of the file tree, while clients combine the zones into a single namespace.

The design keeps subtrees complete whenever possible, so most operations stay within a single zone and require fewer distributed transactions. Cross-zone migration uses links and references, remaining transparent to POSIX paths. Extremely large directories can also be split into multiple virtual subdirectories, allowing finer-grained migration and preventing a single large directory from remaining a long-term burden on one zone.

The high-order bits of each inode encode its zone information. Clients automatically discover the zone topology and connect to all zones. Adding a zone therefore requires no changes to application access patterns.

For reliability, each zone consists of three instances: a service instance, a hot standby instance, and a cold standby instance. The service and hot standby instances use different memory compression strategies. Snapshots and change logs are continuously persisted to disk and can also be backed up to a remote location (see the Trash, background tasks, and audit backups section).

Version evolution and scale validation

Starting with v5.2, Enterprise Edition focused on improving multi-zone stability and reducing metadata memory consumption, bringing file management into the hundreds-of-billions range. In production, a single cluster now manages more than 50 billion files while keeping metadata access latency at the millisecond level.

In v5.3, the maximum number of zones increased to 1,024, allowing a single file system to support more than 500 billion files. The release also introduced automatic hotspot migration and supporting operations tools. Frequently accessed directories can be split into smaller units and migrated concurrently to distribute hotspots more quickly. Periodic self-checks detect and repair intermediate states that may remain after cross-zone migrations.

In v5.4, the focus expanded from file count to client scale. Metadata nodes and network proxies can now be deployed together, and clients can connect to any node. Requests for other zones are forwarded internally by the cluster. Combined with connection reuse, this architecture supports up to a million client connections. In the last section, we’ll cover this design in more detail.

Data lifecycle management: built-in deletion, recovery, and auditing Data lifecycle challenges when deleting petabytes of data

Deleting petabytes of data requires more than reclaiming storage space promptly. The system must also support recovery from accidental deletion, deletion traceability, and audits for orphaned objects.

Object storage can accumulate billions of objects awaiting reclamation. An accidental deletion can disrupt training jobs, while leftover objects must be continuously detected and accounted for.

Trash, background tasks, and audit backups

The trash is enabled by default in Enterprise Edition. Deleted files first move to the trash, where the retention period is configurable (typically seven days). During this period, users can restore files through the console or a restore command. Restoration only updates metadata; it does not copy the underlying data.

Starting with v5.3, the trash in multi-zone environments records each file's original path to ensure that files are restored to the correct location. In v5.4, users can filter deleted files by time range and keywords. This makes it easier to find accidentally deleted files among large volumes of deletions.

Storage reclamation is handled by a unified background tasks framework. Tasks such as chunk compaction, trash cleanup, and cross-cloud replication are scheduled by the metadata service and executed concurrently across clients throughout the cluster.

This approach offers three main benefits:

  • Scalable deletion: Deletion capacity scales with the number of clients. To speed up reclamation, simply add more mount points.
  • Controllable execution: Deletion traffic can be limited by access token. Background tasks can be disabled for specific clients, while the metadata service centrally configures the execution windows for chunk compaction.
  • Observable progress: Both chunk compaction and deletion tasks expose monitoring metrics.

Auditing and disaster recovery are also built into the system. Change logs record every deletion operation and the session that initiated it. Combined with audit logs, they help answer the questions: who deleted what, and when?

The console provides centralized configuration for metadata snapshots and change logs. By default, backups are sent to remote object storage every hour. Local backups are retained for two days, and a retention period of at least 30 days is recommended.

On the object storage side, garbage collection and consistency-checking tools audit orphaned objects. In v5.4, both tools gained an external sorting mode that uses disk space instead of memory for sorting. This keeps memory consumption manageable when checking hundreds of millions of files. External sorting is intended for inspection and assessment only; it does not delete any objects.

Data insights and dataset branching

Deletion decisions require reliable data. The console's monitoring dashboard provides metrics such as the number of files in the trash, pending object chunks for deletion, and fragmented chunks. File searches filter results on the metadata side, supporting hot/cold data analysis and data aging assessments. Directory, user, and group quotas help enforce storage budgets across workloads.

For dataset preparation, v5.4 supports cross-zone directory cloning. Cloning a directory containing 100 million files takes approximately 1 minute and 40 seconds, or about 1 million files per second.

Data path: balancing performance and cost with caching and mirroring Accessing EB-scale data: throughput, storage costs, and cross-cloud access

Training workloads require throughput at the terabyte-per-second level. Dataset loading involves large volumes of random reads, while training checkpoint writes involve sequential writes of large files. These workloads have different IOPS and write-throughput requirements.

At the same time, storing all EB-scale data in a hot storage tier is not possible. Compute resources deployed across multiple clouds also need to access data from nearby locations whenever possible.

Therefore, read performance, storage costs, and data locality must be addressed together.

Multi-level caching and distributed cache groups

Enterprise Edition turns shared caching across clients into a distributed caching solution. Multiple clients can form a cache group and share data blocks through consistent hashing. When a node fails, the system automatically removes it from the group. Cache misses fall back to object storage, so read operations can continue without interruption.

Application clients can also be configured to use cache without serving cached data to other clients. This allows a dedicated cache cluster, made up of stable nodes, to serve frequently accessed training data.

The read path is hierarchical. Data retrieved from a cache group is also retained in the local cache of the requesting client, so subsequent accesses do not need to traverse the network again.

Enterprise Edition also provides a comprehensive set of tools for cache group operations and efficiency:

  • Data warm-up to load data into the cache before workloads need it.
  • Cache group backup to improve cache hit rates while group membership changes.
  • Scale-out protection to let new nodes retrieve data from existing nodes on a cache miss, reducing requests to object storage.
  • No-backfill-on-miss to protect hot data from being displaced by less frequently accessed data.
  • Cache block compaction to reduce the number of files on large cache disks.
  • Range-based warm-up to warm up specific byte ranges within files.

The transport layer has also evolved through the introduction of the custom IORPC protocol in v5.2 and RDMA support starting with v5.3.

The following benchmarks illustrate the performance improvements:

  • v5.2: With 100 nodes equipped with 100 Gbps network interfaces, aggregate read bandwidth reached 1.2 TB/s.
  • v5.3: With 160 Gbps network interfaces and 1 MB random reads, CPU utilization dropped to approximately one-third of that of the TCP-based approach.
  • v5.4: In an environment with 400 Gbps client nodes and 800 Gbps cache nodes, a single client achieved 45 GB/s of read bandwidth, while a single cache node achieved 90 GB/s. Network interface utilization exceeded 90%, and random-read IOPS under high concurrency more than doubled.

Cross-region mirroring and on-demand synchronization

To bring data closer to compute resources, Enterprise Edition provides mirror file systems. A metadata replica is deployed in the mirror region and kept in sync with the source. Clients prioritize reads from local object storage. Writes follow a read/write separation model: write operations are committed to the source cluster to maintain consistency across regions.

Starting with v5.3, read requests can fall back to the source cluster when the mirror is unavailable. In v5.4, mirroring gained on-demand data synchronization. Only metadata is continuously synchronized. Object data is fetched on demand when first accessed and then cached locally. This avoids synchronizing an entire dataset when only a small portion is needed.

If the goal is to accelerate metadata reads alone, read-only metadata nodes can be deployed directly.

Elastic capacity and onboarding existing data

Object storage provides the underlying capacity. Storage can scale up or down on demand, and a single file system can manage multiple buckets across regions and providers while providing caching for all of them.

Existing data in object storage can be onboarded transparently through the import feature. The process creates metadata entries without copying the underlying data. Starting with v5.2, data can be imported on demand when first accessed. Starting with v5.3, all imported objects can benefit from cache acceleration. Hot data is served by caches and mirrors, while cold data remains in object storage. This means that exabyte-scale capacity no longer needs to be provisioned based on peak demand.

Clients and control plane: isolation, observability, and operations at a million connections Control plane challenges at the million-client scale

Hundreds of thousands of clients connect through Kubernetes and CSI, the S3 Gateway, SDKs, and other interfaces. The number of active connections can reach one million.

At this scale, any client could overwhelm a shared metadata cluster. Each client also generates hundreds of metrics, making direct collection impractical due to time-series cardinality. Multi-tenant environments require clear access controls and resource budgets. Upgrades must also minimize disruption to training workloads.

Connection reuse: supporting a million clients

In v5.4, Enterprise Edition expanded client connectivity to the million-client scale by introducing a network proxy layer. The proxy can be deployed together with metadata nodes or separately.

Clients can connect to any metadata node. Requests for the local zone are handled directly, while cross-zone requests are forwarded internally. Multiple client sessions share physical connections between nodes.

In stress tests, 10 internal proxy nodes handled one million client connections while requiring only about 400 physical backend connections to metadata service nodes.

Session management was also optimized. The system uses index-based lookups instead of full scans, while paginated queries and sampled reporting keep the amount of session state under control. Expired sessions are cleaned up in batches.

Multi-tenant isolation, observability, and operations

In multi-tenant environments, Enterprise Edition uses access tokens to define client access boundaries. These controls include allowed IP ranges, read/write permissions, accessible subdirectories, and whether a client can participate in background tasks.

In v5.4, Enterprise Edition extended the existing single-subdirectory restriction with a whitelist mechanism. This allows multiple top-level subdirectories to be configured for a client.

Resource controls cover different types of traffic, including uploads, downloads, deletions, and background tasks. The system also supports session-level CPU quotas to prevent a single tenant from continuously consuming resources needed by the shared cluster. In v5.2, global rate-limit messages were consolidated to reduce the overhead of synchronizing rate-limit state.

The client access layer supports multiple interfaces and client types, including POSIX through FUSE and CSI, the S3 Gateway, the Hadoop SDK, the Python SDK, and Windows clients. This flexibility accommodates different training and data-processing workflows.

For observability, the console integrates Prometheus and Grafana. It provides metrics for file systems, client sessions, and cluster health, and can also integrate with existing monitoring and alerting systems.

For daily operations, Enterprise Edition has supported centralized client upgrades and diagnostic information collection through the console since v5.2. The metadata service also supports rolling upgrades without service interruption.

Conclusion

From v5.2 to v5.4, the evolution of JuiceFS Enterprise Edition for large-scale environments has not been about adding isolated features. Instead, the goal has been to make the metadata engine, data lifecycle, data path, and client and control planes all scale together.

  • Metadata: An in-memory engine, multi-zone architecture, and automatic balancing extend single-node capabilities to hundreds of billions of files and beyond.
  • Data lifecycle: The trash, background tasks, auditing, and backups are integrated into a unified framework.
  • Data path: Distributed caching, RDMA, mirroring, and data import bring hot data closer to compute resources while preserving the capacity elasticity of object storage.
  • Clients and control plane: Connection reuse, access controls, rate limiting, and centralized observability support hundreds of thousands to millions of connections.

These capabilities address common challenges that emerge as infrastructure scales. The goal is to let the file system handle more of the foundational work itself, reducing the need for platform teams to build and maintain additional systems around it.

JuiceFS Enterprise Edition is already running in production environments at the exabyte scale, and its architecture continues to evolve. We hope these design choices offer useful insights to teams planning their AI data infrastructure.

If you have any feedback on this article or ideas to share, we invite you to participate in the discussions on GitHub and join our community on Discord.
