items.title: How UV-C LED Water Disinfection Works – Water Treatment Engineers' Guide
items.summary: By yoyo-uv — drafted with AI assistance and edited by people Abstract With advancements in UV-C LED technology, new possibilities arise for compact and energy-efficient water disinfection systems. While traditional water disinfection systems are based on mercury-filled UV lamps, UV-C LEDs are semiconductor-based technologies that create germicidal UV light. However, a successful water disinfection process depends on more aspects than simply choosing a proper wavelength. Such factors as water quality, UV dose, reactor design, flow rate, and system validation all play a role in inactivating pathogens. In this article, we discuss how UV-C LED water disinfection works, key engineering aspects, and potential applications in modern water treatment systems. 1. Principles of UV-C LED Water Disinfection UV disinfection is a physical water treatment method that uses UV radiation to inactivate harmful microorganisms in water. The range of UV-C waves is from about 200 to 280 nm. Most of the UV-C LED water treatment applications utilize wavelengths from 265 to 280 nm. Upon exposure to the proper UV dose, ultraviolet radiation destroys microorganisms' genetic material, interfering with its reproduction. Thus, bacteria, viruses, and some protozoans can be effectively inactivated with UV-C rays, if sufficient amount of UV radiation is provided. As opposed to chemical water disinfection, there is no need to add any disinfectant to the water during UV treatment. However, there will be no disinfectant residue after the process. According to US Environmental Protection Agency, UV disinfection performance depends on such factors as microorganism, UV dose, water quality, and many other. US EPA 2. How Does a UV-C LED Water Treatment System Work? Typical UV-C LED disinfection system consists of the following components: UV-C LED light sources The chamber for water treatment LED driver and power source Components for thermal management Inlet and outlet for water Additional sensors and electronics for monitoring (optional) During the operation of such systems, the water flows through a chamber which is illuminated by UV-C LEDs. Microorganisms get exposed to UV while flowing through the reactor. The efficiency of the process depends on the amount of UV fluence that microorganisms get in the reactor while passing through it. Fluence is usually measured in millijoules per square centimeters (mJ/cm²). Although under simplified assumptions fluence could be calculated as irradiance multiplied by the exposure time, it does not mean that the calculation is straightforward for the reactor. Thus, the engineer cannot use only electrical power of LEDs. 3. Why Are UV-C LEDs Attractive for Water Treatment? There are several design features of UV-C LEDs which can make them attractive for water treatment applications. Small Size and Integration Opportunities UV-C LEDs are semiconductor devices which can be arranged in different ways. Because of their small size, they can be used for compact treatment chambers, point-of-use water purifiers and water treatment equipment. Rapid Switching UV-C LEDs can quickly turn on and off without any warm-up process which is necessary in some types of UV lamps. It makes them attractive for use in intermittent water consumption situations. For example, the system can turn on UV irradiation as soon as water flow is detected. No Mercury UV-C LEDs do not need mercury as light-emitting substance. Flexibility of System Design Engineers have an opportunity to choose arrangement of LEDs, optical scheme, power and other parameters according to their needs. However, there is no guarantee that UV-C LED-based systems are more energy efficient than conventional UV lamps. Performance, efficiency and even cost depend on specific LED, reactor and conditions of its operation. Duty cycle plays a major role in efficiency. Comparison of efficiency of UV-C LEDs and conventional lamps for the inactivation of microorganisms showed importance of evaluation of both microbial inactivation and electrical energy consumption. PubMed Central (PMC) 4. What Determines Disinfection Efficiency? Choosing the right UV-C LED module is not the only thing to think about when creating a good water disinfection system. There are a number of parameters which have to be taken into account. UV wavelength: Various microorganisms react to various wavelengths of UV light. The best choice of wavelength will depend on target microorganisms and the efficiency of the process. Flow rate: Increased flow rates usually decrease the exposure time unless reactor design or increased UV output compensate for this increase. UV transmittance: Various dissolved materials can absorb ultraviolet light and decrease its intensity. Turbidity: Suspended particles can protect microorganisms from UV exposure. Reactor design: The design of the reactor (LED placement, reactor size and flow pattern) can affect the distribution of UV light. Heat management: LED temperature will affect its performance and efficiency. This is why good heat dissipation is crucial. Research on flow-through reactors using UV-C LED light for disinfection shows that irradiance distribution and flow rate can significantly affect microbial inactivation. National Taipei University of Technology 5. How Can UV-C LED Water Disinfection be Used? UV-C LED technology is especially useful for equipment which is supposed to be compact or work intermittently. Examples of potential uses are residential point-of-use water filters, water dispensers, recreational vehicles, marine water systems, laboratory devices, or OEM water treatment products. Integration requirements may include reactor size, electric power input, water flow rate capability, and installation area. Firms that create small treatment equipment may find it beneficial to consider different configurations of UV-C LED reactors. One such example is YoYo UV's range of water treatment products . The claimed flow rate or microbial reduction capabilities of any manufacturer will need to be analyzed according to specific operational parameters and validation data. 6. Significant Limitations That Engineers Need To Be Aware Of UV-C LED disinfection cannot replace all water treatment processes. Germicidal conventional UV water disinfection does not reduce sediment, heavy metal, dissolved salt, or most other chemical contamination. If the source water is contaminated by any of these components, other treatment systems may be needed. In some cases, pre-filtration is required to enhance the clarity of water before UV exposure. Moreover, UV disinfection does not retain a residual disinfection capacity downstream in the distribution pipes and tanks. In drinking water applications, system engineers need to take into account potential contamination post-treatment. The CDC stresses that UV treatment systems are designed for microbial control, not for chemical contaminant reduction. 7. Future Perspectives in UV-C LED Disinfection for Water Treatment UV-C LED technology allows one to develop compact flexible water disinfection devices. Further advancements in semiconductors, optics, thermal design, and reactor performance validation may open new possibilities. However, a systems engineering approach is still crucial for its successful application. Water treatment professionals should assess microbial performance, UV dosing, energy requirements, operation parameters, and regulatory compliance before adopting a technology. UV-C LEDs are innovative components of modern water treatment systems but their disinfection performance depends on engineering and validation. Discussion for Water Treatment Engineers What is the biggest challenge in developing reliable UV-C LED water disinfection systems today? Energy efficiency UV reactor design UV dose validation System cost We welcome insights and experiences from water treatment engineers, researchers, and OEM equipment manufacturers.
items.summary_html:
• By yoyo-uv — drafted with AI assistance and edited by people
Abstract

With advancements in UV-C LED technology, new possibilities arise for compact and energy-efficient water disinfection systems. While traditional water disinfection systems are based on mercury-filled UV lamps, UV-C LEDs are semiconductor-based technologies that create germicidal UV light.

However, a successful water disinfection process depends on more aspects than simply choosing a proper wavelength. Such factors as water quality, UV dose, reactor design, flow rate, and system validation all play a role in inactivating pathogens.

In this article, we discuss how UV-C LED water disinfection works, key engineering aspects, and potential applications in modern water treatment systems.

1. Principles of UV-C LED Water Disinfection

UV disinfection is a physical water treatment method that uses UV radiation to inactivate harmful microorganisms in water.

The range of UV-C waves is from about 200 to 280 nm. Most of the UV-C LED water treatment applications utilize wavelengths from 265 to 280 nm.

Upon exposure to the proper UV dose, ultraviolet radiation destroys microorganisms' genetic material, interfering with its reproduction.

Thus, bacteria, viruses, and some protozoans can be effectively inactivated with UV-C rays, if sufficient amount of UV radiation is provided.

As opposed to chemical water disinfection, there is no need to add any disinfectant to the water during UV treatment. However, there will be no disinfectant residue after the process.

According to US Environmental Protection Agency, UV disinfection performance depends on such factors as microorganism, UV dose, water quality, and many other. US EPA

2. How Does a UV-C LED Water Treatment System Work?

Typical UV-C LED disinfection system consists of the following components:

  • UV-C LED light sources
  • The chamber for water treatment
  • LED driver and power source
  • Components for thermal management
  • Inlet and outlet for water
  • Additional sensors and electronics for monitoring (optional)

During the operation of such systems, the water flows through a chamber which is illuminated by UV-C LEDs.

Microorganisms get exposed to UV while flowing through the reactor.

The efficiency of the process depends on the amount of UV fluence that microorganisms get in the reactor while passing through it.

Fluence is usually measured in millijoules per square centimeters (mJ/cm²).

Although under simplified assumptions fluence could be calculated as irradiance multiplied by the exposure time, it does not mean that the calculation is straightforward for the reactor.

Thus, the engineer cannot use only electrical power of LEDs.

3. Why Are UV-C LEDs Attractive for Water Treatment?

There are several design features of UV-C LEDs which can make them attractive for water treatment applications.

Small Size and Integration Opportunities

UV-C LEDs are semiconductor devices which can be arranged in different ways.

Because of their small size, they can be used for compact treatment chambers, point-of-use water purifiers and water treatment equipment.

Rapid Switching

UV-C LEDs can quickly turn on and off without any warm-up process which is necessary in some types of UV lamps.

It makes them attractive for use in intermittent water consumption situations.

For example, the system can turn on UV irradiation as soon as water flow is detected.

No Mercury

UV-C LEDs do not need mercury as light-emitting substance.

Flexibility of System Design

Engineers have an opportunity to choose arrangement of LEDs, optical scheme, power and other parameters according to their needs.

However, there is no guarantee that UV-C LED-based systems are more energy efficient than conventional UV lamps.

Performance, efficiency and even cost depend on specific LED, reactor and conditions of its operation.

Duty cycle plays a major role in efficiency.

Comparison of efficiency of UV-C LEDs and conventional lamps for the inactivation of microorganisms showed importance of evaluation of both microbial inactivation and electrical energy consumption. PubMed Central (PMC)

4. What Determines Disinfection Efficiency?

Choosing the right UV-C LED module is not the only thing to think about when creating a good water disinfection system.

There are a number of parameters which have to be taken into account.

  • UV wavelength: Various microorganisms react to various wavelengths of UV light. The best choice of wavelength will depend on target microorganisms and the efficiency of the process.
  • Flow rate: Increased flow rates usually decrease the exposure time unless reactor design or increased UV output compensate for this increase.
  • UV transmittance: Various dissolved materials can absorb ultraviolet light and decrease its intensity.
  • Turbidity: Suspended particles can protect microorganisms from UV exposure.
  • Reactor design: The design of the reactor (LED placement, reactor size and flow pattern) can affect the distribution of UV light.
  • Heat management: LED temperature will affect its performance and efficiency. This is why good heat dissipation is crucial.

Research on flow-through reactors using UV-C LED light for disinfection shows that irradiance distribution and flow rate can significantly affect microbial inactivation. National Taipei University of Technology

5. How Can UV-C LED Water Disinfection be Used?

UV-C LED technology is especially useful for equipment which is supposed to be compact or work intermittently.

Examples of potential uses are residential point-of-use water filters, water dispensers, recreational vehicles, marine water systems, laboratory devices, or OEM water treatment products.

Integration requirements may include reactor size, electric power input, water flow rate capability, and installation area.

Firms that create small treatment equipment may find it beneficial to consider different configurations of UV-C LED reactors.

One such example is YoYo UV's range of water treatment products.

The claimed flow rate or microbial reduction capabilities of any manufacturer will need to be analyzed according to specific operational parameters and validation data.

6. Significant Limitations That Engineers Need To Be Aware Of

UV-C LED disinfection cannot replace all water treatment processes.

Germicidal conventional UV water disinfection does not reduce sediment, heavy metal, dissolved salt, or most other chemical contamination.

If the source water is contaminated by any of these components, other treatment systems may be needed.

In some cases, pre-filtration is required to enhance the clarity of water before UV exposure.

Moreover, UV disinfection does not retain a residual disinfection capacity downstream in the distribution pipes and tanks.

In drinking water applications, system engineers need to take into account potential contamination post-treatment.

The CDC stresses that UV treatment systems are designed for microbial control, not for chemical contaminant reduction.

7. Future Perspectives in UV-C LED Disinfection for Water Treatment

UV-C LED technology allows one to develop compact flexible water disinfection devices.

Further advancements in semiconductors, optics, thermal design, and reactor performance validation may open new possibilities.

However, a systems engineering approach is still crucial for its successful application.

Water treatment professionals should assess microbial performance, UV dosing, energy requirements, operation parameters, and regulatory compliance before adopting a technology.

UV-C LEDs are innovative components of modern water treatment systems but their disinfection performance depends on engineering and validation.

Discussion for Water Treatment Engineers

What is the biggest challenge in developing reliable UV-C LED water disinfection systems today?

  • Energy efficiency
  • UV reactor design
  • UV dose validation
  • System cost

We welcome insights and experiences from water treatment engineers, researchers, and OEM equipment manufacturers.

items.title: From Footprints to Massing: Engineering a Citywide 3D Model of New York
items.summary: My first attempt at extruding a city took an afternoon. Building polygons in, heights in, solids out, and it looked fine in the viewer. Then I tried to use it. The heights had three different sources, the ground was flat, and a bridge had been rendered as an office tower. New York's citywide massing model, built for the Department of Information Technology and Telecommunications with AppGeo, is a useful reference for the gap between that first demo and a dataset someone can actually work with. The inputs, and what they really contain Building footprints come from planimetric mapping: closed polygons with a source date and an identifier. Heights usually arrive in a separate table or raster, joined by an ID that may or may not be stable. Terrain comes from a digital elevation model. In New York, the horizontal units are US survey feet in the state plane coordinate system, and vertical units are feet as well, which is convenient until someone hands you a file in meters. Extrusion and its assumptions The operation is simple. Take the polygon, sample the ground elevation, lift the top by the height value, and close the sides. Then decide what height means. Above ground? Above sea level? Roof line or top of the mechanical penthouse? For massing, roof height is the usual answer, but the choice needs to be written down, because two datasets that disagree by ten feet will produce different shadows at 5 p.m. in December. Height is not one number Some heights come from a surface model, which includes parapets, bulkheads, and sometimes antennas. Some come from an attribute that reflects the roof deck. A single tower can have three plausible heights and no obvious way to pick one. My rule is to document the source per building where possible, and to treat the resulting error as a range, not a fact. At low sun angles, a height error of a few feet moves a shadow by many feet. Tiling a million buildings One citywide mesh is unusable, both for file size and for rendering. Tile the model on a grid, keep a stable ID for every footprint, and build lower levels of detail for distant tiles. Formats matter: 3D Tiles or glTF for streaming viewers, a spatial database for analysis, and a simplified solid for shadow runs. The same building should carry the same ID in all of them, or every downstream join becomes a guess. Shadows at city scale Shadow is where the model earns its keep. Pick a date, a time step, and a sun vector, then intersect each building with the ground and with its neighbors. Terrain matters more than people expect near slopes and waterfronts. Compute on the GPU when you can, cache the results for common dates, and publish the method alongside the output, because a shadow map without a stated time and datum is not evidence. Keys, joins, and silent failures Most errors in a model this size are join errors. A footprint without a height becomes a zero-height building that still renders as a flat plate. A duplicate ID attaches a tower's height to a shed. A demolished building keeps its geometry for a year. None of these throw an exception. They just make the result wrong in a way that looks normal, which is the worst kind of wrong. Filling one missing parcel Proposed buildings are not in the footprint file yet, which is a problem when the question is about a project that has not been built. I sketched the site boundary and asked GenAnywhere for a rough volume at the district's allowed height. It returned a clean box, which I kept in a separate layer. Generated massing is fine for a screening question. It should never be mistaken for a survey of what will stand there. QA rules that catch the weird ones A few automated checks catch most of the damage: heights outside a plausible range for the borough, footprint area against height, buildings that intersect terrain, duplicate identifiers, and anything taller than the tallest recorded tower. Then sample a few blocks on foot. The automated checks find the absurd; the walk finds the merely wrong. What I would change next time I would store height provenance per building from day one, publish a confidence flag with the geometry, version the height table separately from the footprints, and keep a change log that names what moved and when. Those are boring features, and they are the difference between a model that gets trusted and one that gets screenshotted.
items.summary_html:
My first attempt at extruding a city took an afternoon. Building polygons in, heights in, solids out, and it looked fine in the viewer. Then I tried to use it. The heights had three different sources, the ground was flat, and a bridge had been rendered as an office tower. New York's citywide massing model, built for the Department of Information Technology and Telecommunications with AppGeo, is a useful reference for the gap between that first demo and a dataset someone can actually work with.

The inputs, and what they really contain

Building footprints come from planimetric mapping: closed polygons with a source date and an identifier. Heights usually arrive in a separate table or raster, joined by an ID that may or may not be stable. Terrain comes from a digital elevation model. In New York, the horizontal units are US survey feet in the state plane coordinate system, and vertical units are feet as well, which is convenient until someone hands you a file in meters.

Extrusion and its assumptions

The operation is simple. Take the polygon, sample the ground elevation, lift the top by the height value, and close the sides. Then decide what height means. Above ground? Above sea level? Roof line or top of the mechanical penthouse? For massing, roof height is the usual answer, but the choice needs to be written down, because two datasets that disagree by ten feet will produce different shadows at 5 p.m. in December.

Height is not one number

Some heights come from a surface model, which includes parapets, bulkheads, and sometimes antennas. Some come from an attribute that reflects the roof deck. A single tower can have three plausible heights and no obvious way to pick one. My rule is to document the source per building where possible, and to treat the resulting error as a range, not a fact. At low sun angles, a height error of a few feet moves a shadow by many feet.

Tiling a million buildings

One citywide mesh is unusable, both for file size and for rendering. Tile the model on a grid, keep a stable ID for every footprint, and build lower levels of detail for distant tiles. Formats matter: 3D Tiles or glTF for streaming viewers, a spatial database for analysis, and a simplified solid for shadow runs. The same building should carry the same ID in all of them, or every downstream join becomes a guess.

Shadows at city scale

Shadow is where the model earns its keep. Pick a date, a time step, and a sun vector, then intersect each building with the ground and with its neighbors. Terrain matters more than people expect near slopes and waterfronts. Compute on the GPU when you can, cache the results for common dates, and publish the method alongside the output, because a shadow map without a stated time and datum is not evidence.

Keys, joins, and silent failures

Most errors in a model this size are join errors. A footprint without a height becomes a zero-height building that still renders as a flat plate. A duplicate ID attaches a tower's height to a shed. A demolished building keeps its geometry for a year. None of these throw an exception. They just make the result wrong in a way that looks normal, which is the worst kind of wrong.

Filling one missing parcel

Proposed buildings are not in the footprint file yet, which is a problem when the question is about a project that has not been built. I sketched the site boundary and asked GenAnywhere for a rough volume at the district's allowed height. It returned a clean box, which I kept in a separate layer. Generated massing is fine for a screening question. It should never be mistaken for a survey of what will stand there.

QA rules that catch the weird ones

A few automated checks catch most of the damage: heights outside a plausible range for the borough, footprint area against height, buildings that intersect terrain, duplicate identifiers, and anything taller than the tallest recorded tower. Then sample a few blocks on foot. The automated checks find the absurd; the walk finds the merely wrong.

What I would change next time

I would store height provenance per building from day one, publish a confidence flag with the geometry, version the height table separately from the footprints, and keep a change log that names what moved and when. Those are boring features, and they are the difference between a model that gets trusted and one that gets screenshotted.

items.title: Packet Notes #3: Your phone has outbound AI traffic now. Nobody shows you it.
items.summary: I spend my working hours in firewall logs. Policies, sessions, denies, the usual. Then one evening I pointed the same habit at the device I actually carry, and the thing that stood out was not ads or analytics. It was AI. Not "an app has an AI feature". Actual bytes, leaving the phone, going to the endpoints of AI companies. The permission model never covered this Android's permission screen answers questions like: can this app read the camera, the mic, the contacts, the location. Good questions. They just stop short. There is no permission for "this app sends the text you typed to a model hosted somewhere else". The INTERNET permission is granted at install time with no prompt, and once an app has it, where it connects is its own business. The permission screen is a list of maybes. It is not a log. So the honest answer to "which of my apps talk to AI providers" is: on a stock phone, you cannot tell. Not because it is hidden maliciously, but because nothing in the stack was built to answer that question for the user. Why this is different from the tracker problem We have had a decade of practice with trackers. Block a domain list, done. The threat model was mostly "someone is building a profile of me". AI traffic is a different shape: The payload is usually content, not identifiers. Your draft, your photo, your question, the document you opened. It is often invisible in the UI. An assistant feature can be two taps deep in a menu you never open, and still phone home. The destination is a small number of very large endpoints, which makes it easy to see once you look, and easy to miss if you never do. A tracker wants to know who you are. An AI backend wants what you wrote. For a lot of people, the second one matters more. What I did about it I built a firewall that runs on the phone itself. No root, no account, nothing leaves the device. One screen, AI Radar, does only this: it names the apps that are sending data to AI companies, with the byte counts. A second screen, ExfilMeter, does the same for outbound traffic in general. The first time I opened it on my own phone, two apps were on that list that I had not thought about that day at all. I am not going to tell you that is a scandal. It might be completely legitimate. The point is narrower and, I think, harder to argue with: you should be able to see it, and right now the platform does not let you. Three things you can check without installing anything Settings, then your data usage per app, over the last week. Sort by background usage. Anything on that list you do not actively use is worth a question. Open the apps you use most and look for an assistant, summarise, or smart reply feature. If it exists and it is not labelled on-device, it is network traffic. Check the app's data safety section on Google Play for sharing with third parties under "app functionality". That category covers a lot. None of that gives you a log. It gives you a shortlist. The part I keep thinking about Every year an app ships a feature that quietly turns local content into outbound requests, and the user-facing change is a sparkle icon. The permission model does not move. The privacy label does not really move either, because the categories were drawn before any of this. I do not think the fix is panic or a ban. I think the fix is boring: a log on the device, readable by the person who owns the device. What would you want on that screen? Byte counts, destination names, per-app toggles, or the actual request bodies? I genuinely cannot decide where the useful line is, and I am the one building it. Disclosure and links I build TacUNS, a free on-device Android firewall. No root, no account, nothing leaves the phone. Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.tacu.nsfwzerotrust Site: https://www.tacuns.net/ Vibe Aegis, our open-source security scanner for AI-built apps: https://github.com/Tacuns/vibe-aegis

items.title: Microsoft Outage: Fix Fails to Restore Outlook, Teams, Copilot Across 74 Countries
items.summary: Microsoft is struggling to restore services following a global outage that disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and several other Microsoft 365 applications. The company's initial recovery measures have not delivered the anticipated improvements, forcing it to explore alternative ways to restore its infrastructure. The disruption began on Thursday, November 12, with Downdetector receiving reports from 74 countries and territories. In its latest update at 11:44 am IST, Microsoft said it was evaluating additional traffic controls, including throttling, protocol adjustments, and failover routing, to improve infrastructure stability. It was also expanding internal testing to improve traffic monitoring and identify failures. Earlier, the company had begun scaling up virtual machines to increase capacity and reduce server loads. However, it encountered problems synchronising network changes because some machines remained stuck in an abnormal state. Microsoft said it was not aware of any malicious activity causing the incident. The company plans to publish a post-incident report detailing the root cause and corrective measures after mitigation. Downdetector recorded nearly 130,000 reports of Outlook-related problems in the US alone. Users reported difficulties accessing their inboxes, sending and receiving emails, and connecting to workplace applications. Other affected services included Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OneDrive, and SharePoint, although the extent of disruption varied across applications. The disruption primarily originated in Exchange Online, Microsoft's cloud-based email infrastructure that powers Outlook. Microsoft initially attributed the connectivity problems to elevated loads across its infrastructure after a large number of servers became unexpectedly unavailable. The resulting loss of capacity shifted traffic onto the remaining servers, creating further strain. The company subsequently identified an issue with a core process responsible for establishing secure connections on affected servers. The process was becoming overwhelmed, causing servers to stop processing requests. Microsoft also identified a recent network configuration change that correlated with the start of the incident, although it has not published a confirmed root cause. The outage extended to services dependent on Exchange Online. In Teams, calendar access, meeting scheduling, and certain organisational chat features were affected, while core messaging and online meetings remained largely functional. Direct access to files stored in SharePoint remained available, although features dependent on Exchange Online were disrupted. Other affected services included Microsoft Defender XDR, Planner, To Do, Purview, Intune, Power BI, and Microsoft Graph. The disruption also affected third-party AI services. OpenAI reported problems with its Microsoft 365 connectors, warning that new connections could fail and connected tools might not work as expected. Anthropic separately reported failures involving mail, calendar, and search functions in its Microsoft 365 connector, along with disruptions to Claude for Outlook. Microsoft initially attempted to redistribute traffic across its global infrastructure, restart affected servers, and redirect connections to alternative pathways. However, some servers became unresponsive again when traffic was restored. The company subsequently restricted certain types of traffic in affected regions, rolled back network configuration changes, and began rebuilding some servers using an earlier software configuration.

items.summary: Anthropic's initial public offering has drawn about six times the orders for the shares available, according to people familiar with the matter, as interest increases for potentially the biggest first-time share sale ever. The Claude AI model firm and its co-founders are seeking to raise as much as $64.4 billion in the IPO and $26 billion in a private placement, its filings show. Taken together, the offering would be bigger than SpaceX’s IPO, making it the biggest listing of all time. Bloomberg's David Savage reports. (Source: Bloomberg)

items.title: Upgrade Evidence for Packages: Helping AI Agents Patch Safely
items.summary: AI agents now open dependency upgrades faster than most engineering teams can review them. Safe patching is not just about bumping a version, it is about proving the bump held. According to Sonatype's 2026 State of the Software Supply Chain report, 27.76% of 36,870 AI-generated upgrade recommendations pointed to versions that do not exist in any registry. This ai agent package upgrade evidence guide breaks down why unverified upgrades fail and what proof every change should carry. It also shows how to record that proof in your pipeline. You will see where human approval belongs, so your team can let agents patch with confidence and keep a clean, reviewable audit trail for every dependency change. Why Do AI Agent Dependency Upgrades Fail Without Evidence? Transitive dependencies change what nobody reviewed An agent that bumps one direct package rarely changes just one package. The new version can pull in a dozen transitive dependencies, and each carries its own code, maintainers, and risks. Reviewers usually read the manifest diff, yet the real change lives in the lockfile. Public data does not fill the gap either. Sonatype's analysis found that nearly 65% of open source CVEs lacked an NVD-assigned CVSS score. Therefore, severity labels alone cannot tell an agent which upgrade is safe, or tell a reviewer why it was chosen. A green build is not proof of a safe upgrade A passing build only shows that the code compiles and the tests you wrote still pass. It does not show that the version exists in the registry. It also cannot show that the version is free of known flaws, or that the changed code paths were exercised. Moreover, an agent explains its choice in fluent text, which feels like evidence but is not. Without a stored record of what was checked, nobody can reconstruct the decision later. For software supply chain security reviews, that missing record is the real failure, not the bad version itself. What Is AI Agent Package Upgrade Evidence? AI agent package upgrade evidence is the verifiable record that proves an automated dependency change was necessary, correct, tested, and approved. Detection tools stop at the alert, so AI agent package upgrade evidence has to be produced by the step that actually changes the code. Think of it as a commit-level receipt. Each upgrade carries six items, and a reviewer should be able to answer every question without opening a terminal. Together they form a package upgrade audit trail that survives staff changes and audit cycles. Notice that the registry check sits next to the test results. The first confirms the package is real, while the second confirms your application still behaves. How to Build an Upgrade Evidence Record Step by Step Reliable ai agent package upgrade evidence starts in the pipeline, so the pipeline below treats evidence as a build artifact. If the file is missing or incomplete, the merge fails. Capture the dependency diff before and after Snapshot the lockfile before the agent runs, then diff it afterward. Record every direct and transitive change, not only the package the agent targeted. Next, confirm each new version exists in the registry, since models can name releases that were never published. A simple lookup such as npm view handles this for npm packages, and the result belongs in the record. Store the advisory ID that triggered the change as well, so the reason for the upgrade travels with the code. Repeat this for every ecosystem in the repository, because mixed stacks hide gaps. Attach regression testing results to the change Run automated dependency upgrade testing against the new dependency tree and store the report with the change ID. Regression testing should cover the code paths that import the upgraded package, not just the overall pass rate. If any test fails, the agent either repairs the code or abandons the upgrade, and the record should show which happened. Keep the report as a build artifact so auditors can open it months later. No passing tests means no evidence, and no evidence means no merge. A minimal evidence record looks like this: { "change_id" : "upg-0042" , "package" : "lodash" , "ecosystem" : "npm" , "from" : "4.17.15" , "to" : "4.17.21" , "advisory_ids" : [ "CVE-2021-23337" ] , "transitive_changes" : 0 , "registry_verified" : true , "tests" : { "suite" : "regression" , "passed" : 187 , "failed" : 0 } , "approval" : { "tier" : "patch" , "approved_by" : "reviewer@example.com" } , "rollback_ref" : "git:9f3c2ab" } A CI gate can then fail closed: - name : Verify upgrade evidence run : | npm view "lodash@$NEW_VERSION" version jq -e '.registry_verified == true and .tests.failed == 0 and .rollback_ref != null' "evidence/$CHANGE_ID.json" Where Should Human Approval Sit in Safe Package Patching? Not every upgrade deserves the same scrutiny. A practical human approval workflow ties review depth to the version change. Patch releases with complete evidence can auto-merge to staging after a spot check. Minor releases need one reviewer who reads the evidence pack. Major releases get a full review and a tested rollback plan. Tool comparisons such as LibX vs Snyk vs Dependabot show that scanners handle detection well. Yet dependency security only improves when the fix is also tested and recorded. Automated vulnerability remediation closes that loop by upgrading the package, generating the code change, testing it, and handing the reviewer an evidence pack. As a result, the reviewer's job shifts from hunting for facts to approving them. Package Upgrade Evidence Checklist for Engineering Teams Use this checklist to judge whether your ai agent package upgrade evidence is strong enough before an agent merges anything. Each item maps to a field in the evidence record, so the checklist doubles as a review template. Teams that adopt even four of these items gain a defensible package upgrade audit trail for the next software supply chain security review. Lockfile diff stored, including transitive dependencies. Advisory ID linked to the reason for the change. Registry lookup confirms the exact version exists. Regression tests run and attached as an artifact. Approval tier matches the version change. Rollback reference points to a tested commit. Evidence file required by the CI gate, with the build failing when it is missing. Verified Upgrades Beat Fast Upgrades Agents will keep proposing upgrades, and the teams that benefit most will be the ones that demand proof with every change. Xccelera builds an AI security dependency upgrader and vulnerability auto-resolver. It finds vulnerable and outdated dependencies, upgrades them, remediates the affected code, and tests each fix before it ships. Every scan, upgrade, and fix is recorded as evidence, and human approval stays in the loop where your policies require it. That combination turns agent speed into something engineering leaders can trust and auditors can verify. If your backlog of security upgrades keeps growing faster than your review capacity, start by asking what evidence each patch leaves behind.

items.summary: Nvidia is searching for a permanent replacement for larger-than-life Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, a daunting challenge at the world’s most valuable chipmaker. The company has tapped an outside firm to identify potential candidates following revelations of multiple extramarital affairs by Huang. Longtime Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO. Bloomberg's Tom Mackenzie has more details. (Source: Bloomberg)

items.title: Nvidia scandal sparks US national security furore and calls to take tough line on China
items.summary: Former CEO Jensen Huang and US commerce secretary to appear before Congress amid bipartisan concern that America’s security was put at risk Nvidia scandal – latest updates Analysis: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached? Nvidia’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang and Donald Trump’s commerce secretary are expected to testify before Congress in the coming weeks, as the fallout from Huang’s reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy reverberated across the US, sparking bipartisan concerns for national security and calls for a tougher stance against Beijing. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Huang and Nvidia must answer as to whether America’s security had been jeopardised, adding that the Trump administration also must account for what it did once it learned about Huang’s reported relationship with Alice Huang, who is accused of spying for China.

items.title: How to Track Company Signals and Feed Them to Your AI Agents
items.summary: A UK company has 14 days to tell the registrar that a director has joined or left, so an agent that reads the register overnight can write to an account about news that is already two weeks old. You avoid that failure with the setup around the agent: a watchlist of target accounts, a source that pushes changes, an events table that stores three dates per event, and an approval step before any message goes out. Pick 50 accounts and the events worth a call Start small. Drimble’s guidance on company monitoring recommends watching your top 50 target accounts and alerting only on “phone-worthy” events: officer changes, new sites, status changes and capital events. A longer list is easy to build and hard to act on. My take is that an agent makes a noisy watchlist worse, because it drafts a message for every event you hand it. Drimble’s guide to webhooks and signals for AI agents lists the events most worth wiring up: incorporations and status changes, registered-address moves, director appointments and resignations, new filings, job postings and local news mentions. Pick the two or three that match what you sell. Add the rest only after the first ones earn replies. Connect to the registers that publish changes If your accounts sit in one country, go to the source. Companies House runs a Streaming API that pushes changes over a long-running HTTP connection, with separate streams for company information, filing history, insolvency cases, charges, officers and persons with significant control. Each event carries a timepoint, so a client that drops its connection can resume where it stopped, although the rewind window is limited. Each account gets two concurrent connections, which suits a single listener feeding a queue. Cross-border lists are harder, because every register has its own format and its own publishing rhythm. An aggregator earns its place here. Drimble monitors official registers in ten markets, from the UK and Ireland to Canada and Australia, and delivers alerts by email or through its buying signals webhooks. A daily digest email suits a solo user, teams can push events into the CRM as tasks, and larger operations can consume the webhook feed in their own tooling. Store three dates on every event Every signal carries three dates, and your events table should hold all of them. The event date says when the change happened. The publication date says when the register or filing made it public. The observation date says when your system saw it. The Companies House officers stream shows why the distinction matters. Each record includes the appointment or resignation date next to a published_at timestamp, so you can measure the gap on every change. In the US, a public company has four business days to file a Form 8-K after a director or certain officers leave or join, under Item 5.02. Companies that do not report to the SEC file no 8-Ks at all, so signals about them have to come from other sources. Drimble’s guidance adds a practical rule: show the observation date next to every event, because some registers publish daily and others weekly. Pass all three dates to the agent. A message about a director who resigned three weeks ago reads differently from one about an appointment filed yesterday, and the agent can only tell the difference if the dates reach it. Deliver events by webhook and store them first A webhook pushes each event to you as it happens, so you skip polling. The delivery rules follow the standard playbook. Stripe’s webhook documentation recommends verifying the signature on every request, returning a 2xx status quickly before running any heavy logic, and deduplicating on the event ID. Stripe also does not guarantee delivery order, so build your table to accept events out of sequence. Drimble’s guide adds the step that matters for agents. Write every verified event into an events table with a stable identifier and a timestamp, and let the agent read from that table instead of from the webhook itself. The agent can then build a daily digest from the table, and you can replay the table after an outage. Webhooks tell your system that something changed. An agent also needs to ask questions afterward, and that is where the Model Context Protocol fits. MCP is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems, and the Drimble MCP server works in Claude, ChatGPT and other MCP clients, with every record linked to a company identifier, source and capture date. My take is to use both: webhooks fill the events table, and MCP lets the agent look up the company record behind an event when it drafts. Let the agent draft and a person send Give the agent one job. It takes an event plus the account record from your CRM and drafts a short message for the account owner. Drimble’s guidance keeps sending behind one-click approval, and I would do the same until the drafts have proven themselves on real accounts. Measure the reply rate for each signal type. If messages about director changes draw replies and messages about address moves draw none, remove address moves from the watchlist. Set an expiry on the queue as well. Drimble’s guidance holds that most public signals lose value after about 30 days , so an event older than that should leave the queue unless a person pulls it back. Treat officer names as personal data Officer events name individuals. The UK Information Commissioner’s Office states that information about a limited company is not personal data , while a director’s name can be personal data when the information relates to that person as an individual. Decide how your agent stores and uses those names before you switch on officer alerts. Take legal advice on the basis for any message that addresses a named person. The feed outlasts the agent The agent is the easiest part of this system to swap. The watchlist, the events table with its three dates and the reply-rate log stay with you, and together they show which events earn a call. Start with 50 accounts, one signal type and a month of data, then widen the feed once the numbers justify it.

items.title: The Microsoft outage is disrupting email. These business leaders barely use it anyway.
items.summary: These CEOs say they limit their use of email. Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagic; Alisha Jucevic/Bloomberg; Daniel Delgado Jr./Disney A major Microsoft 365 outage sparked jokes and complaints as workers lost email and Teams access. Microsoft said overloaded infrastructure and unresponsive servers led to the disruptions. These business leaders say they hardly use email at all. A widespread Microsoft outage on Thursday left thousands of users struggling to access their emails, disrupting workplaces and government operations around the world. The outage affected Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and other Microsoft 365 services. In updates on X, Microsoft said overloaded infrastructure and unresponsive servers were contributing to the disruptions, which continued into Friday. "We regret that today's outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue," Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said in a Thursday post on X. " We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it, and for now I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity." The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Some employees around the world are celebrating the outage, saying they can't possibly work without their Teams and emails, and are jokingly suggesting their bosses give them Friday off. Others, in angry social media posts, are calling on Microsoft to resolve the issue soon so they can get back to work. But for some of the world's most successful business leaders, going without email is already a way of life. Several CEOs and entrepreneurs have previously told Business Insider that they rarely use email, preferring phone calls, text messages, or even handwritten letters. Kevin O'Leary "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary said in a December interview with Business Insider that he had given up on email after being inundated with thousands of messages daily. "I don't do emails anymore because I get anywhere from 2,000 to 4,000 a day," he said. O'Leary said he had tried different filtering systems but couldn't escape the constant stream of messages. People who need to reach him now use messaging apps instead, he added. Brian Chesky Brian Chesky says email is one of the most inferior forms of communication. Stefanie Keenan/Getty Images for Airbnb The Airbnb CEO is another email skeptic. "I don't know if I write an email a week," Chesky told Time in a September interview. He said he responds to emails daily but rarely initiates them, preferring texts, calls, and in-person conversations. "I just find it inferior to almost every other form of communication," Chesky said, explaining that texts feel more personal and faster. John Paul DeJoria DeJoria, the billionaire cofounder of haircare brands John Paul Mitchell Systems and Patrón Tequila, takes things further. "I don't even own a computer," DeJoria told Business Insider in a June interview . The 82-year-old entrepreneur said he doesn't have an email address. Instead, he uses his assistant's computer when necessary and prefers calls or handwritten letters. Wolfgang Puck Wolfgang Puck says he prefers to do work over calls. Denise Truscello/Getty Images for Drink Las Vegas The celebrity chef also favors phone calls over email when managing his restaurant empire. "I don't enjoy emails very much. I like talking to people directly. I think you understand people better that way," Puck told Business Insider earlier this year. Melanie Perkins "When I shut my laptop, I actually tune out," Perkins says. Nina Franova/Getty Images for SXSW Sydney The Canva CEO isn't against using email, but limits it to protect her personal time. "I don't have email or Slack on my phone," Perkins said on a podcast last year. "When I shut my laptop, I actually tune out." She said she remains reachable through emergency calls or pages, but otherwise tries to separate work from downtime. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The Jensen Huang scandal is casting a shadow over data centers halfway across the world
items.summary: The Jensen Huang scandal could increase scrutiny of AI infrastructure companies in Southeast Asia, according to industry sources. Samsul Said/Bloomberg via Getty Images Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia after allegations of an affair with a Singapore-based Chinese spy. Megaspeed, the company at the center of the scandal, has been accused of funneling Nvidia chips to China. The scandal could increase scrutiny and costs for AI infrastructure operators in Southeast Asia. Jensen-Gate isn't just Nvidia's problem anymore. Data center operators across Southeast Asia might be getting caught in the fallout. In case you missed it, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has had a rough week. On Sunday, The New York Times published an exposé that the executive had an affair with Singapore-based Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , believed to be passing sensitive Nvidia information to Beijing. Alice Huang worked at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that is the largest Nvidia customer in Southeast Asia, per Bloomberg. US authorities have investigated the company on suspicion that it helped Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia AI chips in violation of US export restrictions . Huang resigned from his role on Thursday. Industry sources in data center financing and operations told Business Insider that Jensen-Gate could increase scrutiny on Southeast Asia's AI infrastructure companies . Jensengate could lead to increased oversight Chris Miller , the author of "Chip War" and a professor at Tufts University, said to Yahoo Finance on Monday that it was widely known that Megaspeed was "primarily building data centers in Southeast Asia to serve Chinese customers, especially Alibaba in their case." He added that Megaspeed isn't alone, and that there are many data centers in Malaysia, Thailand, and Singapore that buy advanced American chips and sell them to customers in China. He expects these relationships to face more oversight from Washington after Huang's scandal. SEA AI infrastructure operations may get slower and more expensive More scrutiny means slower and more expensive processes. Lior Prosor, the managing partner of Deep33, an NYC-headquartered venture fund that invests in AI infrastructure, told Business Insider that the Huang affair would intensify scrutiny of American tech deployments in Southeast Asia, especially which customers' hands they end up in. "That could increase financing costs and create additional hurdles for some operators," Prosor said. He said this could temporarily create a broader risk premium for Southeast Asian operators, even those with no connection to Megaspeed. Chinmoy Baruah, the CEO of Dublin-based semiconductor company ChipX, said he expects approvals for AI infrastructure projects in the region to take longer, as investors and partners will ask more detailed questions on compliance. ChipX has committed to building wafer fabrication plants in Malaysia. "That may slow some projects at the margin, particularly those with less transparent structures," Baruah told Business Insider. Michael Heinrich, the CEO of Singapore-based decentralized AI compute company 0G, said he could see fundraising for AI infrastructure get more selective over the next year. "The next round of capital will go to the operators who can prove where their chips are, who uses them, and who owns the business," Heinrich said. Bitter medicine, but better long-term health The Huang scandal won't have a lasting impact on demand for Southeast Asian AI infrastructure, but rather on the standards for it, said Baruah. He said the region's fundamentals — growing digital economies, supportive governments, improving connectivity, and rising AI adoption — remain strong. This incident, however, will make rules clearer and increase diligence among operators, chip suppliers, and regulators. "That is a positive outcome for Southeast Asia, because it strengthens the region's position as a reliable, long-term destination for global digital infrastructure investment, not a shortcut around the rules," Baruah said. Prosor from Deep33 added that AI compute is in "extraordinarily short supply, and capital will flow to wherever companies can reliably build up compute. "Southeast Asia remains an important part of that equation," he said. Southeast Asia's data center boom The Huang scandal comes as the data center industry in Southeast Asia is booming. Ember Energy, a London-headquartered energy think tank, wrote in a 2025 report that ASEAN — a bloc of 11 member states in Southeast Asia — was emerging as a "global data center hot spot" due to lower construction costs and electricity levies. Malaysia, for instance, had live data center operations totaling about 1.3 gigawatts in June, which was a tenfold increase from 2022, per a report by BloombergNEF, a think tank under Bloomberg. It has another 4.7 gigawatts planned or under construction, the report added. Indonesia had about 450 megawatts of live data-center capacity as of June, with more than four times that amount currently under construction or committed, per the BloombergNEF report. A rough week for Nvidia Huang's resignation comes after a tumultuous few days for Nvidia . Its stock took a hit after the US midterm elections on November 3, which flipped control of Congress to the Democrats, many of whom had made anti-data-center messaging a major part of their campaigns. A few days after reports on Huang's affair, on Wednesday, the Times published another report that said Huang had had a second extramarital relationship, this time with Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell . The Wall Street Journal wrote on Wednesday that Nvidia's board was preparing to oust Huang. Early Thursday morning, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned from the role, and CFO Colette Kress would take over as interim CEO. Read the original article on Business Insider

A few days after reports on Huang's affair, on Wednesday, the Times published another report that said Huang had had a second extramarital relationship, this time with Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell. The Wall Street Journal wrote on Wednesday that Nvidia's board was preparing to oust Huang.

items.title: The Nightmare at NVIDIA
items.summary: It took Jensen Huang forty years to go from working as a ‘dishwasher, waiter, busboy’ to starting NVIDIA and turning it into a trillion-dollar company by 2023. But it took only a fortnight and a handful of investigative reports to unravel his charismatic leadership at one of the world’s most valuable companies—in what is now widely seen as one of the more humiliating resignations in Silicon Valley. Over the last few days, he’s been the subject of reports about a romantic relationship with a Chinese spy. In an apology letter, he acknowledged that he was unfaithful to his wife. In quick succession, came another report from The New York Times, which revealed he had an ‘extramarital affair’ with the company’s VP of Healthcare, Kimberly Powell. Barely a few hours into his resignation, Reuters reported that he had an intimate relationship with a second NVIDIA employee. He saved NVIDIA from bankruptcy and led it through the gaming, crypto, and AI boom, and created $5 trillion in value. But his personal life choices and moral misgivings have tainted this historic journey. The company’s shares are down approximately 12% since November 6, wiping out an estimated $540 billion in market capitalisation. CFO Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO until a permanent successor is named. Can There Be a True Successor? “It seems likely that the board of the company will attempt to recruit a semiconductor industry veteran to ensure that the firm is headed by a CEO who already has deep industry ties and something like the stature of Huang,” Paul Triolo, Partner at DGA Global, tells AIM. Over the last week, there has been speculation among analysts and industry on who, if any, could succeed Huang, who has been at the helm of NVIDIA since 1993. According to numerous analysts and industry experts, Ian Buck, NVIDIA’s VP of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing, has emerged as a leading candidate. A company veteran since 2004, Buck played a central role in developing CUDA and now oversees products for major cloud providers. Futurum Equities’ Shay Boloor told Reuters that Buck was the strongest long-term internal contender. Among external candidates, Semafor mentioned Apple’s Johny Srouji, who led the development of its proprietary silicon. A few surprising contenders floated by industry commentators include Arm CEO Rene Haas, a former NVIDIA executive, and even AMD CEO Lisa Su. US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, suggested another name in a Truth Social post: Apple CEO Tim Cook, writing that there was “only one man to take his place”. But it would be difficult for any replacement to emulate Huang’s ability to shape the company’s long-term technology roadmap. Kress, or whoever eventually takes the permanent CEO role, will have to lead NVIDIA through an increasingly uncertain AI economy, where questions about the sustainability of massive infrastructure investments and the possibility of an AI bubble are becoming harder to ignore. “The change will not impact the firm's long-term direction,” says Triolo. But only “if the new CEO can quickly rebuild industry relationships and leverage the firm's substantial engineering capability, which remains intact.” On the other hand, Stacy Ragson, Managing Director at equity research firm Bernstein, in an assessment shared with AIM before Huang resigned, said that NVIDIA is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he ‘is’ NVIDIA. In a 2024 interview with Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, Huang revealed that 60 people reported directly to him. He deliberately kept the organisation relatively flat, arguing that information about the company's challenges, priorities, and future direction should reach senior executives simultaneously rather than pass through layers of management. This made him the central point connecting NVIDIA’s engineering, product development, and commercial strategy. The difficulty for his successor is replicating the alignment that allowed NVIDIA to move from gaming GPUs to CUDA, accelerated computing and, eventually, full-stack AI infrastructure. “Wrangling more than 60 VPs to a cohesive vision of the company takes a certain kind of person; otherwise the firm’s direction risks dissolving into noise,” says SemiAnalysis, in its analysis post Huang’s resignation. “Our view is that the company was never built for him not to be there.” SemiAnalysis also notes how Huang ‘woved’ to keep the company in a ‘startup mode’, where major decisions in product development and engineering could be made in the final moments before release. “For example, the GB200 design came together a lot closer to the product cycle than probably anyone would have liked,” says SemiAnalysis, citing a former executive at NVIDIA. Under his leadership, NVIDIA became a major venture investor, startup financier, cloud infrastructure backer, and M&A participant. Tomasz Tunguz, General Partner at venture capital firm Theory Ventures, described NVIDIA in his blog post as the “Central Bank of AI”. He argued that NVIDIA has become deeply embedded in the US AI economy, shaping how startups raise capital, how acquisitions take place, and how policy around the sector evolves. “Under a CFO-led regime facing heightened board scrutiny, any tightening of those equity checks, payment terms or lease backstops will slow AI buildouts just as the broader economy slows when the Federal Reserve tightens credit,” Tunguz noted. He also expects second-order effects on the startup ecosystem. “Under Huang, NVIDIA acted simultaneously as chip supplier, lead venture investor, anchor cloud customer, and lease guarantor across more than 200 startups,” he noted. “Those deals ran on Huang's personal conviction and relationships. NVIDIA now needs a leader who can sustain these founder partnerships without the co-founder who built them. A sudden transition at the top introduces real uncertainty into the market and especially in startups.” Despite record revenues, several neocloud operators are struggling with debt that outpaces cash flows, weakening bond-market confidence and fuelling a broader bearish outlook among investors. The ecosystem is now entering a post-Huang era, with mounting financial pressures Huang backing of these cloud and AI compute providers went beyond supplying GPUs. Under his leadership, NVIDIA took equity stakes in companies such as CoreWeave and Nebius, invested in Lambda and Nscale, and helped them secure financing for large data-centre projects. SemiAnalysis explained that neoclouds around the world had been able to raise capital largely because of Huang’s backing, rather than simply because they had evaluated NVIDIA’s chips and chosen them over competitors. NVIDIA’s financial backstops, including revenue guarantees, landlord guarantees, and lease agreements, allowed operators without investment-grade credit ratings to borrow at investment-grade rates. “If the Jensen pull is not there, there might be a large contraction in this ecosystem,” said SemiAnalysis. What Happens to Open-Source? Huang’s departure does not just concern NVIDIA’s technology roadmap. It could also affect the open-source AI ecosystem. Huang has been one of the industry's most vocal champions of open-weight AI models. In July, NVIDIA joined Meta, Microsoft, and several other technology companies in signing an open letter urging US lawmakers not to impose premature restrictions on open models. NVIDIA has backed this ambition with substantial capital. In September, it agreed to acquire Hugging Face , the open-source AI model repository, for $12.93 billion. A month earlier, it committed $7 billion to coding-focused AI startup Poolside—comprising a $6 billion technology-licensing deal and a $1 billion equity investment—with more than 100 of its engineers joining NVIDIA’s open-source Nemotron project. Melvin Mathew, AI and equities analyst and writer at Milk Road, believes the biggest beneficiaries could be frontier AI labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic. “If NVIDIA becomes less aggressive about supporting open-weight AI and the US tightens access to advanced chips, I think the competitive environment could shift significantly in favour of the American frontier labs,” he noted in a post on X. The early signs are already emerging. The Information had previously reported that DeepSeek was using thousands of restricted Blackwell chips obtained through overseas data centres, allegedly circumventing US export restrictions. Reuters reported on November 12 that Chinese AI companies were scrambling to secure NVIDIA-powered computing capacity at overseas data centres, fearing that Washington could tighten restrictions on remote access to advanced chips. Open-weight AI is unlikely to disappear, particularly as China accelerates its domestic chip ambitions through companies such as Huawei. Moreover, leading tech companies and startups are leaning into open-weight AI models to reduce their AI spending. But Huang’s departure could weaken the case for broader access to AI computing, potentially changing the competitive dynamics between American frontier labs and Chinese open-model developers. Several frontier AI leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have pursued more cautious, largely proprietary approaches. Amodei had warned that increasingly capable open models could be difficult to control and safeguard. For now, the investigations remain far from conclusive. The company's independent board inquiry and the scrutiny from US lawmakers and federal authorities will have to establish what Huang knew, what role he played, and whether NVIDIA itself crossed any legal or regulatory boundaries. NVIDIA has been through numerous nightmares over the last few decades. With this one, there’s no Huang to save the day.

items.title: Sex, Lies and AI Chips: Jensen Huang’s Last Days as Nvidia CEO
items.summary: Last weekend, all hell broke loose around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. On Friday, his intimate relationship with a suspected Chinese spy was made public. Then Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, came to Huang’s home and asked him whether a news report about the relationship was true, according to a person briefed on the interaction. Huang told him it was. By Sunday evening, Huang had publicly apologized for the affair, and Nvidia’s board had said it would investigate his conduct. Teter had to urge directors to do so—the board, which includes executives who’ve known Huang for decades, had been reluctant to act. In conversations with senior Nvidia executives, Huang maintained that the affair with the woman, Alice Huang, was his only infidelity, according to people familiar with the situation. Had that been the case, perhaps he would have made it through the maelstrom.

items.title: What smart people in business and tech are saying about Jensen Huang's ouster
items.summary: Nvidia's board announced Thursday that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO. Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty Images Nvidia founder Jensen Huang is out. After another report about an affair, Nvidia's board announced Thursday that Huang had resigned. This is what smart people in business and tech are saying about Huang's departure. Nvidia is without its founder for the first time in more than 30 years. On Thursday, Nvidia's board announced CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation , ending the tenure of a leader who had overseen the chipmaker's rise to become one of the world's most valuable companies. Huang's ouster came after days of reports about his personal life. First, The New York Times reported that the Nvidia leader had a close relationship with someone US officials suspect to be a Chinese intelligence asset. On Sunday, Huang acknowledged having an affair, and Nvidia's board launched an investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The Times had reported that the Nvidia founder had grown close to Alice Huang , who US officials believed had been recruited to gather information for the Chinese government. Then on Wednesday, the Times reported that Huang had another affair with Kimberly Powell , an Nvidia executive who reported to him. By Thursday morning, one of the world's richest men and a face of the AI boom was out of a job. Clem Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue Bloomberg/Getty Images Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said, "This whole thing sucks." "I wish none of it had happened. It's a really sad day!" Delangue wrote on social media. Delangue, whose company Nvidia agreed to acquire for roughly $12.9 billion, said that he'll continue to fight for open-source AI. "I want to make one thing clear: we'll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever," he wrote. "This is too important to slow down now. Let's go!" Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co. Dan Ives. Astrida Valigorsky/Getty Images Tech megabull Dan Ives said that Nvidia's board "had no choice." "Time to look forward for Nvidia without Jensen," Ives wrote on X. "Dark chapter for Jensen and Nvidia." Ives also pointed to his earlier statement about what he expects the stock to do without Huang at the helm, which was published before the resignation was announced. "We see the stock valuation at $225 without Jensen ($300 with Jensen as CEO)." President Donald Trump Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images President Donald Trump suggested a familiar name to take Huang's place. "NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. Cook stepped down as Apple CEO in September. Lloyd Blankfein, former CEO of Goldman Sachs Bloomberg/Getty Images Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein waxed poetic about the moment. "Sad about Jensen. Shakespearean," Blankfein wrote on X. "But as de Gaulle said, 'The graveyards are filled with indispensable men.'" (While the quote is often attributed to the legendary French statesman Charles de Gaulle, at least one researcher has raised questions about its origins .) Sen. Elizabeth Warren Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who is likely to chair the powerful Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation won't end Congress' desire for answers. "Jensen Huang's decision to resign from NVIDIA does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Warren wrote on X. Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital Shaun Maguire called the decision "bad for America" but doubted Huang had bad intentions. Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire said Huang will "leave a huge void, with the loss of a: technical, aggressive, founder-CEO." "The American AI community needs to work double-time in an attempt to fill this void," Maguire wrote in a lengthy post on X. Maguire said, "Infidelity is obviously bad," but Huang's "contributions to American innovation and AI leadership cannot be overstated." Jim Cramer, host of CNBC's Mad Money Jim Cramer said Apple's new filing was "gloves off." John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images CNBC anchor Jim Cramer, who has interviewed Huang on several occasions, said Nvidia had no choice. "It had to happen. There's way too much evidence," Cramer said on CNBC after the news became official. Cramer praised Kress who the board named as Nvidia's interim leader. "I like Colette very much," he said. "I think she's going to be terrific in trying to figure out where the pieces are. Martin Casado, A16z general partner TK. Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Investor Martin Casado called Thursday a "Dark, dark day." "Horrible decision for the U.S. and the western world," he wrote on X. Ross Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management Ross Gerber has been bearish on Tesla. Emma McIntyre/Getty Images Ross Gerber said Huang's departure is "certainly a low moment for us long term Nvidia investors." "Jensen has resigned which is sadly the correct action in this case. Nvidia needs to be bigger than one man," Gerber wrote on X. "AI will go on and Nvidia will continue to be the core player." Gerber compared the moment to when Steve Jobs stepped away from Apple. "I was around when Jobs died, and many thought it was the end of Apple," Gerber wrote. "It was only the beginning." Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management Peter Foley/Bloomberg via Getty Images Gene Munster, a tech analyst and managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, said in an X post that Nvidia will rebound. "The unknown is now known," Munster wrote. "This morning $NVDA will gap down ($150 floor) on the Jensen news, then rallies as the market focuses on what actually matters." Munster said Nvidia's earnings next Tuesday should confirm his view. "AI demand is still accelerating," he wrote. "Nvidia GPUs remain the clear winners." Sarah Guo, founder of Conviction Big Event Media/Getty Images for HumanX Conference Investor Sarah Guo said that Huang's ouster is "a big loss." Before the news was announced, Guo described the Nvidia founder as "one of the most extraordinary entrepreneurs of all time." "He's bent the arc of technological progress, and the growth engine of the American economy rests on the shoulders of the company he built," Guo wrote on Thursday. Stephen Witt, author of a Huang biography Journalist Stephen Witt, who wrote "The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and the World's Most Coveted Microchip," said Huang "was Nvidia." "It's like the Bulls without Jordan," Witt said on CNBC on Thursday, alluding to NBA legend Michael Jordan's retirement after winning six titles in Chicago. "I don't know how they are going to replace this guy." Witt said Huang's range, from "world-class computer scientist" to deal-closer, will be difficult to replicate. "Jensen could take a diagram of Nvidia equipment, an exploded diagram, and draw it by hand from memory," Witt said. Anthony Pompliano, crypto investor and entrepreneur Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images for Anthony Pompliano Anthony Pompliano, a crypto investor and entrepreneur, wrote on X: "There is a good chance today is the bottom of the AI sell-off." Pompliano added, "No greater capitulation than the resignation of the CEO of the largest company in the world." Elad Gil, founder and CEO of Gil Capital, The prominent VC said the Nvidia drama should prompt founders to reassess their boards. "Good reminder for all founders to revisit who is on their board," Gil wrote on X, pointing to the OpenAI coup and Uber as precedents. He advised founders to reset their boards "during good times" to avoid abrupt action in bad ones. Travis Kalanick, Uber's cofounder who resigned as CEO in 2017, replied: "I concur." Naval Ravikant, AngelList's cofounder and chairman Naval Ravikant said that you cannot simply replace the founder. Steve Jennings/Getty Images for TechCrunch The angel investor and entrepreneur argued that founders are not easily replaceable. "You'd think we'd have learned from Steve Jobs and Travis Kalanick that one does not just simply replace the founder…" Ravikant wrote, invoking two high-profile cases where boards ousted founders. Elon Musk replied, "True words." Lex Fridman, host of the Lex Fridman Podcast Fridman called Nvidia's decision to let Huang go "a huge mistake" and said he stood with him. Fridman said the move was "Apple firing Steve Jobs all over again, but much bigger," given AI's importance. He said he had stayed quiet out of respect for Huang's family and team and because he personally hates infidelity. Still, Fridman wrote that Huang "is human, and makes mistakes like all of us do." He said his own interactions with Huang had shown kindness and humility, and he pushed back against the "mass hysteria" around spy allegations. Tobi Lütke, Shopify's cofounder and CEO Shopify CEO says companies often undervalue founders and put them in a corner. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Lütke called Nvidia's CEO transition a "generational blunder." Lütke said that was his view "at least based on the information that's available." Responding to a comment that Nvidia lacked a succession plan after 33 years under Huang, Lütke said there could never be a "true succession" for a founder like Huang, and warned Nvidia could become an imitation of the company he built. "There is no replacing a founder like Jensen," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue
