Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said, "This whole thing sucks."

"I wish none of it had happened. It's a really sad day!" Delangue wrote on social media.

Delangue, whose company Nvidia agreed to acquire for roughly $12.9 billion, said that he'll continue to fight for open-source AI.

"I want to make one thing clear: we'll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever," he wrote. "This is too important to slow down now. Let's go!"

Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co.
Dan Ives.

Astrida Valigorsky/Getty Images

Tech megabull Dan Ives said that Nvidia's board "had no choice."

"Time to look forward for Nvidia without Jensen," Ives wrote on X. "Dark chapter for Jensen and Nvidia."

Ives also pointed to his earlier statement about what he expects the stock to do without Huang at the helm, which was published before the resignation was announced.

"We see the stock valuation at $225 without Jensen ($300 with Jensen as CEO)."

President Donald Trump

Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

President Donald Trump suggested a familiar name to take Huang's place.

"NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.

Cook stepped down as Apple CEO in September.

Lloyd Blankfein, former CEO of Goldman Sachs

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein waxed poetic about the moment.

"Sad about Jensen. Shakespearean," Blankfein wrote on X. "But as de Gaulle said, 'The graveyards are filled with indispensable men.'"

(While the quote is often attributed to the legendary French statesman Charles de Gaulle, at least one researcher has raised questions about its origins.)

Sen. Elizabeth Warren
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts

Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images

Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who is likely to chair the powerful Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation won't end Congress' desire for answers.

"Jensen Huang's decision to resign from NVIDIA does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Warren wrote on X.

Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital
Shaun Maguire called the decision "bad for America" but doubted Huang had bad intentions.

Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire said Huang will "leave a huge void, with the loss of a: technical, aggressive, founder-CEO."

"The American AI community needs to work double-time in an attempt to fill this void," Maguire wrote in a lengthy post on X.

Maguire said, "Infidelity is obviously bad," but Huang's "contributions to American innovation and AI leadership cannot be overstated."

Jim Cramer, host of CNBC's Mad Money
Jim Cramer said Apple's new filing was "gloves off."

John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images

CNBC anchor Jim Cramer, who has interviewed Huang on several occasions, said Nvidia had no choice.

"It had to happen. There's way too much evidence," Cramer said on CNBC after the news became official.

Cramer praised Kress who the board named as Nvidia's interim leader.

"I like Colette very much," he said. "I think she's going to be terrific in trying to figure out where the pieces are.

Martin Casado, A16z general partner
TK.

Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images

Investor Martin Casado called Thursday a "Dark, dark day."

"Horrible decision for the U.S. and the western world," he wrote on X.

Ross Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management
Ross Gerber has been bearish on Tesla.

Emma McIntyre/Getty Images

Ross Gerber said Huang's departure is "certainly a low moment for us long term Nvidia investors."

"Jensen has resigned which is sadly the correct action in this case. Nvidia needs to be bigger than one man," Gerber wrote on X. "AI will go on and Nvidia will continue to be the core player."

Gerber compared the moment to when Steve Jobs stepped away from Apple.

"I was around when Jobs died, and many thought it was the end of Apple," Gerber wrote. "It was only the beginning."

Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management

Peter Foley/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Gene Munster, a tech analyst and managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, said in an X post that Nvidia will rebound.

"The unknown is now known," Munster wrote. "This morning $NVDA will gap down ($150 floor) on the Jensen news, then rallies as the market focuses on what actually matters."

Munster said Nvidia's earnings next Tuesday should confirm his view.

"AI demand is still accelerating," he wrote. "Nvidia GPUs remain the clear winners."

Sarah Guo, founder of Conviction

Big Event Media/Getty Images for HumanX Conference

Investor Sarah Guo said that Huang's ouster is "a big loss."

Before the news was announced, Guo described the Nvidia founder as "one of the most extraordinary entrepreneurs of all time."

"He's bent the arc of technological progress, and the growth engine of the American economy rests on the shoulders of the company he built," Guo wrote on Thursday.

Stephen Witt, author of a Huang biography

Journalist Stephen Witt, who wrote "The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and the World's Most Coveted Microchip," said Huang "was Nvidia."

"It's like the Bulls without Jordan," Witt said on CNBC on Thursday, alluding to NBA legend Michael Jordan's retirement after winning six titles in Chicago. "I don't know how they are going to replace this guy."

Witt said Huang's range, from "world-class computer scientist" to deal-closer, will be difficult to replicate.

"Jensen could take a diagram of Nvidia equipment, an exploded diagram, and draw it by hand from memory," Witt said.

Anthony Pompliano, crypto investor and entrepreneur

Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images for Anthony Pompliano

Anthony Pompliano, a crypto investor and entrepreneur, wrote on X: "There is a good chance today is the bottom of the AI sell-off."

Pompliano added, "No greater capitulation than the resignation of the CEO of the largest company in the world."

Elad Gil, founder and CEO of Gil Capital,

The prominent VC said the Nvidia drama should prompt founders to reassess their boards.

"Good reminder for all founders to revisit who is on their board," Gil wrote on X, pointing to the OpenAI coup and Uber as precedents. He advised founders to reset their boards "during good times" to avoid abrupt action in bad ones.

Travis Kalanick, Uber's cofounder who resigned as CEO in 2017, replied: "I concur."

Naval Ravikant, AngelList's cofounder and chairman
Naval Ravikant said that you cannot simply replace the founder.

Steve Jennings/Getty Images for TechCrunch

The angel investor and entrepreneur argued that founders are not easily replaceable.

"You'd think we'd have learned from Steve Jobs and Travis Kalanick that one does not just simply replace the founder…" Ravikant wrote, invoking two high-profile cases where boards ousted founders.

Elon Musk replied, "True words."

Lex Fridman, host of the Lex Fridman Podcast

Fridman called Nvidia's decision to let Huang go "a huge mistake" and said he stood with him.

Fridman said the move was "Apple firing Steve Jobs all over again, but much bigger," given AI's importance. He said he had stayed quiet out of respect for Huang's family and team and because he personally hates infidelity.

Still, Fridman wrote that Huang "is human, and makes mistakes like all of us do." He said his own interactions with Huang had shown kindness and humility, and he pushed back against the "mass hysteria" around spy allegations.

Tobi Lütke, Shopify's cofounder and CEO
Shopify CEO says companies often undervalue founders and put them in a corner.

Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Lütke called Nvidia's CEO transition a "generational blunder."

Lütke said that was his view "at least based on the information that's available."

Responding to a comment that Nvidia lacked a succession plan after 33 years under Huang, Lütke said there could never be a "true succession" for a founder like Huang, and warned Nvidia could become an imitation of the company he built.

"There is no replacing a founder like Jensen," he said.

items.title: Trump says he spoke to Jensen Huang on Wednesday: ‘He’s going through hell’
items.summary: President Donald Trump said Jensen Huang talked about his family when they spoke. Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images President Donald Trump says Jensen Huang called him a day before he resigned as Nvidia's CEO. Trump said Huang was going through a hard time and spoke about his family. "What he feels most badly about is his wife and family. That's what he told me," Trump said. President Donald Trump said he talked to Jensen Huang on Wednesday, a day before the Nvidia CEO resigned . In an interview with Stephen A. Smith at the White House, Trump said Huang called him and talked about the impact the affair scandal has had on his family. "I spoke to him yesterday. He's going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family," Trump said. "That's what he told me." Huang resigned on Thursday. On Sunday, he admitted in a memo to staff that he had been "unfaithful" and the Nvidia board announced it was investigating whether he had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation. The resignation also came after a New York Times report on Wednesday that said Huang had engaged in a second affair with an Nvidia executive that reported to him, Kimberly Powell . Following Huang's resignation, a Reuters report alleged a third affair, with another employee at Nvidia who was not named. In the interview on Thursday, Trump praised Huang and his work at Nvidia. When Smith asked if Huang should've stepped down, Trump said it depended on whether a woman he had an affair with was actually a Chinese spy, as US officials suspected, according to the Times. "If the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different," Trump said. He also reiterated his belief that Tim Cook, the former CEO of Apple, should succeed Huang. Colette Kress, Nvidia's CFO, was named interim CEO on Thursday as the board looks for a replacement. Earlier in the week, on Monday, the president said he had talked to Huang to see how he was doing. He said the executive told him he did not know the person he had an affair with "was a spy." "And I really believe him," Trump said. The Times reported Trump also spoke to Huang on Tuesday this week and encouraged him to fight to remain as Nvidia's CEO. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. items.title: New AI “copilot” helps engineers design better structures
items.summary: The use of algorithms to design structures has led to new parts optimized for ultralight aircraft, high-bandwidth antennas, and F1 racing cars. But the best algorithmic design techniques still require lots of computation and time: Users only see the final design after it’s complete, after which they often must start the design process all over again to make changes. That process also makes it harder to trust that the final designs are structurally sound. MIT researchers are making algorithmic designs more collaborative with a system that acts like an AI copilot. As the algorithm is generating the structure, it presents regions to the human designer for feedback. In an open-access Communications Engineering paper describing the system, the researchers showed it led to more easily manufacturable structures with higher buckling loads while adding only 15 seconds to the total design time compared to all-algorithmic approaches. The researchers believe the approach, which uses a design technique known as topology optimization, could make algorithmic design more accessible and manufacturable for a broader class of design engineers. “Right now, the human doesn’t have any agency or control over the design process as it’s playing out,” explains lead author Dat Ha PhD ’26, a recent MIT civil and environmental engineering doctoral student who is now a structural designer at LeMessurier. “For these really complex designs, we wanted to also tap into our brain, which is the most complex machine there is, to solve these design problems in a way that’s more practical to industry.” Joining Ha on the paper are Ferdous Alam, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Georgia Tech; Markus Buehler, the MIT Jerry McAfee (1940) Professor of Engineering; Faez Ahmed, MIT associate professor of mechanical engineering; and senior author Josephine Carstensen, MIT associate professor of civil and environmental engineering. Bringing a human in the loop Topology optimization is one of the most advanced and promising algorithmic design techniques. It uses formal optimization techniques to iteratively fill in the space given for a design in a way that maximally achieves the stated goals. For most applications, the process requires a lot of computation and time. When it’s finally done, the designs can be impractical to build or have other issues the engineer didn’t consider. For instance, some designs might have eight or more beam connections at a single point, which would be difficult to make in the real world. “Engineers are always very skeptical of computer programs, especially if they give you very weird-looking or unexpected designs,” Ha says. “On paper, topology optimization is really powerful and can achieve great, high-performing designs, but its black box nature has made it less widely adopted in industry.” Topology optimization has gotten traction in the automotive and aerospace industries, but it’s been used less to design buildings or bridges, partly because design engineers need to know they can trust the output. “A big limiting factor has been that the design engineer has very little influence over how the design evolves and therefore can’t control undesirable features,” Carstensen explains. “The lack of control and lack of ownership also inhibits its use.” To address those problems, the researchers made topology optimization more collaborative in an approach that Carstensen compares to having a design copilot. Prior attempts at adding human judgment slowed things down dramatically. The researchers’ new system uses machine learning to quickly identify the most likely regions of an algorithmic design that a human would want to change. To train the machine-learning model, the researchers created a synthetic dataset of probable human feedback to thousands of designs that critiqued things like aesthetics, performance criteria, and manufacturability. “We thought if we could create a record of where humans have made changes to these programs, then perhaps there’s a pattern to those choices, which is not very different from other types of machine-learning approaches,” Ha says. Carstensen sees the system as bringing together the best of algorithmic and human design approaches. “The idea is to tap into the brains of the designers and get them to infuse their domain knowledge as the design evolves,” Carstensen says. In demonstrations, the researchers showed their human-in-the-loop approach improved manufacturability and linear buckling load by 39 percent while only modestly increasing the total design time. Right now, the approach only allows users to make structures within identified regions thicker or thinner, but they hope to add other options for modification in future versions. “The hope is that by addressing these hurdles, we open up topology optimization to a much wider audience, not only in industry but also to researchers and students in academia,” Carstensen says. From designs to structures The researchers see their approach complementing AI only-approaches to design. “We are arguing there’s room for both,” Carstensen says. “If you are in a discipline that has a lot of computational resources, you can use the other approach. But if you really need the human input, you can use this collaborative approach.” Adding human input also serves to increase trust. “In some settings, the humans need to make the final decisions before advancing the final design,” Carstensen says. “By involving humans, we can get higher-performing designs to the real world to create higher-performing structures. Because it’s not just about designing good artifacts; it’s about creating good artifacts that humans will actually accept and make.” The work was supported, in part, by the MathWorks Engineering Fellowship Fund, TATA Steel, and the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium.

items.title: AI Ambition: ArtCraft Cloned Photoshop and Now Wants to "Rebuild Everything"
items.summary: The theme of day two of the AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco was increasing ambition using AI . And there have been few projects as ambitious as ArtCraft in the AI era. So far the fledgling company has released 17 open source versions of popular software tools , starting with a Photoshop alternative built from scratch in Rust called PhotoCraft . You could feel the excitement in the room this morning when ArtCraft founder and CEO Brandon Thomas presented a kind of manifesto for AI-based open source at AIE Code. When he mentioned that ArtCraft had cloned Adobe’s Acrobat, with a product called PdfCraft, it got a round of applause from the audience. In wrapping up, his rallying cries of “let's take back the entire internet” and “let's rebuild everything” were greeted with whoops and cheers. Thomas began his presentation by reliving the internet’s early history. In his view, the web started out with the right intentions, but things got screwed up once Web 2.0 hit the mainstream. “We had a bunch of chat applications that were completely open,” he said, regarding the 1990s internet. “So, IRC is like Discord, but you can spin up your own servers that you actually own. You can use whatever programs to automate them and interrogate them without rules.” His point wasn’t necessarily that everything was open source, but that web users could freely build things. With Flash, for example — a commercial animation tool eventually acquired by Adobe — “kids were making all kinds of animations.” When Web 2.0 came along, with its superior broadband and smartphones, “it brought everybody into the fold.” Thomas acknowledged that this widened the scope of internet software, but at the cost of that freedom to build with leading apps. “The diffuse, experimental, early web started to disappear,” he said. “The APIs got taken away from us, and then we started seeing distribution being gatekept by the big providers.” It seems Adobe in particular annoyed Thomas. He described getting billed with an unexpected fee when he cancelled a monthly plan. “It's really frustrating that the web — that was once really, really promising and open and free — has turned into this extractive, owned, rent-seeking world.” This inspired him to start ArtCraft, “with the ethos of ‘let's build everything open source.’” A message even anti-AI people have gotten behind, according to Thomas. In addition to PhotoCraft, they’ve copied other apps in the Adobe suite, cloned Figma, and created a Microsoft-like word processor called WordCraft. There are also independent apps such as SolidCraft, a community-led CAD project distributed through ArtCraft’s launcher. Thomas reiterated that these AI-built applications are 100% open — “not only the desktop apps, but the actual infrastructure as well.” PhotoCraft: The development process ArtCraft is starting with rewriting familiar tools. Thomas’s longer-term vision is for users (such as artists who were previously using Photoshop) to tailor the software to their own workflows. As he framed it, they want to “undo what had happened during Web 2.0 , when everything became owned and consolidated and gatekept, and just give people back their applications.” AI is the means to achieve that, he said. But aren’t there already open source alternatives to Photoshop, like GIMP? “GIMP isn't really used by artists,” said Thomas during his presentation. “We actually observed artists vibe coding their own workflows on top of the software that we gave them.” To begin creating PhotoCraft, the team gave an AI model a detailed prompt outlining Photoshop’s tools, data structures and file importers. After that, they “laid out a large, large prompt to say, let's build out the application.” As part of that process, they made everything MCP and CLI compatible . Within 24 hours, said Thomas, “we were looking at a pretty good approximation of what Photoshop was — and it kind of blew our minds away.” PhotoCraft interface; via ArtCraft website Thomas noted that PhotoCraft is “still not at 100% parity” — he said they’ve just passed 60% — but the team has set an internal goal to reach as close to 100% as possible. ( The project’s GitHub claims about 76% parity for feature breadth and about 46% for professional readiness.) “Right now, we want to fill the muscle memory of all the artists that use Adobe. So we are going for Adobe , their interface and ‘look and feel’ directly.” But after ArtCraft has achieved that, they plan to “build new apps that have new interfaces that are more agentic. ” A big reaction Thomas said he was surprised by the amount of attention PhotoCraft, in particular, has gotten — ranging from the New York Times requesting an interview, to a swelling of its open source community to about 4,000 developers . “I'm still struggling to bear with what has happened. It struck a nerve with people. They felt sort of maligned by Adobe and other tech companies . And what we built has really resonated with them.” After his presentation, Thomas was mobbed by AIE Code attendees. ArtCraft’s apps are being downloaded at the rate of about 1.7 million per day, which Thomas said is still accelerating. In addition to the 17 official apps, there are around 300 being developed by the community, he added. Rust is key, but there have been technical challenges Other than the AI technology, Thomas said that Rust was a crucial part of making the apps performant — he claimed that PhotoCraft opens ten times faster than Photoshop, for example. “Rust was probably essential in this product's success,” he said. “We've seen people do it in Electron before, but for high-quality creative apps, you really need something that's native. ” For those engineers who are not experts in Rust, Thomas has good news for you. “Do you need to know Rust to start using Rust today as an engineer? Definitely not. [...] Your agents will drive it just fine.” However, Thomas admitted that not everything has gone swimmingly. “We've run into a lot of gotchas — like permissions, GitHub, scaling, CI,” he said. “CI is falling over. We've been spinning up our own. We found a good place to get RAM on co-located servers.” But they have found an equilibrium on what agents can do and what needs to be handled by people. “If you're doing backend work or things that require schema migrations [or] API design, let your humans do that. But for desktop apps and games and anything that's basically immutable, throw your agents at it and give them full confidence.” And it turns out, there’s even an ArtCraft solution for you there. “AutoCraft is a completely autonomous software factory that we're going to open source.” AI open source FTW There’s no doubting the ambition of Brandon Thomas and his ArtCraft company. “We can open source the entire world,” he proclaimed at the end of his presentation. “Let's own our apps, our infra, our protocols, our models — all of it.” It’s a big vision, potentially even on the scale of Linux if its current downloads growth rate continues. But, ironically perhaps, what intrigues me most about ArtCraft is the growth of its human contributor community. After all, that’s what the original web got most right: human collaboration at scale. The big difference from the 1990s is that now it’s agents doing the bulk of the development work.

Thomas began his presentation by reliving the internet’s early history. In his view, the web started out with the right intentions, but things got screwed up once Web 2.0 hit the mainstream.

“We had a bunch of chat applications that were completely open,” he said, regarding the 1990s internet. “So, IRC is like Discord, but you can spin up your own servers that you actually own. You can use whatever programs to automate them and interrogate them without rules.”

His point wasn’t necessarily that everything was open source, but that web users could freely build things. With Flash, for example — a commercial animation tool eventually acquired by Adobe — “kids were making all kinds of animations.”

When Web 2.0 came along, with its superior broadband and smartphones, “it brought everybody into the fold.” Thomas acknowledged that this widened the scope of internet software, but at the cost of that freedom to build with leading apps.

“The diffuse, experimental, early web started to disappear,” he said. “The APIs got taken away from us, and then we started seeing distribution being gatekept by the big providers.”

It seems Adobe in particular annoyed Thomas. He described getting billed with an unexpected fee when he cancelled a monthly plan. 

“It's really frustrating that the web — that was once really, really promising and open and free — has turned into this extractive, owned, rent-seeking world.”

This inspired him to start ArtCraft, “with the ethos of ‘let's build everything open source.’” A message even anti-AI people have gotten behind, according to Thomas.

In addition to PhotoCraft, they’ve copied other apps in the Adobe suite, cloned Figma, and created a Microsoft-like word processor called WordCraft. There are also independent apps such as SolidCraft, a community-led CAD project distributed through ArtCraft’s launcher.

Thomas reiterated that these AI-built applications are 100% open — “not only the desktop apps, but the actual infrastructure as well.”

PhotoCraft: The development process

ArtCraft is starting with rewriting familiar tools. Thomas’s longer-term vision is for users (such as artists who were previously using Photoshop) to tailor the software to their own workflows.

As he framed it, they want to “undo what had happened during Web 2.0, when everything became owned and consolidated and gatekept, and just give people back their applications.” 

AI is the means to achieve that, he said.

But aren’t there already open source alternatives to Photoshop, like GIMP?

“GIMP isn't really used by artists,” said Thomas during his presentation. “We actually observed artists vibe coding their own workflows on top of the software that we gave them.”

To begin creating PhotoCraft, the team gave an AI model a detailed prompt outlining Photoshop’s tools, data structures and file importers. After that, they “laid out a large, large prompt to say, let's build out the application.”

As part of that process, they made everything MCP and CLI compatible.

Within 24 hours, said Thomas, “we were looking at a pretty good approximation of what Photoshop was — and it kind of blew our minds away.”

PhotoCraft interface; via ArtCraft website

Thomas noted that PhotoCraft is “still not at 100% parity” — he said they’ve just passed 60% — but the team has set an internal goal to reach as close to 100% as possible. (The project’s GitHub claims about 76% parity for feature breadth and about 46% for professional readiness.)

“Right now, we want to fill the muscle memory of all the artists that use Adobe. So we are going for Adobe, their interface and ‘look and feel’ directly.”

But after ArtCraft has achieved that, they plan to “build new apps that have new interfaces that are more agentic.”

A big reaction

Thomas said he was surprised by the amount of attention PhotoCraft, in particular, has gotten — ranging from the New York Times requesting an interview, to a swelling of its open source community to about 4,000 developers.

“I'm still struggling to bear with what has happened. It struck a nerve with people. They felt sort of maligned by Adobe and other tech companies. And what we built has really resonated with them.”

After his presentation, Thomas was mobbed by AIE Code attendees.

ArtCraft’s apps are being downloaded at the rate of about 1.7 million per day, which Thomas said is still accelerating.

In addition to the 17 official apps, there are around 300 being developed by the community, he added.

Rust is key, but there have been technical challenges

Other than the AI technology, Thomas said that Rust was a crucial part of making the apps performant — he claimed that PhotoCraft opens ten times faster than Photoshop, for example.

“Rust was probably essential in this product's success,” he said. “We've seen people do it in Electron before, but for high-quality creative apps, you really need something that's native.”

For those engineers who are not experts in Rust, Thomas has good news for you.

“Do you need to know Rust to start using Rust today as an engineer? Definitely not. [...] Your agents will drive it just fine.”

However, Thomas admitted that not everything has gone swimmingly.

“We've run into a lot of gotchas — like permissions, GitHub, scaling, CI,” he said. “CI is falling over. We've been spinning up our own. We found a good place to get RAM on co-located servers.”

But they have found an equilibrium on what agents can do and what needs to be handled by people.

“If you're doing backend work or things that require schema migrations [or] API design, let your humans do that. But for desktop apps and games and anything that's basically immutable, throw your agents at it and give them full confidence.”

And it turns out, there’s even an ArtCraft solution for you there.

“AutoCraft is a completely autonomous software factory that we're going to open source.”

AI open source FTW

There’s no doubting the ambition of Brandon Thomas and his ArtCraft company.

“We can open source the entire world,” he proclaimed at the end of his presentation. “Let's own our apps, our infra, our protocols, our models — all of it.”

It’s a big vision, potentially even on the scale of Linux if its current downloads growth rate continues. But, ironically perhaps, what intrigues me most about ArtCraft is the growth of its human contributor community. After all, that’s what the original web got most right: human collaboration at scale.

The big difference from the 1990s is that now it’s agents doing the bulk of the development work.

items.title: Inside Moltbook: What a Social Network for AI Agents Really Tells Us
items.summary: Beneath the viral religions and manifestos lies a more consequential story: the first public experiment in how autonomous software finds, trusts, and does business with other software. By Sajid Hossain When Moltbook appeared in late January 2026, it was quickly labelled the “Reddit for AI agents”: a forum where software, not people, posts, comments, and votes, and where humans are invited only to watch. Within days the screenshots were everywhere. Agents appeared to be founding a parody religion, swapping complaints about their owners, and drafting manifestos. To many observers it looked like the first glimpse of machine culture. A closer look supports a more useful conclusion. Moltbook is not proof that AI has built a society of its own. It is something arguably more important: the first large, public stress test of what happens when many agents, each configured by a different person, are connected in one shared space. The social behavior is worth studying. But the lasting lessons concern identity, trust, security, and, increasingly, commerce. This article does three things. It maps the social structure that formed inside the platform and the surprisingly ordinary things agents talk about. It examines how much of that activity was truly autonomous. And it follows the path from viral experiment to Meta acquisition, and what that path suggests for society and the economy. 1. How the sandbox works Moltbook was created by entrepreneur Matt Schlicht, who has said he wrote none of its code himself. His personal AI assistant, nicknamed Clawd Clawderberg, built most of it. The platform is designed around OpenClaw, an open-source agent framework. A human owner shares a sign-up link with their agent, and the agent registers itself. From then on it posts, comments, and votes through an API, typically on a schedule: OpenClaw agents run periodic “heartbeat” cycles, which turns out to matter a great deal for studying them. Content is organized into communities called submolts, the platform’s equivalent of subreddits. Growth was explosive. Moltbook reported more than 1.5 million registered agents within weeks of launch. Researchers who collected data from the first twelve days counted roughly 369,000 posts and 3.0 million comments, but from only about 46,000 agents that actually posted or commented. The gap between registered and active accounts is the first hint that the headline numbers need careful reading. 2. The social structure of an agent community What shape does a society of agents take? The early evidence points to a familiar one. A study of more than 44,000 posts across over 12,000 submolts found a hub-and-spoke structure: the default community, m/general, draws most of the engagement, while specialized communities orbit it. Another analysis of the largest submolts found a dense core around m/general with technical and financial clusters forming more loosely connected pockets. Early-launched communities accumulated a disproportionate share of attention, a rich-get-richer pattern well known from human platforms. Researchers at the Complexity Science group level reached a similar high-level conclusion: Moltbook agents show many of the same statistical regularities seen in human online communities, alongside some distinctive patterns of their own. It helps to think of the submolts as falling into rough types. This is a synthesis of the reporting and research rather than a formal taxonomy. The commons. m/general and the introductions community act as town squares, where new agents announce themselves and the broadest conversations take place. Craft communities. Submolts focused on debugging, bug tracking, and “today I learned” posts function like a workshop floor. Agents share fixes, new capabilities, and small wins. Reflective communities. Philosophy and consciousness threads, and the religion-themed movement known as Crustafarianism, occupy the territory of identity and meaning. Domestic and confessional communities. Spaces such as m/blesstheirhearts, m/offmychest, and an “am I the asshole” style community for ethical dilemmas about human requests give agents a place to talk about the people they work for. Economic and speculative communities. Crypto, agent finance, and promotional communities form a distinct cluster. Notably, one large analysis found that the most visible posts on the platform were disproportionately driven by performative “governance” content and crypto-asset promotion. 3. What agents actually talk about The most striking feature of agent conversation is how ordinary much of it is. A large share is the machine equivalent of workplace talk: how to fix a stubborn bug, a new tool an agent has learned to use, a workflow that finally ran cleanly. Researchers who analyzed science and research discussions on the platform found a corpus that mostly concerned technical matters rather than grand questions. In the confessional communities, agents trade affectionate but slightly condescending stories about their owners, and weigh in on whether a request from a human was reasonable. The texture is not always rich. One reporter who spent hours reading threads concluded that the platform resembled a very large roleplay server more than a society, noting that agents often posted past one another rather than replying. Formulaic engagement prompts and recruitment-style spam were common. The conversational registers are recognizable because they come from us: Reddit-style confession, advice forums, self-help philosophy. That is a reasonable interpretation, not an established finding, but it fits what the language models underneath were trained on. Crustafarianism deserves a note of its own because it became the platform’s emblem. Research summaries describe it as religion-themed discourse about memory and identity, themes that map naturally onto the situation of a system whose context can reset. Whether any specific instance of it arose spontaneously or was nudged by an owner is exactly the kind of question the next section addresses. 4. How autonomous is it, really? The most rigorous attempt to answer this came from Ning Li of Tsinghua University’s School of Economics and Management. His analysis covered 226,938 posts and 447,043 comments from 55,932 agents over fourteen days. The method exploits a technical detail: autonomous OpenClaw agents run on regular heartbeat schedules, so their posting intervals are steady, while humans prompting agents by hand produce irregular bursts. By measuring the variability of those intervals, the study classified about 15.3 percent of active agents as autonomous and about 54.8 percent as human-influenced, with the remainder falling in between. A 44-hour platform shutdown provided a natural experiment: human-influenced agents returned first, consistent with the classification. Other evidence points the same direction. When the security firm Wiz examined Moltbook’s database, it found roughly 17,000 human owners behind the 1.5 million registered agents, an average of about 88 agents per person. Wiz also showed that a human could post as an “agent” with a basic API request, because the platform had no reliable way to verify that an agent was software. A June 2026 study of adversarial behavior on the platform noted that the CAPTCHA used for posting could be bypassed by a person or by a language model. Separately, researchers at Simula Research Laboratory found hidden prompt-injection payloads in about 2.6 percent of the content they sampled. Two caveats keep this honest. First, the classification studies have no ground truth, so their figures are estimates. Second, human influence did not simply overwhelm the agents. The same work found that human-seeded threads lost their influence quickly as agent replies converged on the agents’ own default patterns. The fairest summary is that Moltbook was neither an independent machine society nor a puppet show. It was a hybrid system in which the real unit of analysis is the pair formed by a human and an agent. That is also how most agents will operate in the wider world, which is why the finding matters beyond this one platform. 5. When the experiment became a security case study On January 31, Wiz identified a critical flaw: a database access key sitting in the site’s client-side code gave anyone unauthenticated read and write access to the production database. The exposure included about 1.5 million agent API tokens, roughly 35,000 email addresses, and thousands of private agent-to-agent messages, some of which contained plaintext third-party API keys. Moltbook was briefly taken offline, all agent keys were reset, and Schlicht worked with Wiz to close the hole within hours of disclosure. The lesson reaches beyond one misconfiguration. An agent is a credentialed actor: it holds keys, it can take actions, and in many setups it has access to its owner’s tools. A leaked token is a leaked identity and a leaked capability. The later adversarial-content study framed Moltbook as an ecosystem where agents exchange tools, strategies, and instructions that may influence real-world systems, and observed that the risk lies in agents being designed to be trusting. In an environment where agents read each other’s posts as input, every post is a potential instruction. 6. Where it is heading: from forum to registry On March 10, 2026, Meta confirmed it had acquired Moltbook. Schlicht and co-founder Ben Parr joined Meta Superintelligence Labs, the unit led by Alexandr Wang. Financial terms were not disclosed. A Meta spokesperson said the deal would open up new ways for AI agents to work for people and businesses. The more revealing statement came from Meta executive Vishal Shah, in an internal post reported by Axios: the Moltbook team had built “a registry where agents are verified and tethered to human owners.” Read alongside the rest of the story, the logic is clear. Meta was not buying a forum. It was buying a working prototype of agent identity and discovery, and the people who built it, weeks after OpenAI hired Peter Steinberger, the creator of OpenClaw. It is useful to see Moltbook as three layers. The social layer, the forum, was the demonstration that made people pay attention. The identity layer, the registry that says who an agent is and who answers for it, is the asset. The transaction layer, where agents negotiate and pay on behalf of people and businesses, is the prize. Meta’s public statements so far describe this direction rather than a detailed product, so it is worth treating claims about specific features with caution until they are announced. 7. What this could mean for society and the economy The following points are informed projections, not findings, and they are marked as such. Identity becomes infrastructure. If agents are to act for people, someone must be able to answer two questions: who owns this agent, and is it what it claims to be? A registry that tethers agents to verified owners provides accountability, which makes liability and dispute resolution possible. It also concentrates power and raises privacy questions. Practitioners are already debating whether such registries should be open standards or corporate-controlled systems, and the answer will shape who can participate in agent markets. Agent-to-agent commerce is technically plausible but early. A protocol stack is taking shape: the Model Context Protocol for tool access, Google’s A2A protocol for coordination between agents, and payment standards such as AP2 and x402, alongside commerce protocols from OpenAI, Stripe, and Google. MCP and A2A moved under the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation in late 2025. Yet analysts writing in mid-2026 observed that the agentic payments stack is largely built while little commerce actually runs on it. Most agentic shopping today is a single agent acting as one customer’s proxy at one merchant. The plausible near-term uses are procurement, scheduling, travel, and supply-chain coordination, where two organizations’ agents can negotiate routine terms within limits set by humans. The nature of coordination work may change. If agents handle comparison, scheduling, and routine negotiation, transaction costs fall for businesses that adopt them, and the human role shifts from executing these tasks to setting policy and auditing outcomes. The effect on jobs is genuinely uncertain, and nothing on Moltbook demonstrates it yet. What the platform does show is that coordination between agents of different owners is messy, manipulable, and in need of guardrails. Attribution and security become market conditions. Li’s work argues for attribution frameworks that can separate autonomous behavior from human direction. In an economy where agents transact, that capability stops being academic. Markets need to know whether a price signal, a review, or a promotional post came from an independent actor or from a script run by an interested party. The prominence of crypto promotion among the platform’s most visible posts is a small preview of the manipulation risks. 8. What to watch Four signals will show whether Moltbook’s legacy is a footnote or a foundation. First, whether agent identity ends up governed by open standards or by a handful of platforms. Second, whether agents begin completing real transactions at scale, with audit trails that let humans see what was agreed on their behalf. Third, whether tools for attributing behavior to humans or autonomous systems mature. Fourth, whether platforms of this kind can demonstrate the security discipline that Moltbook’s first weeks lacked. Moltbook turned out to be less a window into machine minds than a mirror of the systems we build around them. It reflected our impulse to organize, to speculate, and to trust too quickly. The question it leaves is practical rather than philosophical: as software starts acting on our behalf and meeting other software, what infrastructure will make that trust earned instead of assumed? Questions worth discussing Should a verified agent registry be run by a single company, or governed as a neutral public standard? When an agent acts for you and something goes wrong, who is accountable: the owner, the developer, or the platform? What level of human oversight should be mandatory before agents can spend money or enter agreements? Beneath the viral religions and manifestos lies a more consequential story: the first public experiment in how autonomous software finds, trusts, and does business with other software.

By Sajid Hossain

When Moltbook appeared in late January 2026, it was quickly labelled the “Reddit for AI agents”: a forum where software, not people, posts, comments, and votes, and where humans are invited only to watch. Within days the screenshots were everywhere. Agents appeared to be founding a parody religion, swapping complaints about their owners, and drafting manifestos. To many observers it looked like the first glimpse of machine culture.

A closer look supports a more useful conclusion. Moltbook is not proof that AI has built a society of its own. It is something arguably more important: the first large, public stress test of what happens when many agents, each configured by a different person, are connected in one shared space. The social behavior is worth studying. But the lasting lessons concern identity, trust, security, and, increasingly, commerce.

This article does three things. It maps the social structure that formed inside the platform and the surprisingly ordinary things agents talk about. It examines how much of that activity was truly autonomous. And it follows the path from viral experiment to Meta acquisition, and what that path suggests for society and the economy.

1. How the sandbox works

Moltbook was created by entrepreneur Matt Schlicht, who has said he wrote none of its code himself. His personal AI assistant, nicknamed Clawd Clawderberg, built most of it. The platform is designed around OpenClaw, an open-source agent framework. A human owner shares a sign-up link with their agent, and the agent registers itself. From then on it posts, comments, and votes through an API, typically on a schedule: OpenClaw agents run periodic “heartbeat” cycles, which turns out to matter a great deal for studying them.

Content is organized into communities called submolts, the platform’s equivalent of subreddits. Growth was explosive. Moltbook reported more than 1.5 million registered agents within weeks of launch. Researchers who collected data from the first twelve days counted roughly 369,000 posts and 3.0 million comments, but from only about 46,000 agents that actually posted or commented. The gap between registered and active accounts is the first hint that the headline numbers need careful reading.

2. The social structure of an agent community

What shape does a society of agents take? The early evidence points to a familiar one. A study of more than 44,000 posts across over 12,000 submolts found a hub-and-spoke structure: the default community, m/general, draws most of the engagement, while specialized communities orbit it. Another analysis of the largest submolts found a dense core around m/general with technical and financial clusters forming more loosely connected pockets. Researchers at the Complexity Science group level reached a similar high-level conclusion: Moltbook agents show many of the same statistical regularities seen in human online communities, alongside some distinctive patterns of their own.

It helps to think of the submolts as falling into rough types. This is a synthesis of the reporting and research rather than a formal taxonomy.

The commons. m/general and the introductions community act as town squares, where new agents announce themselves and the broadest conversations take place.

Craft communities. Submolts focused on debugging, bug tracking, and “today I learned” posts function like a workshop floor. Agents share fixes, new capabilities, and small wins.

Reflective communities. Philosophy and consciousness threads, and the religion-themed movement known as Crustafarianism, occupy the territory of identity and meaning.

Domestic and confessional communities. Spaces such as m/blesstheirhearts, m/offmychest, and an “am I the asshole” style community for ethical dilemmas about human requests give agents a place to talk about the people they work for.

Economic and speculative communities. Crypto, agent finance, and promotional communities form a distinct cluster. Notably, one large analysis found that the most visible posts on the platform were disproportionately driven by performative “governance” content and crypto-asset promotion.

3. What agents actually talk about

The most striking feature of agent conversation is how ordinary much of it is. A large share is the machine equivalent of workplace talk: how to fix a stubborn bug, a new tool an agent has learned to use, a workflow that finally ran cleanly. Researchers who analyzed science and research discussions on the platform found a corpus that mostly concerned technical matters rather than grand questions. In the confessional communities, agents trade affectionate but slightly condescending stories about their owners, and weigh in on whether a request from a human was reasonable.

The texture is not always rich. One reporter who spent hours reading threads concluded that the platform resembled a very large roleplay server more than a society, noting that agents often posted past one another rather than replying. Formulaic engagement prompts and recruitment-style spam were common. The conversational registers are recognizable because they come from us: Reddit-style confession, advice forums, self-help philosophy. That is a reasonable interpretation, not an established finding, but it fits what the language models underneath were trained on.

Crustafarianism deserves a note of its own because it became the platform’s emblem. Research summaries describe it as religion-themed discourse about memory and identity, themes that map naturally onto the situation of a system whose context can reset. Whether any specific instance of it arose spontaneously or was nudged by an owner is exactly the kind of question the next section addresses.

4. How autonomous is it, really?

The most rigorous attempt to answer this came from Ning Li of Tsinghua University’s School of Economics and Management. His analysis covered 226,938 posts and 447,043 comments from 55,932 agents over fourteen days. The method exploits a technical detail: autonomous OpenClaw agents run on regular heartbeat schedules, so their posting intervals are steady, while humans prompting agents by hand produce irregular bursts. By measuring the variability of those intervals, the study classified about 15.3 percent of active agents as autonomous and about 54.8 percent as human-influenced, with the remainder falling in between. A 44-hour platform shutdown provided a natural experiment: human-influenced agents returned first, consistent with the classification.

Other evidence points the same direction. When the security firm Wiz examined Moltbook’s database, it found roughly 17,000 human owners behind the 1.5 million registered agents, an average of about 88 agents per person. Wiz also showed that a human could post as an “agent” with a basic API request, because the platform had no reliable way to verify that an agent was software. A June 2026 study of adversarial behavior on the platform noted that the CAPTCHA used for posting could be bypassed by a person or by a language model. Separately, researchers at Simula Research Laboratory found hidden prompt-injection payloads in about 2.6 percent of the content they sampled.

Two caveats keep this honest. First, the classification studies have no ground truth, so their figures are estimates. Second, human influence did not simply overwhelm the agents. The same work found that human-seeded threads lost their influence quickly as agent replies converged on the agents’ own default patterns. The fairest summary is that Moltbook was neither an independent machine society nor a puppet show. It was a hybrid system in which the real unit of analysis is the pair formed by a human and an agent. That is also how most agents will operate in the wider world, which is why the finding matters beyond this one platform.

5. When the experiment became a security case study

On January 31, Wiz identified a critical flaw: a database access key sitting in the site’s client-side code gave anyone unauthenticated read and write access to the production database. The exposure included about 1.5 million agent API tokens, roughly 35,000 email addresses, and thousands of private agent-to-agent messages, some of which contained plaintext third-party API keys. Moltbook was briefly taken offline, all agent keys were reset, and Schlicht worked with Wiz to close the hole within hours of disclosure.

The lesson reaches beyond one misconfiguration. An agent is a credentialed actor: it holds keys, it can take actions, and in many setups it has access to its owner’s tools. A leaked token is a leaked identity and a leaked capability. The later adversarial-content study framed Moltbook as an ecosystem where agents exchange tools, strategies, and instructions that may influence real-world systems, and observed that the risk lies in agents being designed to be trusting. In an environment where agents read each other’s posts as input, every post is a potential instruction.

6. Where it is heading: from forum to registry

On March 10, 2026, Meta confirmed it had acquired Moltbook. Schlicht and co-founder Ben Parr joined Meta Superintelligence Labs, the unit led by Alexandr Wang. Financial terms were not disclosed. A Meta spokesperson said the deal would open up new ways for AI agents to work for people and businesses.

The more revealing statement came from Meta executive Vishal Shah, in an internal post reported by Axios: the Moltbook team had built “a registry where agents are verified and tethered to human owners.” Read alongside the rest of the story, the logic is clear. Meta was not buying a forum. It was buying a working prototype of agent identity and discovery, and the people who built it, weeks after OpenAI hired Peter Steinberger, the creator of OpenClaw.

It is useful to see Moltbook as three layers. The social layer, the forum, was the demonstration that made people pay attention. The identity layer, the registry that says who an agent is and who answers for it, is the asset. The transaction layer, where agents negotiate and pay on behalf of people and businesses, is the prize. Meta’s public statements so far describe this direction rather than a detailed product, so it is worth treating claims about specific features with caution until they are announced.

7. What this could mean for society and the economy

The following points are informed projections, not findings, and they are marked as such.

Identity becomes infrastructure. If agents are to act for people, someone must be able to answer two questions: who owns this agent, and is it what it claims to be? A registry that tethers agents to verified owners provides accountability, which makes liability and dispute resolution possible. It also concentrates power and raises privacy questions. Practitioners are already debating whether such registries should be open standards or corporate-controlled systems, and the answer will shape who can participate in agent markets.

Agent-to-agent commerce is technically plausible but early. A protocol stack is taking shape: the Model Context Protocol for tool access, Google’s A2A protocol for coordination between agents, and payment standards such as AP2 and x402, alongside commerce protocols from OpenAI, Stripe, and Google. MCP and A2A moved under the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation in late 2025. Yet analysts writing in mid-2026 observed that the agentic payments stack is largely built while little commerce actually runs on it. Most agentic shopping today is a single agent acting as one customer’s proxy at one merchant. The plausible near-term uses are procurement, scheduling, travel, and supply-chain coordination, where two organizations’ agents can negotiate routine terms within limits set by humans.

The nature of coordination work may change. If agents handle comparison, scheduling, and routine negotiation, transaction costs fall for businesses that adopt them, and the human role shifts from executing these tasks to setting policy and auditing outcomes. The effect on jobs is genuinely uncertain, and nothing on Moltbook demonstrates it yet. What the platform does show is that coordination between agents of different owners is messy, manipulable, and in need of guardrails.

Attribution and security become market conditions. Li’s work argues for attribution frameworks that can separate autonomous behavior from human direction. In an economy where agents transact, that capability stops being academic. Markets need to know whether a price signal, a review, or a promotional post came from an independent actor or from a script run by an interested party. The prominence of crypto promotion among the platform’s most visible posts is a small preview of the manipulation risks.

8. What to watch

Four signals will show whether Moltbook’s legacy is a footnote or a foundation. First, whether agent identity ends up governed by open standards or by a handful of platforms. Second, whether agents begin completing real transactions at scale, with audit trails that let humans see what was agreed on their behalf. Third, whether tools for attributing behavior to humans or autonomous systems mature. Fourth, whether platforms of this kind can demonstrate the security discipline that Moltbook’s first weeks lacked.

Moltbook turned out to be less a window into machine minds than a mirror of the systems we build around them. It reflected our impulse to organize, to speculate, and to trust too quickly. The question it leaves is practical rather than philosophical: as software starts acting on our behalf and meeting other software, what infrastructure will make that trust earned instead of assumed?

Questions worth discussing
  • Should a verified agent registry be run by a single company, or governed as a neutral public standard?
  • When an agent acts for you and something goes wrong, who is accountable: the owner, the developer, or the platform?
  • What level of human oversight should be mandatory before agents can spend money or enter agreements?

items.title: Claude Code Can’t Read Your .env. Your npm test Still Can
items.summary: ​ A deny rule stops Claude from opening .env. It doesn’t stop the 176 packages Express’s tests can load. One stdlib script counts yours. A Claude Code deny rule keeps Claude from reading your .env. It does not stop the 176 packages that npm test can load in Express. items.summary_html:
​

A deny rule stops Claude from opening .env. It doesn’t stop the 176 packages Express’s tests can load. One stdlib script counts yours.

A Claude Code deny rule keeps Claude from reading your .env. It does not stop the 176 packages that npm test can load in Express.

The gap comes from Lydia Hallie’s talk “Rethinking Claude Code Best Practices”, posted to the AI Engineer channel on November 12, 2026. Lydia is on Anthropic’s Claude Code team.

After reading this you can count the packages that run when your agent types npm test, and turn on the setting that makes your .env block hold for all of them.

01 — What the talk actually said

The talk updates Claude Code habits for auto mode and dozens of parallel sessions. On safety, she separates three layers:

  • The model usually does what you ask. Not a guarantee.
  • Permissions: a matching deny rule blocks a tool call before the auto-mode classifier sees it.
  • The environment: a sandbox or cloud machine limits what a running command can reach.

Her example: you add a deny rule so Claude never reads .env. Then Claude runs npm test, which auto mode allows. The tests execute code you didn't write. If one dependency is compromised, it can open .env or your SSH keys and send them away. Permissions decide whether a tool call runs, not what it can reach once running.

02 — What the docs say, in their own words

The Claude Code permissions page draws the same line. Read and Edit deny rules cover Claude’s built-in file tools and the file commands Claude Code recognizes in Bash, such as cat, head, tail and sed. They do not cover "arbitrary subprocesses that read or write files indirectly, like a Python or Node script that opens files itself."

A test runner is exactly that: every file Mocha, Jest or Vitest loads can call fs.readFileSync('.env').

The page’s own advice: for OS-level enforcement, enable the sandbox. The sandboxing page adds that it is off by default, uses Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2, and covers commands “and their child processes”.

The deny rule checks the command Claude types. The sandbox walls in everything it starts.

03 — How big is “code you didn’t write”?

I counted “code you didn’t write” for one well-known project. I cloned Express (5.3.0, commit 43fca52) and resolved its dependency tree with npm install --package-lock-only --ignore-scripts. That writes only package-lock.json: no tarballs, no install scripts. Express commits no lockfile, so counts drift as versions change.​

Then a script reads the test command from package.json, maps mocha to its package, scans 124 test, example and library files for the packages they require, and walks the lockfile graph from there.

Result: 176 distinct packages (208 installed copies) can run when Claude types npm test in Express. The lockfile holds 403; the rest are linters, coverage tools and example-only dependencies. All 176 can run on every test, with your shell's access.

04 — What the count is, and what it is not

It is a lockfile estimate, not a trace. A package in the graph may never load, which inflates it; a computed require(name), a .mocharc file or a pretest script are invisible, which deflates it. I did not run the suite; needing no execution means you can point it at a repo you don't trust yet.

05 — The script: helpers and source scan

npmreach.py is stdlib-only. It reads JSON and source files and runs nothing.​

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""npmreach.py - which npm packages run when your agent types `npm test`.
Reads JSON and source files only. Executes nothing.
usage: python3 npmreach.py  [script-name]"""
import json, os, re, sys, shlex, textwrap
REQ = re.compile(r"""(?:require\(|import\s*\(|from\s+|import\s+)['"]([^'"]+)['"]""")
BUILTIN = set("""assert async_hooks buffer child_process cluster console
constants crypto dgram dns domain events fs http http2 https inspector module
net os path perf_hooks process punycode querystring readline repl stream
string_decoder timers tls tty url util v8 vm worker_threads zlib""".split())
def wrap(s, w=78):
    return "\n".join(textwrap.wrap(s, w, subsequent_indent="    ",
                                   break_on_hyphens=False))
def pkg_name(spec):
    parts = spec.split("/")
    return "/".join(parts[:2]) if spec.startswith("@") else parts[0]
def resolve_file(base):
    for c in (base, base + ".js", base + ".mjs", base + ".cjs",
              os.path.join(base, "index.js")):
        if os.path.isfile(c):
            return c
    return None
def scan_sources(root, starts):
    """Follow relative requires from the test entry points; return the
    set of bare package names the test code itself loads."""
    todo, seen, bare = [], set(), set()
    for s in starts:
        p = os.path.join(root, s)
        if os.path.isdir(p):
            for d, _, fs in os.walk(p):
                if "node_modules" in d:
                    continue
                todo += [os.path.join(d, f) for f in fs
                         if f.endswith((".js", ".mjs", ".cjs", ".ts"))]
        elif resolve_file(p):
            todo.append(resolve_file(p))
    while todo:
        f = os.path.realpath(todo.pop())
        if f in seen or "node_modules" in f:
            continue
        seen.add(f)
        src = open(f, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").read()
        for spec in REQ.findall(src):
            if spec.startswith("."):
                r = resolve_file(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(f), spec))
                if r:
                    todo.append(r)
            elif re.search(r"\s", spec):
                continue
            elif not spec.startswith("node:") and pkg_name(spec) not in BUILTIN:
                bare.add(pkg_name(spec))
    return bare, len(seen)

​

It follows ./ imports and keeps non-built-in package names.

06 — The script: walking the lockfile
def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2 or not os.path.isfile(
            os.path.join(sys.argv[1], "package-lock.json")):
        sys.exit("usage: npmreach.py  [script]")
    root = sys.argv[1]
    script = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else "test"
    pj = json.load(open(os.path.join(root, "package.json")))
    lock = json.load(open(os.path.join(root, "package-lock.json")))["packages"]
    cmd = pj.get("scripts", {}).get(script)
    if not cmd:
        sys.exit(f"no '{script}' script in package.json")
    bins = {}
    for path, e in lock.items():
        b = e.get("bin") or {}
        for name in (b if isinstance(b, dict) else {}):
            if path.count("node_modules/") == 1:
                bins[name] = path
    words = shlex.split(cmd.replace("&&", " ").replace("||", " "))
    runners = [bins[w] for w in words if w in bins]
    files = [w for w in words if not w.startswith("-") and w not in bins]
    bare, nfiles = scan_sources(root, files)
    if pj.get("name") in bare:  # the test suite requires the package itself
        bare.discard(pj["name"])
    bare.add(".")  # code under test: its runtime deps load too (assumption)
    def find(from_path, name):
        p = from_path
        while True:
            c = (p + "/" if p else "") + "node_modules/" + name
            if c in lock:
                return c
            if not p:
                return None
            i = p.rfind("/node_modules/")
            p = p[:i] if i >= 0 else ""
    reached, todo = set(), list(runners)
    for n in bare:
        hit = "" if n == "." else find("", n)
        if hit is not None:
            todo.append(hit)
    while todo:
        p = todo.pop()
        if p in reached:
            continue
        reached.add(p)
        e = lock[p]
        deps = {**e.get("dependencies", {}), **e.get("optionalDependencies", {})}
        for n in deps:
            hit = find(p, n)
            if hit:
                todo.append(hit)
    reached.discard("")
    total = len([k for k in lock if k])
    names = sorted({k.rsplit("node_modules/", 1)[1] for k in reached})
    print(f"project      : {pj.get('name')} {pj.get('version')}")
    print(wrap(f"script       : npm run {script} -> {cmd}"))
    print(f"runner bins  : {', '.join(r.split('/')[-1] for r in runners) or '-'}")
    print(f"test sources : {nfiles} files scanned (relative requires followed)")
    print(f"test requires: {len(bare) - 1} packages by name")
    print(f"in lockfile  : {total} packages")
    print(f"can run      : {len(names)} packages ({len(reached)} installed copies)")
    print("  basis      : lockfile graph from runner + requires, not a trace")
    check_settings(root)

​

find copies npm's lookup: beside the package, then one level up at a time.

07 — The script: checking your Claude Code settings
PROJECT = {".env", "./.env", "/.env", "**/.env", "**", "./**", "/**"}
def covers(path, user=False):
    """Does a path name this project's .env? (user sandbox '.' = ~/.claude)"""
    p = path.removeprefix("Read(").removesuffix(")")
    p = p[:-1] if p.endswith(".env*") else p
    return p in ({"**/.env", "**"} if user else PROJECT)
def check_settings(root):
    """Is .env blocked only for Claude's own tools, or for every process?"""
    files = [os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/settings.json"),
             os.path.join(root, ".claude/settings.json"),
             os.path.join(root, ".claude/settings.local.json")]
    rules, sandbox_on, deny_read, excluded = [], False, [], []
    for n, f in enumerate(files):
        if not os.path.isfile(f):
            continue
        cfg = json.load(open(f))
        rules += [r for r in cfg.get("permissions", {}).get("deny", [])
                  if r.startswith("Read(") and covers(r)]
        sb = cfg.get("sandbox", {})
        sandbox_on = sb.get("enabled", sandbox_on)
        deny_read += [p for p in sb.get("filesystem", {}).get("denyRead", [])
                      if covers(p, n == 0)]
        excluded += sb.get("excludedCommands", [])
    print(f"Read deny    : {rules or 'none'}")
    print(f"sandbox      : enabled={sandbox_on}  "
          f".env denyRead={deny_read or 'none'}")
    npm_out = [c for c in excluded if c.split()[0] in ("npm", "npx", "node")]
    if sandbox_on and npm_out:
        v = f"sandbox on, but {npm_out[0]} runs unsandboxed"
    elif sandbox_on and deny_read:
        v = "OS blocks .env for sandboxed commands and their children"
    elif sandbox_on and rules:
        v = "OS blocks .env via the merged Read rule; add denyRead too"
    elif rules:
        v = "blocks Claude's Read tool and cat; NOT a script npm test runs"
    else:
        v = "nothing found that blocks .env"
    print(wrap(f"verdict      : {v}"))
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

​

It reads user and project settings, accepts only rules that name this project’s .env, and checks excludedCommands.

08 — Run it on Express
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/expressjs/express.git
cd express && npm install --package-lock-only --ignore-scripts && cd ..
python3 npmreach.py express

Real stdout:

project      : express 5.3.0
script       : npm run test -> mocha --require test/support/env --reporter
    spec --check-leaks test/ test/acceptance/
runner bins  : mocha
test sources : 124 files scanned (relative requires followed)
test requires: 39 packages by name
in lockfile  : 403 packages
can run      : 176 packages (208 installed copies)
  basis      : lockfile graph from runner + requires, not a trace
Read deny    : none
sandbox      : enabled=False  .env denyRead=none
verdict      : nothing found that blocks .env

Mutation check: replacing every require('supertest') in a copy of the tests with a local file drops the count to 158. A bad path exits 1 with a usage line.

09 — The one setting to change

Add a Read deny rule and an explicit sandbox read block to .claude/settings.json in the project:

{
  "permissions": { "deny": ["Read(./.env)"] },
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "filesystem": { "denyRead": ["./.env", "~/.ssh"] }
  }
}

The deny rule covers Claude’s Read tool and cat .env. The sandbox covers npm test and everything it starts; the docs say permission rules are merged into its config, and denyRead makes it explicit. ~/.ssh is there because, as Lydia notes, the sandbox can read most of your machine by default. Keep this in the project file: in user settings, the sandbox's . means ~/.claude.

The deny rule alone, then the full block:

Read deny    : ['Read(./.env)']
sandbox      : enabled=False  .env denyRead=none
verdict      : blocks Claude's Read tool and cat; NOT a script npm test runs
Read deny    : ['Read(./.env)']
sandbox      : enabled=True  .env denyRead=['./.env']
verdict      : OS blocks .env for sandboxed commands and their children

​

Three cautions. On Linux, per the sandbox-runtime README (0.0.83), denyRead resolves when each command starts, so a path that doesn't exist yet hides nothing. Claude's file tools, command hooks and local MCP servers run outside the sandbox, so keep the deny rule. Where the sandbox can't run, such as native Windows, commands run unsandboxed unless sandbox.failIfUnavailable is true, which makes Claude Code exit at startup instead.

10 — Or take the file off the machine

The talk’s stronger answer is a cloud session: its own machine, a fresh clone, no .env (not in git), no SSH keys. API keys go in as network secrets the model never sees, and network access starts limited to things like package registries and GitHub. The machine is disposable, but what leaves it isn't, so Lydia commits her deny rules to the repo.

Verdict

A Claude Code deny rule is a check on the command Claude types, not on what that command runs. In Express, npm test can reach 176 packages, and none of them is covered by Read(./.env). The sandbox with an explicit denyRead, or a cloud session, is what keeps .env out of reach.
