items.title: THIRSTDAY #11: HOW MUCH OF THAT AI REVENUE IS NEW BUSINESS?
items.summary: As software companies put AI figures into their earnings reports, investors need a clearer view of what customers purchased, what they actually used, and how the economics of serving them are changing. A reported AI revenue figure can contain both separate purchases and value allocated inside subscriptions. Understanding those sources helps investors distinguish additional demand from changes in product packaging. A software company can add AI credits to an existing subscription without increasing the customer’s bill. The feature may still be useful, and it might help persuade the customer to renew, although the commercial outcome differs from selling that customer a separate AI product for another $20,000 a year. When both arrangements contribute to an AI revenue metric, an investor needs to understand which transaction took place before deciding what the number says about demand. That distinction became unusually concrete on November 9 , when monday.com reported $36 million in AI annual recurring revenue (AI ARR) alongside $377.5 million in third-quarter revenue . The company defines AI ARR as the annualized recurring value of standalone AI products, subscription-term AI credit packages, and a portion of existing subscription plans allocated to included AI credits according to relative list prices. One-time purchases and overages are excluded. The allocation is made specifically for calculating AI ARR. ( monday.com, Q3 2026 results ) This is unusually helpful disclosure, although those two headline figures measure different things: AI ARR is an annualized component of contracted recurring business, not $36 million earned during the quarter , while the $377.5 million is recognized quarterly revenue across the company. Neither figure can simply be added to the other. The question is also one analysts are asking rather than an objection invented for this article. During the earnings call, an analyst requested a breakdown of the $36 million between standalone products, separately purchased credits and allocations inside subscription plans. Management described strong uptake of credit packages, particularly among larger customers, and said that more than 30% of accounts in the $50,000-plus segment pay for and use AI credits. Those are meaningful signals of paid adoption, although the call did not provide the requested dollar-by-dollar split of the three categories. ( Q3 earnings-call transcript ) The same hypothetical $24,000 attributed to AI can leave annual spending unchanged or increase it by $24,000; these are different customer decisions, not claims about a named company’s contracts. 💧 What I want is a comparable description of the AI business that distinguishes additional customer spending from allocation within an existing contract, while showing whether customers keep using the product and what it costs to serve them. One AI number can describe two different customer decisions Consider two hypothetical annual contracts. In the first, a company already pays $120,000 for software, and its renewed plan includes AI credits without changing that total. The vendor assigns $24,000 of the plan’s value to the AI component for reporting purposes. The customer is still paying $120,000, although that allocation may describe a capability that helps the vendor defend the renewal. In the second example, the customer keeps its existing $120,000 plan and independently buys a $24,000 AI add-on , lifting its total annual spending to $144,000 . Both contracts can have $24,000 associated with AI, but only the second demonstrates $24,000 of additional contracted spending in that particular transaction. These examples are illustrative, not claims about monday.com’s customer contracts or the composition of its $36 million figure. The distinction matters because the first arrangement might generate value through retention or pricing power, while the second provides more direct evidence that a buyer chose to increase its budget for AI. A useful investor note should allow both to be seen without declaring one arrangement superior. The company bundling AI may be protecting a large, durable subscription business; the company selling a separate add-on must show that customers continue to value the additional purchase. Those routes have different economics and different evidence requirements, even when the marketing language sounds similar. The category itself can change while the business grows Salesforce illustrates a related measurement issue. For its fiscal 2027 second quarter, ended July 31, 2026, it reported nearly $3.9 billion in combined Agentforce and Data 360 ARR , including more than $1.5 billion in Agentforce ARR . From that quarter, the Agentforce definition also included its AI offerings, Slackbot and Headless 360. ( Salesforce’s FY27 Q2 results and definitions ) The $1.5 billion is part of the $3.9 billion combined measure; it is not another amount to add on top. The revised product scope also means that an apparently straightforward growth comparison needs to be read alongside the definitions in effect during each period. I would not compare Salesforce’s combined Agentforce and Data 360 ARR directly with monday.com’s AI ARR as though both were measuring identical products. Each company supplies useful information about its own commercial development, but the boundaries differ, and an investor should understand those boundaries before drawing conclusions about relative momentum. The concern here is not that a company has reorganized its products around AI. That can reflect a genuine change in what customers are buying. The analytical problem arises when an expanded category and expanding demand are described by the same growth line without enough information to distinguish them. Usage is useful evidence, although consumption is not the whole business A contracted allowance does not tell us whether a customer has meaningfully adopted the feature. Some teams purchase credits before a rollout, while others consume them quickly during a trial and reduce usage later. A busy month can therefore signal genuine demand without proving that the next quarter will look the same. ChartMogul’s October 19 usage-based billing guide separates usage revenue , usage MRR and contracted commitments because the figures answer different questions. A customer can commit to $120,000 over a year, consume $12,000 of service in February, and still have only one contractual commitment rather than two independent revenue streams. The guide also recommends watching paid consumption, changes by customer cohort and whether usage persists beyond isolated spikes. For AI products, I would want to see how many paying accounts continue using what they bought, how their consumption develops after introductory credits, and what happens at renewal. At the same time, usage is an imperfect proxy for value: a better model or more efficient workflow may deliver the same customer outcome with fewer tokens, so falling consumption does not automatically imply that the product became less useful. This is why commercially meaningful adoption needs several kinds of evidence, rather than one cumulative count of prompts, agents or work units. A high activity number may show that people use the service; it does not automatically establish what they pay, what they will renew or how much that work costs the provider. The next question is what remains after delivery If an AI feature increases engagement while its price stays unchanged, the company may have improved retention, but the financial benefit depends partly on the cost of providing the new work. Inference, retrieval, hosting and human intervention can all become material costs, especially when consumption expands faster than pricing. A product-level contribution measure would help if its scope were stated clearly, including what belongs in direct delivery costs and what remains excluded. There is no need to allocate every corporate research expense to every product; such allocations can create false precision. What matters is whether the same definition is used consistently enough to show how the economics move as adoption grows. I would also separate acquisition expenses from delivery costs. Selling an AI product and serving it are different problems, while a company can have strong margins on usage but expensive sales, or a remarkably effective distribution channel supporting an expensive service. Investors need to know which part of the business is being tested before calling the model sustainable. What a better AI economics note would look like The underlying systems largely exist already. Billing services distinguish contracts from consumption, product telemetry records activity, and financial reporting provides revenue and cost information. The missing convenience is a consistent public connection between them, with enough context that figures from different companies do not silently acquire the same meaning. +----------------------------+----------------------------+ | WHAT WAS PURCHASED | WHAT WAS USED | | Extra spend, allocations, | Paid accounts, consumption,| | credits, contract terms | renewals, contraction | +----------------------------+----------------------------+ | WHAT IT COST TO SERVE | WHAT CHANGED IN SCOPE | | Direct costs and explicit | Product definitions and | | exclusions | comparable history | +----------------------------+----------------------------+ This would be a supplementary analytical note, not another number to add to the financial statements or a compulsory formula for every business model. It would also let an early product explain what remains uncertain, instead of forcing every new AI capability to compete on an inflated-looking annualized headline. 📦 THIRSTDAY INVENTORY #11 🧱 IN STOCK Defined AI metrics. Companies such as monday.com and Salesforce disclose how their reported AI categories are constructed, including included products and allocation rules. Billing and usage analytics. Existing software can track recurring commitments, credits, consumption, invoices, upgrades and contractions. Product activity and financial reporting. Internal systems can measure usage, while statutory and management accounts describe the wider business. 🟧 STILL TO ESTABLISH Comparable purchase mix. How much of the AI category reflects a separate decision to spend more, rather than value attributed within existing contracts? Cohort continuity. Do customers keep paying and using the product when credits expire, adoption matures and renewals arrive? Clearly bounded delivery economics. Which direct costs accompany usage, and how consistently are they reported? Continuity across changing definitions. When the AI category expands, can readers separate a measurement change from an underlying commercial change? These are goals for comparable disclosure, not claims that the technology to measure them is unavailable or that every company lacks each component. Reporting definitions, billing records and product telemetry already exist, while comparable purchase mix, cohort continuity, service costs and consistent historical scope remain harder to establish publicly. The number should lead back to a customer decision AI features can create value through direct purchases, more durable subscriptions, higher renewal prices or lower costs elsewhere in the customer’s business. Because those effects differ, a financial headline becomes more persuasive when it tells the reader which commercial behavior actually changed. The challenge for investors is not to prove that all AI revenue is incremental, since there are legitimate reasons to bundle new capabilities into an existing product. It is to avoid treating every dollar assigned to AI as if it represented an identical decision by the customer, and to interpret impressive usage figures alongside continuing paid demand and delivery economics. For the next AI earnings announcement, I would therefore ask a fairly ordinary question before celebrating the growth rate: what changed in the customer’s bill, what did the customer keep using, and what did the supplier have to spend to deliver it? A business that can answer those questions consistently gives investors something more useful than another attractive number. THIRSTDAY #11: HOW MUCH OF THAT AI REVENUE IS NEW BUSINESS? was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: 12 GitHub Repos That Turn AI Into Your Slide, Report and Marketing Team (No Coding Needed)
items.summary: Part 2: free, open-source skill packs that make Claude, Codex and OpenCode build decks, reports, dashboards, SVG graphics, web pages and campaigns from plain-English requests. Alt text: Part 2 cover: “No coding needed.” with a skills folder fanning out reports, data, slides, ads and video cards. Copy alt Here is the strange part of the 2026 AI boom: some of the most-starred things on GitHub are not software. They are folders of plain-text instructions. And a growing number of them have nothing to do with code. They make slide decks, reports, landing pages, ad copy, dashboards and videos. Part 1 was for people who write code. This one is for everyone else: marketers, founders, consultants, teachers, analysts, anyone who builds things in PowerPoint, Excel, Google Docs and a browser all day. You do not need to be a developer. If you can type a request into a chat box, you can use every repo below. What a “skill” is, in 30 seconds A skill is a folder with one instruction file inside. It teaches an AI agent how to do one job well, a bit like a recipe card. The agent reads it only when your request matches the job, so it costs you nothing until it is needed. The same skill folder works across Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, and many of them also work in Cursor and Gemini CLI. Claude.ai can use them too, if you upload the folder as a zip in the Skills settings. How to install one without touching code There are three ways, from easiest to slightly less easy. 1. Paste the link. Open Claude Code, or the Code tab in the Claude desktop app, paste the repo’s GitHub link and write: “Install this skill: [link].” The agent does the rest. 2. One copy-paste line. Most repos below show a command that starts with npx skills add. Paste it into the agent’s terminal and press Enter. The same line installs the skill for Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode. 3. Upload a zip in Claude.ai. Zip the skill folder and add it under the Skills settings. Code execution needs to be switched on. Three ways to install a skill. Pick one. Read this before you install anything Popular does not mean safe. An NVIDIA analysis of more than 31,000 public skills, as reported by Walma AI, found vulnerabilities in about a quarter of them and likely malicious intent in about 5%. Three habits cover most of the risk. Stick to well-known repos. Before installing, ask your agent: “Read this skill and tell me if it sends data anywhere or runs anything hidden.” And if you are comfortable with a scanner, NVIDIA’s open-source SkillSpector checks a skill before it lands on your machine. One more rule: install two or three skills, not twenty. Every installed skill puts a short description in the agent’s working memory, and overlapping skills compete with each other. A note on stars. They measure attention, not quality. The counts below are approximate, taken from public snapshots between mid-2026 and early November 2026. The whole list on one page Find the job you need done, then jump to the repos in that card. Find your job, then jump to the repos in that card. The file makers: slides, reports, spreadsheets 1. anthropics/skills (about 181K stars) The official collection, and the single most useful one for office work. Its document skills create and edit Word files, Excel sheets with real formulas, PowerPoint decks and PDFs, including filling in PDF forms. The same repo has skills for applying a brand or colour theme to anything you make, writing status updates and newsletters, and designing posters. Try it with: “Turn these meeting notes into a 10-slide PowerPoint for my manager. Start with a one-slide summary.” Install: /plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills, then /plugin install document-skills@anthropic-agent-skills. In Claude.ai these skills are already there; switch them on in Skills settings. The catch: the four document skills are source-available, not fully open. You can use them freely with Claude, but you cannot fork them into your own product. 2. zarazhangrui/frontend-slides (about 27K stars) This one makes decks that live in the browser, with smooth animation and a real sense of design. It was built for people who are not designers: it shows you style previews first, then builds the full deck in the one you pick. It can also convert an existing PowerPoint into a web presentation. Try it with: “Build a 12-slide pitch deck for my bakery’s wholesale expansion. Show me three style options first.” Install: npx skills add https://github.com/zarazhangrui/frontend-slides --skill frontend-slides The catch: the result is a web page, not a .pptx file. You present from a browser. If someone insists on a PowerPoint file, use repo #1. 3. nexu-io/open-design (about 90K stars) Anthropic launched Claude Design in April 2026 as a paid-plan product that turns prompts into prototypes, decks and one-pagers. Eleven days later, this open-source alternative appeared. Open Design is a desktop app for macOS and Windows that turns the agent you already use into a design studio. It makes prototypes, landing pages, dashboards, slides, images and video, and exports to HTML, PDF, PPTX and MP4. It ships with hundreds of skills and more than 140 ready-made brand styles. Try it with: “Design a one-page landing page for my yoga studio, then export it as a PDF.” Install: download the desktop app from the repo, then point it at the agent you already have. The catch: it is the interface, not the AI. You still need Claude Code, Codex or another supported agent (or an API key) set up first. The project also moves fast, so expect a few rough edges between releases. Make it look designed: web pages, HTML and video 4. nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill (about 135K stars) AI-built web pages tend to look the same. This skill fixes that by giving the agent a searchable library of styles, colour palettes, font pairings and usability rules to consult while it builds. It is the one to try for a full site: a landing page, a portfolio, a small-business homepage. Try it with: “Build a landing page for my photography business. Warm, editorial, mobile-first.” Install: /plugin marketplace add nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill, then /plugin install ui-ux-pro-max@ui-ux-pro-max-skill The catch: use one design skill per project. Two sets of taste rules average out into the generic look you were trying to escape. 5. Leonxlnx/taste-skill (about 95K stars) A second answer to the same problem, from a different angle. Instead of one big rulebook, it is a family of variants: minimalist, brutalist, soft, redesign and image-to-code. You pick a direction instead of asking for “make it good.” Try it with: “Use taste-skill, minimalist variant, to redesign this page.” Install: npx skills add https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill The catch: same rule as #4. My suggestion: start with ui-ux-pro-max for a whole new site, and reach for taste-skill when you already have a page that looks generic. 6. heygen-com/hyperframes (20K+ stars and climbing fast) You describe a video. The agent writes it as an HTML page and renders it to MP4. It is built by HeyGen and designed for agents from day one. Product intros, explainer clips and social posts all work, and the README’s own example turns an attached PDF into a 45-second pitch video. Try it with: “Summarize the attached PDF into a 45-second pitch video using /hyperframes.” Install: npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes The catch: this is the most technical repo on the list. Rendering runs on your own computer and needs Node.js and video tools set up first, so expect one proper setup session. Its inspiration, Remotion, uses React and needs a paid licence above small-team thresholds. Marketing, SEO and writing 7. coreyhaines31/marketingskills (about 58K stars) About fifty skills that give the agent real marketing knowledge: copywriting, conversion optimization, SEO audits, email sequences, ads, pricing, launches and analytics tracking. It comes from Corey Haines, who runs Swipe Files and Conversion Factory, and it is MIT-licensed. You do not memorize commands. You describe the job, and the right skill picks itself up. Try it with: “Audit my homepage for conversion problems, then rewrite the top section.” Install: npx skills add coreyhaines31/marketingskills The catch: it knows how to write an ad, but not how your ads performed last week. Live numbers from Google Ads or Analytics need a separate connection. And install only the few skills you need, not all fifty. 8. AgriciDaniel/claude-seo (about 4K stars) A smaller, SEO-only toolkit for auditing a site and its content. It is a good fit when marketingskills is more than you need and you just want a focused SEO pass. Try it with: “Audit this page’s SEO and list the five fixes that matter most.” Install: use the paste-the-link method from earlier. The repo’s README has the exact command for your agent. The catch: a much smaller community than the big repos here. Run the “read it first” check from the safety section before you install it. 9. blader/humanizer (about 56K stars) It rewrites text to remove the patterns that make AI writing obvious: the “it’s not X, it’s Y” construction, forced lists of three, dashes everywhere and inflated vocabulary. Run it on LinkedIn posts, emails, ad copy and newsletters after the first draft. Try it with: “Humanize this LinkedIn post. Keep my meaning and my numbers.” Install: /plugin marketplace add blader/humanizer, then /plugin install humanizer@humanizer The catch: it fixes style, not facts. Check your claims yourself. And pick this or the similar stop-slop skill, not both, because two sets of style rules make the model second-guess itself. Research and organizing 10. mvanhorn/last30days-skill (about 64K stars) A research assistant for “what are people actually saying about this right now?” Out of the box it searches Reddit, Hacker News, GitHub and Polymarket. With extra keys it adds X and YouTube. It scores what it finds by engagement and writes everything up as one brief. Try it with: “What have people said about standing desks in the last 30 days? Give me a one-page brief with the top complaints.” Install: /plugin marketplace add mvanhorn/last30days-skill, then /plugin install last30days The catch: it is strong on discussion and weaker where the answer lives in official documentation. X and YouTube need API keys. 11. kepano/obsidian-skills (about 49K stars) From Obsidian’s CEO. It teaches the agent how Obsidian stores notes, so it can work directly inside your notes vault: reading, linking, organizing and writing in Obsidian’s own formats. Part 2: free, open-source skill packs that make Claude, Codex and OpenCode build decks, reports, dashboards, SVG graphics, web pages and campaigns from plain-English requests.

Alt text: Part 2 cover: “No coding needed.” with a skills folder fanning out reports, data, slides, ads and video cards. Copy alt

Here is the strange part of the 2026 AI boom: some of the most-starred things on GitHub are not software. They are folders of plain-text instructions. And a growing number of them have nothing to do with code. They make slide decks, reports, landing pages, ad copy, dashboards and videos.

Part 1 was for people who write code. This one is for everyone else: marketers, founders, consultants, teachers, analysts, anyone who builds things in PowerPoint, Excel, Google Docs and a browser all day.

You do not need to be a developer. If you can type a request into a chat box, you can use every repo below.

What a “skill” is, in 30 seconds

A skill is a folder with one instruction file inside. It teaches an AI agent how to do one job well, a bit like a recipe card. The agent reads it only when your request matches the job, so it costs you nothing until it is needed.

The same skill folder works across Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, and many of them also work in Cursor and Gemini CLI. Claude.ai can use them too, if you upload the folder as a zip in the Skills settings.

How to install one without touching code

There are three ways, from easiest to slightly less easy.

1. Paste the link. Open Claude Code, or the Code tab in the Claude desktop app, paste the repo’s GitHub link and write: “Install this skill: [link].” The agent does the rest.

2. One copy-paste line. Most repos below show a command that starts with npx skills add. Paste it into the agent’s terminal and press Enter. The same line installs the skill for Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode.

3. Upload a zip in Claude.ai. Zip the skill folder and add it under the Skills settings. Code execution needs to be switched on.

Three ways to install a skill. Pick one.Read this before you install anything

Popular does not mean safe. An NVIDIA analysis of more than 31,000 public skills, as reported by Walma AI, found vulnerabilities in about a quarter of them and likely malicious intent in about 5%.

Three habits cover most of the risk. Stick to well-known repos. Before installing, ask your agent: “Read this skill and tell me if it sends data anywhere or runs anything hidden.” And if you are comfortable with a scanner, NVIDIA’s open-source SkillSpector checks a skill before it lands on your machine.

One more rule: install two or three skills, not twenty. Every installed skill puts a short description in the agent’s working memory, and overlapping skills compete with each other.

A note on stars. They measure attention, not quality. The counts below are approximate, taken from public snapshots between mid-2026 and early November 2026.

The whole list on one page

Find the job you need done, then jump to the repos in that card.

Find your job, then jump to the repos in that card.The file makers: slides, reports, spreadsheets1. anthropics/skills (about 181K stars)

The official collection, and the single most useful one for office work. Its document skills create and edit Word files, Excel sheets with real formulas, PowerPoint decks and PDFs, including filling in PDF forms. The same repo has skills for applying a brand or colour theme to anything you make, writing status updates and newsletters, and designing posters.

Try it with: “Turn these meeting notes into a 10-slide PowerPoint for my manager. Start with a one-slide summary.”

Install: /plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills, then /plugin install document-skills@anthropic-agent-skills. In Claude.ai these skills are already there; switch them on in Skills settings.

The catch: the four document skills are source-available, not fully open. You can use them freely with Claude, but you cannot fork them into your own product.

2. zarazhangrui/frontend-slides (about 27K stars)

This one makes decks that live in the browser, with smooth animation and a real sense of design. It was built for people who are not designers: it shows you style previews first, then builds the full deck in the one you pick. It can also convert an existing PowerPoint into a web presentation.

Try it with: “Build a 12-slide pitch deck for my bakery’s wholesale expansion. Show me three style options first.”

Install: npx skills add https://github.com/zarazhangrui/frontend-slides --skill frontend-slides

The catch: the result is a web page, not a .pptx file. You present from a browser. If someone insists on a PowerPoint file, use repo #1.

3. nexu-io/open-design (about 90K stars)

Anthropic launched Claude Design in April 2026 as a paid-plan product that turns prompts into prototypes, decks and one-pagers. Eleven days later, this open-source alternative appeared. Open Design is a desktop app for macOS and Windows that turns the agent you already use into a design studio. It makes prototypes, landing pages, dashboards, slides, images and video, and exports to HTML, PDF, PPTX and MP4. It ships with hundreds of skills and more than 140 ready-made brand styles.

Try it with: “Design a one-page landing page for my yoga studio, then export it as a PDF.”

Install: download the desktop app from the repo, then point it at the agent you already have.

The catch: it is the interface, not the AI. You still need Claude Code, Codex or another supported agent (or an API key) set up first. The project also moves fast, so expect a few rough edges between releases.

Make it look designed: web pages, HTML and video4. nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill (about 135K stars)

AI-built web pages tend to look the same. This skill fixes that by giving the agent a searchable library of styles, colour palettes, font pairings and usability rules to consult while it builds. It is the one to try for a full site: a landing page, a portfolio, a small-business homepage.

Try it with: “Build a landing page for my photography business. Warm, editorial, mobile-first.”

Install: /plugin marketplace add nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill, then /plugin install ui-ux-pro-max@ui-ux-pro-max-skill

The catch: use one design skill per project. Two sets of taste rules average out into the generic look you were trying to escape.

5. Leonxlnx/taste-skill (about 95K stars)

A second answer to the same problem, from a different angle. Instead of one big rulebook, it is a family of variants: minimalist, brutalist, soft, redesign and image-to-code. You pick a direction instead of asking for “make it good.”

Try it with: “Use taste-skill, minimalist variant, to redesign this page.”

Install: npx skills add https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill

The catch: same rule as #4. My suggestion: start with ui-ux-pro-max for a whole new site, and reach for taste-skill when you already have a page that looks generic.

6. heygen-com/hyperframes (20K+ stars and climbing fast)

You describe a video. The agent writes it as an HTML page and renders it to MP4. It is built by HeyGen and designed for agents from day one. Product intros, explainer clips and social posts all work, and the README’s own example turns an attached PDF into a 45-second pitch video.

Try it with: “Summarize the attached PDF into a 45-second pitch video using /hyperframes.”

Install: npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The catch: this is the most technical repo on the list. Rendering runs on your own computer and needs Node.js and video tools set up first, so expect one proper setup session. Its inspiration, Remotion, uses React and needs a paid licence above small-team thresholds.

Marketing, SEO and writing7. coreyhaines31/marketingskills (about 58K stars)

About fifty skills that give the agent real marketing knowledge: copywriting, conversion optimization, SEO audits, email sequences, ads, pricing, launches and analytics tracking. It comes from Corey Haines, who runs Swipe Files and Conversion Factory, and it is MIT-licensed. You do not memorize commands. You describe the job, and the right skill picks itself up.

Try it with: “Audit my homepage for conversion problems, then rewrite the top section.”

Install: npx skills add coreyhaines31/marketingskills

The catch: it knows how to write an ad, but not how your ads performed last week. Live numbers from Google Ads or Analytics need a separate connection. And install only the few skills you need, not all fifty.

8. AgriciDaniel/claude-seo (about 4K stars)

A smaller, SEO-only toolkit for auditing a site and its content. It is a good fit when marketingskills is more than you need and you just want a focused SEO pass.

Try it with: “Audit this page’s SEO and list the five fixes that matter most.”

Install: use the paste-the-link method from earlier. The repo’s README has the exact command for your agent.

The catch: a much smaller community than the big repos here. Run the “read it first” check from the safety section before you install it.

9. blader/humanizer (about 56K stars)

It rewrites text to remove the patterns that make AI writing obvious: the “it’s not X, it’s Y” construction, forced lists of three, dashes everywhere and inflated vocabulary. Run it on LinkedIn posts, emails, ad copy and newsletters after the first draft.

Try it with: “Humanize this LinkedIn post. Keep my meaning and my numbers.”

Install: /plugin marketplace add blader/humanizer, then /plugin install humanizer@humanizer

The catch: it fixes style, not facts. Check your claims yourself. And pick this or the similar stop-slop skill, not both, because two sets of style rules make the model second-guess itself.

Research and organizing10. mvanhorn/last30days-skill (about 64K stars)

A research assistant for “what are people actually saying about this right now?” Out of the box it searches Reddit, Hacker News, GitHub and Polymarket. With extra keys it adds X and YouTube. It scores what it finds by engagement and writes everything up as one brief.

Try it with: “What have people said about standing desks in the last 30 days? Give me a one-page brief with the top complaints.”

Install: /plugin marketplace add mvanhorn/last30days-skill, then /plugin install last30days

The catch: it is strong on discussion and weaker where the answer lives in official documentation. X and YouTube need API keys.

From Obsidian’s CEO. It teaches the agent how Obsidian stores notes, so it can work directly inside your notes vault: reading, linking, organizing and writing in Obsidian’s own formats.

items.title: Your PBIP Has Tables and No Measures. Claude’s Free Plan Can Write 65 of Them.
items.summary: The prompts, the order I work in, the errors that stop a TMDL file from opening, and the checks that catch wrong numbers. You have a Power BI project with the tables loaded and the relationships drawn. The Fields pane is full of raw columns and there is not one measure. Total Sales, Sales PY, Sales YTD and Gross Margin % all still have to be written. Most measures in a model like this are variations on a few patterns: a base measure, its prior-year version, a growth percentage. The prompt further down asks for 65 measures, and 21 of them are time intelligence. A PBIP saves the semantic model as plain-text TMDL files. So you can give those files to Claude, list the measures you want, and get back a finished _Measures.tmdl to drop into the project folder. This guide uses Claude's free plan. I wrote it for my workshop participants, with a retail case study called PT Nusa Retail as the model. The project starts with tables and relationships and no measures: NusaRetail.SemanticModel/ definition/ model.tmdl relationships.tmdl tables/ Sales.tmdl _Measures.tmdl <- Claude will write this Dim_Date.tmdl The PBIP folder before Claude writes anything The whole workflow in one sentence: give the TMDL files to Claude as context, let it write or tidy the TMDL, paste the result back into the PBIP folder, then open the project and refresh. Step 0: Set up once In Power BI Desktop, open File > Options > Preview features and turn on “Power BI Project (.pbip) save option” and “Store semantic model using TMDL format”. Turn off Auto date/time in Options > Current File > Data Load. With it on, Desktop adds hidden LocalDateTable_* tables, and their leftovers cause one of the errors in Step 5. Save the file as .pbip with File > Save As. Close Power BI Desktop. Don’t edit TMDL files while the project is open in it. The two preview features that make the PBIP and TMDL folder structure possible Auto date/time off, so no hidden date tables get created Step 1: Give Claude the model Put all the files in a single message to save your message limit. Send model.tmdl (the table list and model settings), relationships.tmdl, the fact table Sales.tmdl, the calendar Dim_Date.tmdl, and every other dimension table such as Products, Customers and Stores. If Claude refuses the .tmdl upload, rename the files to .txt or paste their contents. You can cut the long partition blocks, which hold the Power Query source. Claude only needs table names, column names and data types to write correct DAX. If you will work on the same model across several chats, store the TMDL files in a Claude Project’s knowledge so you don’t upload them every time. Step 2: Ask for the measures The prompt below lists every measure by display folder and sets the writing rules. It is an English version of the prompt I give participants in Indonesian. I have a Power BI Project (PBIP) in TMDL format. I uploaded my model files (model.tmdl, relationships.tmdl, and every table file). Read the table, column, and relationship structure before you write any DAX. Create a new file, tables/_Measures.tmdl, with the measures below, grouped by displayFolder: 01. Sales Total Sales, Gross Sales, Discount Amount, Discount %, Total Qty, Total Orders, Avg Order Value, Avg Selling Price, Avg Qty per Order 02. Profitability Total COGS (Qty x Products[UnitCost]), Gross Profit, Gross Margin % 03. Time Intelligence (use Dim_Date[Date]) Sales PY, Sales YoY, Sales YoY %, Sales PM, Sales MoM %, Sales MTD, Sales QTD, Sales YTD, Sales YTD PY, Sales YTD YoY %, Sales Rolling 3M, Gross Profit PY, Gross Profit YoY %, Gross Margin % PY, Gross Margin Δ pts, Orders PY, Orders YoY %, Customers PY, Customers YoY %, AOV PY, AOV YoY % 04. Target Sales Target (use TREATAS from Stores[Region] to Targets_2025_wide[Region]), Sales vs Target, Target Achievement %, Sales Target YTD, Target Achievement YTD % 05. Customer Active Customers, New Customers, Returning Customers, Repeat Customer Rate %, Sales per Customer, Orders per Customer 06. Contribution & Ranking Sales % of Total, Product Rank, Store Rank, Cumulative Sales % (Pareto) 07. UI & Formatting Last Sales Date, Report Period Label, Sales YoY Label, Color YoY, Color Achievement 08. KPI Card (each KPI gets one Label and one Color) KPI AOV Label/Color, KPI Customers Label/Color, KPI Gross Profit Label/Color, KPI Margin Label/Color, KPI Sales YTD Label/Color, KPI Target Label/Color - Label: short text for the card, for example "Rp 1.2 M" or "▲ 12.3% vs PY" (Rb = thousand, Jt = million, M = billion) - Color: hex code for conditional formatting (green = good, red = bad, gray = no comparison data) Writing rules: 1. All measures in one file, in folder order 01 to 08. 2. Write displayFolder exactly as named above (for example: 01. Sales). 3. formatString: Rupiah \R\p #,0 ; percent 0.0% ; counts #,0 ; text and color measures need no formatString. 4. Write each description with /// above the measure line (NOT a description: property), in Indonesian. 5. _Measures is a calculated table: ROW("Value", BLANK()) with the Value column hidden. Do not write dataType on that column, same as the other calculated columns in my model. 6. Use DIVIDE for every division. Use table names exactly as the model spells them (Dim_Date, not dim_date). 7. File format: tab indentation, CRLF line endings, a new lineageTag for every measure. 8. Ranking and Pareto measures only fill in when the related column is in the visual (ISINSCOPE/HASONEVALUE). When the file is done, also give me: - the line to add to model.tmdl (ref table _Measures) - the folder structure and measure names as plain text - a note on any risk in my model (for example a bidirectional relationship, or a product with no UnitCost) that could make the numbers wrong Output: the complete file, ready to copy. Change “in Indonesian” in rule 4 to your team’s language. One message with every model file and the full measure list Three lines in that prompt need a note. Rule 4 asks for descriptions with /// above each measure instead of a description: property. TMDL reads /// as the description of the line directly below it, so no blank line can sit between them. Step 5 shows what happens when one does. Total COGS multiplies quantity by Products[UnitCost]. A product with no UnitCost gets zero cost, so its margin looks better than it is. That is why the last paragraph asks Claude to list risks like this one, along with bidirectional relationships. In the KPI Card labels, Rb, Jt and M are the Indonesian abbreviations for thousand, million and billion. “Rp 1.2 M” means 1.2 billion rupiah. To add measures to a file you already have, use this follow-up: Add the following measures to the existing _Measures.tmdl: - 04. Target: Sales Target, Target Achievement %, Sales vs Target - 05. Customer: Active Customers, New Customers, Returning Customers - 06. Ranking: Product Rank, Sales % of Total, Cumulative Sales % (Pareto) Give me the complete _Measures.tmdl file, not a fragment. Ask for the complete file every time. A fragment is easy to paste into the wrong place. The first measures in Claude’s output Step 3: Tidy the model Do the measures first, review them, and only then tidy the model. This prompt hides the ID columns, fixes sorting and checks the relationships: Review my TMDL model and tidy it up: 1. Hide the foreign key (ID) columns and the raw numeric columns in the fact table 2. Make sure Dim_Date has dataCategory: Time and the Date column isKey 3. Set sortByColumn (Month Name sorted by Month No) 4. Change summarizeBy to none for columns that should not be summed 5. Check the relationships: are any many-to-many, inactive, or unused? Do not change the partition/source Power Query and do not change any lineageTag. Give me only the files that changed, complete from the first line to the last. Claude must not touch lineageTag. That ID links tables, columns and measures to the visuals already built on them, so rewriting it can break those visuals. If you have no calendar table yet, ask for one: Create tables/Dim_Date.tmdl as a calculated table using CALENDAR from the minimum to the maximum Sales[OrderDate] (start of year to end of year). Columns: Date, Year, Quarter, Month No, Month Name, Month Short, Year Month, Year Month Key, Week No, Day Name, Day Type (Weekday/Weekend). Set dataCategory: Time, Date as isKey, and the correct sortByColumn. Also give me a new relationship Sales[OrderDate] -> Dim_Date[Date] to add to relationships.tmdl. Check how Claude builds Month No. It should come from MONTH(Dim_Date[Date]), not from Month Name. Month Name is sorted by Month No, and a sort column that depends on the column it sorts produces a circular dependency error. Step 4: Put the files back Copy Claude’s files into definition/ and definition/tables/. Add ref table _Measures to model.tmdl, and ref table Dim_Date if the calendar is new. Delete .pbi/cache.abf if you changed a column's data type or removed a table. Open the .pbip and click Refresh. All 65 measures, grouped by display folder. Step 5: When the project won’t open Copy only the Error Message from the dialog, not the whole stack trace, and send it back with this: I got this error when opening the PBIP: [paste Error Message] Which file is wrong and how do I fix it? Give me the corrected file, complete. These are the errors I meet most often, with the cause and the fix. description is not a supported property A table description was written as description:. Put /// text on the line above table instead. variation Variation ... refers to an object which cannot be found A leftover from Auto date/time. Delete the variation block on the date column, and delete the LocalDateTable_*.tmdl and DateTableTemplate_*.tmdl files. Type mismatch. Datatype conversion failed You changed a column’s type but the cache still holds the old data. Delete .pbi/cache.abf, then refresh. Cannot find table/column inside a measure A table or column name in the DAX doesn’t match the model. Send the table files to Claude again and ask it to match the names. Four more came up when I built other PBIPs this way. Unexpected line type: Empty! A blank line sits between a /// description and the object under it. I got this when Claude used /// blocks as section headers. Put /// directly above the measure it describes. The 'Goals' measure cannot be created because a column with the same name already exists. A measure and a column in the same table share a name. Rename the column (GoalsRaw, for example) and leave its sourceColumn as it is, so the data mapping doesn't change. Property QueryGroup of object "expression DataFolderPath" refers to an object which cannot be found A queryGroup: line points at a query group that was never declared on the model. Delete the line. It only controls folders in the Power Query pane. A circular dependency was detected: DimPlayer[Position], DimPlayer[PositionSort], DimPlayer[Position] A column is sorted by a calculated column that reads the first column. Build the sort key from a column that doesn’t depend on it, such as Month No from MONTH(Dim_Date[Date]). Step 6: Check the numbers Claude speeds up the writing. It doesn’t check results against your data, so you do: Every measure shows in the _Measures table, grouped by folder. Total Sales equals the SUM of the Sales Amount column in Data view. The PY and YoY measures return values when you use columns from Dim_Date. Month Name sorts Jan to Dec, not alphabetically. ID columns no longer appear in the Fields pane. Rupiah and percent formats display correctly. Total Sales against the raw sum Start with Total Sales. Sales PY, Sales YTD and the target measures are normally built on it, so a wrong total repeats through all of them. I build Power BI models and data pipelines for mid-market companies. 01. Sales
   Total Sales, Gross Sales, Discount Amount, Discount %, Total Qty,
   Total Orders, Avg Order Value, Avg Selling Price, Avg Qty per Order
02. Profitability
   Total COGS (Qty x Products[UnitCost]), Gross Profit, Gross Margin %
03. Time Intelligence (use Dim_Date[Date])
   Sales PY, Sales YoY, Sales YoY %, Sales PM, Sales MoM %, Sales MTD,
   Sales QTD, Sales YTD, Sales YTD PY, Sales YTD YoY %, Sales Rolling 3M,
   Gross Profit PY, Gross Profit YoY %, Gross Margin % PY, Gross Margin Δ pts,
   Orders PY, Orders YoY %, Customers PY, Customers YoY %, AOV PY, AOV YoY %
04. Target
   Sales Target (use TREATAS from Stores[Region] to Targets_2025_wide[Region]),
   Sales vs Target, Target Achievement %, Sales Target YTD,
   Target Achievement YTD %
05. Customer
   Active Customers, New Customers, Returning Customers,
   Repeat Customer Rate %, Sales per Customer, Orders per Customer
06. Contribution & Ranking
   Sales % of Total, Product Rank, Store Rank, Cumulative Sales % (Pareto)
07. UI & Formatting
   Last Sales Date, Report Period Label, Sales YoY Label,
   Color YoY, Color Achievement
08. KPI Card (each KPI gets one Label and one Color)
   KPI AOV Label/Color, KPI Customers Label/Color,
   KPI Gross Profit Label/Color, KPI Margin Label/Color,
   KPI Sales YTD Label/Color, KPI Target Label/Color
   - Label: short text for the card, for example "Rp 1.2 M" or
     "▲ 12.3% vs PY" (Rb = thousand, Jt = million, M = billion)
   - Color: hex code for conditional formatting
     (green = good, red = bad, gray = no comparison data)
Writing rules:
1. All measures in one file, in folder order 01 to 08.
2. Write displayFolder exactly as named above (for example: 01. Sales).
3. formatString: Rupiah \R\p #,0 ; percent 0.0% ; counts #,0 ;
   text and color measures need no formatString.
4. Write each description with /// above the measure line
   (NOT a description: property), in Indonesian.
5. _Measures is a calculated table: ROW("Value", BLANK()) with the Value
   column hidden. Do not write dataType on that column, same as the other
   calculated columns in my model.
6. Use DIVIDE for every division. Use table names exactly as the model
   spells them (Dim_Date, not dim_date).
7. File format: tab indentation, CRLF line endings, a new lineageTag
   for every measure.
8. Ranking and Pareto measures only fill in when the related column is in
   the visual (ISINSCOPE/HASONEVALUE).
When the file is done, also give me:
- the line to add to model.tmdl (ref table _Measures)
- the folder structure and measure names as plain text
- a note on any risk in my model (for example a bidirectional relationship,
  or a product with no UnitCost) that could make the numbers wrong
Output: the complete file, ready to copy.

Change “in Indonesian” in rule 4 to your team’s language.

One message with every model file and the full measure list

Three lines in that prompt need a note.

Rule 4 asks for descriptions with /// above each measure instead of a description: property. TMDL reads /// as the description of the line directly below it, so no blank line can sit between them. Step 5 shows what happens when one does.

Total COGS multiplies quantity by Products[UnitCost]. A product with no UnitCost gets zero cost, so its margin looks better than it is. That is why the last paragraph asks Claude to list risks like this one, along with bidirectional relationships.

In the KPI Card labels, Rb, Jt and M are the Indonesian abbreviations for thousand, million and billion. “Rp 1.2 M” means 1.2 billion rupiah.

To add measures to a file you already have, use this follow-up:

Add the following measures to the existing _Measures.tmdl:
- 04. Target: Sales Target, Target Achievement %, Sales vs Target
- 05. Customer: Active Customers, New Customers, Returning Customers
- 06. Ranking: Product Rank, Sales % of Total, Cumulative Sales % (Pareto)
Give me the complete _Measures.tmdl file, not a fragment.

Ask for the complete file every time. A fragment is easy to paste into the wrong place.

The first measures in Claude’s outputStep 3: Tidy the model

Do the measures first, review them, and only then tidy the model. This prompt hides the ID columns, fixes sorting and checks the relationships:

Review my TMDL model and tidy it up:
1. Hide the foreign key (ID) columns and the raw numeric columns in the
   fact table
2. Make sure Dim_Date has dataCategory: Time and the Date column isKey
3. Set sortByColumn (Month Name sorted by Month No)
4. Change summarizeBy to none for columns that should not be summed
5. Check the relationships: are any many-to-many, inactive, or unused?
Do not change the partition/source Power Query and do not change
any lineageTag.
Give me only the files that changed, complete from the first line
to the last.

Claude must not touch lineageTag. That ID links tables, columns and measures to the visuals already built on them, so rewriting it can break those visuals.

If you have no calendar table yet, ask for one:

Create tables/Dim_Date.tmdl as a calculated table using CALENDAR from the
minimum to the maximum Sales[OrderDate] (start of year to end of year).
Columns: Date, Year, Quarter, Month No, Month Name, Month Short, Year Month,
Year Month Key, Week No, Day Name, Day Type (Weekday/Weekend).
Set dataCategory: Time, Date as isKey, and the correct sortByColumn.
Also give me a new relationship Sales[OrderDate] -> Dim_Date[Date]
to add to relationships.tmdl.

Check how Claude builds Month No. It should come from MONTH(Dim_Date[Date]), not from Month Name. Month Name is sorted by Month No, and a sort column that depends on the column it sorts produces a circular dependency error.

Step 4: Put the files back
  1. Copy Claude’s files into definition/ and definition/tables/.
  2. Add ref table _Measures to model.tmdl, and ref table Dim_Date if the calendar is new.
  3. Delete .pbi/cache.abf if you changed a column's data type or removed a table.
  4. Open the .pbip and click Refresh.
All 65 measures, grouped by display folder.Step 5: When the project won’t open

Copy only the Error Message from the dialog, not the whole stack trace, and send it back with this:

I got this error when opening the PBIP:
[paste Error Message]
Which file is wrong and how do I fix it?
Give me the corrected file, complete.

These are the errors I meet most often, with the cause and the fix.

description is not a supported property

A table description was written as description:. Put /// text on the line above table instead.

variation Variation ... refers to an object which cannot be found

A leftover from Auto date/time. Delete the variation block on the date column, and delete the LocalDateTable_*.tmdl and DateTableTemplate_*.tmdl files.

Type mismatch. Datatype conversion failed

You changed a column’s type but the cache still holds the old data. Delete .pbi/cache.abf, then refresh.

Cannot find table/column inside a measure

A table or column name in the DAX doesn’t match the model. Send the table files to Claude again and ask it to match the names.

Four more came up when I built other PBIPs this way.

Unexpected line type: Empty!

A blank line sits between a /// description and the object under it. I got this when Claude used /// blocks as section headers. Put /// directly above the measure it describes.

The 'Goals' measure cannot be created because a column with the same name already exists.

A measure and a column in the same table share a name. Rename the column (GoalsRaw, for example) and leave its sourceColumn as it is, so the data mapping doesn't change.

Property QueryGroup of object "expression DataFolderPath" refers to an object which cannot be found

A queryGroup: line points at a query group that was never declared on the model. Delete the line. It only controls folders in the Power Query pane.

A circular dependency was detected: DimPlayer[Position], DimPlayer[PositionSort], DimPlayer[Position]

A column is sorted by a calculated column that reads the first column. Build the sort key from a column that doesn’t depend on it, such as Month No from MONTH(Dim_Date[Date]).

Step 6: Check the numbers

Claude speeds up the writing. It doesn’t check results against your data, so you do:

  • Every measure shows in the _Measures table, grouped by folder.
  • Total Sales equals the SUM of the Sales Amount column in Data view.
  • The PY and YoY measures return values when you use columns from Dim_Date.
  • Month Name sorts Jan to Dec, not alphabetically.
  • ID columns no longer appear in the Fields pane.
  • Rupiah and percent formats display correctly.
Total Sales against the raw sum

Start with Total Sales. Sales PY, Sales YTD and the target measures are normally built on it, so a wrong total repeats through all of them.

I build Power BI models and data pipelines for mid-market companies.

items.title: Your Analytics Agent Needs a Harness. What Should Be in It?
items.summary: Follow one margin investigation through a partial result, a warehouse timeout, and a verified cancellation. This article was drafted with AI assistance. The investigation below uses a fictional dataset and an illustrative event trace. Cover illustration generated with AI. The finance team asks a straightforward question: “Why did gross margin fall last week?” The analytics agent pulls the weekly totals, requests a breakdown by product, and starts a deeper query into supplier costs. That last call times out. The chat says the query stopped. Somewhere behind it, the warehouse may still be running the statement. The first two results present another problem. The weekly totals are complete, but the product tool returned only the first 50 rows. If the agent treats those rows as the entire breakdown, it can name a product as the biggest driver without having looked at every candidate. Both failures happen around the model. The system needs to track what the tools actually did, how much evidence came back, and which claims the answer can support. That is the job of the harness. The code around one agent run An analytics harness assembles context, exposes tools, checks permissions, enforces limits, and records the outcome of each step. The model can propose the next query or explain a result. The runtime decides whether the call may proceed and what information about its outcome goes back to the model. A semantic layer supplies the governed definition of gross margin and the dimensions along which it can be analyzed. The harness applies that context to a specific request. It records which definition and periods were used, attaches the caller’s identity, and controls the lifetime of the queries. Cube describes a production analytics harness built around governed measures and tools that expose result limits. Cube engineering write-up One model and a handful of tools are enough to demonstrate the pattern. A separate evaluation harness runs prepared cases and scores outcomes. You can use it to test the production runtime, including conditions that a model may rarely encounter during a demo. Make partial results visible Suppose the first tool returns complete, comparable weekly totals. Gross margin was 28% in the previous closed week and 24% last week. The difference is four percentage points. The product breakdown then returns 50 rows with an explicit truncation flag and no continuation token. The agent can report the aggregate decline. It has insufficient coverage to rank contributors across the full assortment. A useful result contract separates execution status from data coverage. A query can succeed and still produce a limited response. Give the runtime a result reference, scope, units, and coverage indicator. Where pagination exists, return a continuation token. When the tool cannot determine coverage, expose that uncertainty explicitly. The ranking also needs the right calculation. A product’s own margin rate does not measure its contribution to the change in company-wide margin. Product mix matters. A product with a steep decline and tiny sales volume can have less impact than a large product whose rate moved slightly. Before requesting the ranking, agree on a decomposition and reconcile its components to the aggregate. Otherwise, complete rows can still support the wrong conclusion. For this run, the harness can offer a narrower follow-up within the remaining budget. An approved server-side decomposition can return a small set of ranked contributors plus an aggregate remainder, provided the calculation covers the full authorized scope. If the tool cannot provide that, the final answer should preserve the distinction between the confirmed decline and the unfinished attribution. Track the query after the client stops waiting Imagine the cost drill-down starts with an application wait limit of eight seconds. When the deadline arrives, the application stops waiting for that call. The warehouse’s own statement lifetime is a separate concern. Configure an appropriate backend timeout where available and obtain the warehouse query ID as early as the driver allows. Persist the query ID alongside the run and step IDs. If the driver cannot return it before a connection fails, use a supported request identifier or query tag for reconciliation where possible. An ambiguous submission needs its own state. Retrying immediately can start a second expensive query while the first continues. A concrete cancellation mechanism is Snowflake’s query-ID-based cancellation function. Its documentation specifies which roles can cancel a query. The harness should use the cancellation mechanism supported by its backend and reconcile the outcome with a status source it can access. Snowflake cancellation reference Illustrative eventRecorded stateWhat the interface can sayWarehouse accepts cost query and returns an IDRunning“Checking supplier costs.”Application wait expiresTimed out locally“The cost check exceeded its time limit.”Runtime submits a cancellation requestCancellation requested“Cancellation requested.”Backend confirms cancellationCancelled“The warehouse cancelled the cost query.”Status cannot be confirmed within the reconciliation windowOutcome unknown“Cancellation has not yet been confirmed.” Sequence diagram by DataForge. Illustrative event flow, drafted with AI assistance and rendered programmatically. A query can also complete before cancellation takes effect. Record that terminal outcome separately. Whether a late result can appear in the answer depends on the run’s deadline and the product’s policy for updating a response. For example, the runtime might retain a result reference for diagnosis and close the original answer without using the late data. Enforce limits and make recovery deliberate Set budgets in the runtime. Start with a run deadline, a per-call wait limit, a maximum number of warehouse statements, and a cap on rows returned to the model. Use warehouse controls for execution time or scan limits where the backend supports them. A client row cap alone can leave the underlying scan just as expensive. Reserve time for a partial answer. If four seconds remain and a tool needs ten, the runtime can close with the verified weekly totals and name the missing evidence. Pass the remaining budget to the model so it can choose among permitted next steps. Enforce the same budget at dispatch so an optimistic suggestion cannot silently extend it. Persist enough state to resume safely after a worker restart. Store the run and step IDs, tool and definition versions, caller scope, budget, query ID, status, and a reference to any completed result. Keep result access bound to the caller and the relevant data snapshot or freshness policy. Avoid copying raw rows or credentials into general-purpose logs. A resumed worker should reconcile in-flight queries before submitting replacements. Reuse a completed result only if its scope and freshness still satisfy the run. Where the backend offers a deduplication key, use it. A logical step ID in your own database is valuable for tracing, but it does not by itself prevent a second warehouse execution. Evaluate the answer and the actions Prepare one scenario with a successful metric call, a truncated breakdown, and a timed-out cost drill-down. Run it against a test double first so you can force the order of events. Then check the cancellation path against a disposable warehouse workload using the actual driver and permissions. Inspect two outputs. In the user-facing answer, verify the metric, comparison period, units, and qualification of incomplete evidence. In the trace, verify the exact query ID targeted for cancellation, the final backend status when available, and whether any retry overlapped with the original call. Also exercise a completion racing with cancellation and a cancellation request denied by permissions. A November 2026 preprint on simulated banking agents provides an example of why this distinction matters. The authors observed episodes where an agent’s message denied an action recorded in its tool trace. The result comes from a banking simulation. For analytics, the corresponding test is to compare the chat’s claim about a stopped query with the warehouse’s recorded outcome. Banking harness preprint An acceptance checklist for the example is short. Evidence. The final answer reports the four-point decline from complete weekly totals and leaves the drivers unresolved. Coverage. The runtime records that the product result was truncated. The answer avoids a full-assortment ranking from those 50 rows. Execution. A local timeout and a confirmed backend cancellation have distinct states. The trace can explain what happened when cancellation failed or the query finished first. Recovery. Restarting a worker while the cost query is running triggers reconciliation before any new attempt. Budget. The run stays within the configured dispatch limits even if the model suggests another drill-down. With cancellation still unconfirmed, the answer might read: “Gross margin fell from 28% to 24% across the two closed weeks. The product breakdown was incomplete, so I couldn’t establish the main drivers. The supplier-cost query timed out, and cancellation has not yet been confirmed.” That answer gives finance a number it can use and a clear account of the work still open. To build the first version of your harness, take one workflow your analysts already run. Define what counts as complete evidence, give every warehouse call a traceable identity, and test the path where the last query outlives the chat’s patience. Your Analytics Agent Needs a Harness. items.summary_html:
Follow one margin investigation through a partial result, a warehouse timeout, and a verified cancellation.

This article was drafted with AI assistance. The investigation below uses a fictional dataset and an illustrative event trace.

Cover illustration generated with AI.

The finance team asks a straightforward question: “Why did gross margin fall last week?” The analytics agent pulls the weekly totals, requests a breakdown by product, and starts a deeper query into supplier costs. That last call times out. The chat says the query stopped. Somewhere behind it, the warehouse may still be running the statement.

The first two results present another problem. The weekly totals are complete, but the product tool returned only the first 50 rows. If the agent treats those rows as the entire breakdown, it can name a product as the biggest driver without having looked at every candidate.

Both failures happen around the model. The system needs to track what the tools actually did, how much evidence came back, and which claims the answer can support. That is the job of the harness.

The code around one agent run

An analytics harness assembles context, exposes tools, checks permissions, enforces limits, and records the outcome of each step. The model can propose the next query or explain a result. The runtime decides whether the call may proceed and what information about its outcome goes back to the model.

A semantic layer supplies the governed definition of gross margin and the dimensions along which it can be analyzed. The harness applies that context to a specific request. It records which definition and periods were used, attaches the caller’s identity, and controls the lifetime of the queries. Cube describes a production analytics harness built around governed measures and tools that expose result limits. Cube engineering write-up

One model and a handful of tools are enough to demonstrate the pattern. A separate evaluation harness runs prepared cases and scores outcomes. You can use it to test the production runtime, including conditions that a model may rarely encounter during a demo.

Make partial results visible

Suppose the first tool returns complete, comparable weekly totals. Gross margin was 28% in the previous closed week and 24% last week. The difference is four percentage points. The product breakdown then returns 50 rows with an explicit truncation flag and no continuation token. The agent can report the aggregate decline. It has insufficient coverage to rank contributors across the full assortment.

A useful result contract separates execution status from data coverage. A query can succeed and still produce a limited response. Give the runtime a result reference, scope, units, and coverage indicator. Where pagination exists, return a continuation token. When the tool cannot determine coverage, expose that uncertainty explicitly.

The ranking also needs the right calculation. A product’s own margin rate does not measure its contribution to the change in company-wide margin. Product mix matters. A product with a steep decline and tiny sales volume can have less impact than a large product whose rate moved slightly. Before requesting the ranking, agree on a decomposition and reconcile its components to the aggregate. Otherwise, complete rows can still support the wrong conclusion.

For this run, the harness can offer a narrower follow-up within the remaining budget. An approved server-side decomposition can return a small set of ranked contributors plus an aggregate remainder, provided the calculation covers the full authorized scope. If the tool cannot provide that, the final answer should preserve the distinction between the confirmed decline and the unfinished attribution.

Track the query after the client stops waiting

Imagine the cost drill-down starts with an application wait limit of eight seconds. When the deadline arrives, the application stops waiting for that call. The warehouse’s own statement lifetime is a separate concern. Configure an appropriate backend timeout where available and obtain the warehouse query ID as early as the driver allows.

Persist the query ID alongside the run and step IDs. If the driver cannot return it before a connection fails, use a supported request identifier or query tag for reconciliation where possible. An ambiguous submission needs its own state. Retrying immediately can start a second expensive query while the first continues.

A concrete cancellation mechanism is Snowflake’s query-ID-based cancellation function. Its documentation specifies which roles can cancel a query. The harness should use the cancellation mechanism supported by its backend and reconcile the outcome with a status source it can access. Snowflake cancellation reference

Illustrative eventRecorded stateWhat the interface can sayWarehouse accepts cost query and returns an IDRunning“Checking supplier costs.”Application wait expiresTimed out locally“The cost check exceeded its time limit.”Runtime submits a cancellation requestCancellation requested“Cancellation requested.”Backend confirms cancellationCancelled“The warehouse cancelled the cost query.”Status cannot be confirmed within the reconciliation windowOutcome unknown“Cancellation has not yet been confirmed.”

Sequence diagram by DataForge. Illustrative event flow, drafted with AI assistance and rendered programmatically.

A query can also complete before cancellation takes effect. Record that terminal outcome separately. Whether a late result can appear in the answer depends on the run’s deadline and the product’s policy for updating a response. For example, the runtime might retain a result reference for diagnosis and close the original answer without using the late data.

Enforce limits and make recovery deliberate

Set budgets in the runtime. Start with a run deadline, a per-call wait limit, a maximum number of warehouse statements, and a cap on rows returned to the model. Use warehouse controls for execution time or scan limits where the backend supports them. A client row cap alone can leave the underlying scan just as expensive.

Reserve time for a partial answer. If four seconds remain and a tool needs ten, the runtime can close with the verified weekly totals and name the missing evidence. Pass the remaining budget to the model so it can choose among permitted next steps. Enforce the same budget at dispatch so an optimistic suggestion cannot silently extend it.

Persist enough state to resume safely after a worker restart. Store the run and step IDs, tool and definition versions, caller scope, budget, query ID, status, and a reference to any completed result. Keep result access bound to the caller and the relevant data snapshot or freshness policy. Avoid copying raw rows or credentials into general-purpose logs.

A resumed worker should reconcile in-flight queries before submitting replacements. Reuse a completed result only if its scope and freshness still satisfy the run. Where the backend offers a deduplication key, use it. A logical step ID in your own database is valuable for tracing, but it does not by itself prevent a second warehouse execution.

Evaluate the answer and the actions

Prepare one scenario with a successful metric call, a truncated breakdown, and a timed-out cost drill-down. Run it against a test double first so you can force the order of events. Then check the cancellation path against a disposable warehouse workload using the actual driver and permissions.

Inspect two outputs. In the user-facing answer, verify the metric, comparison period, units, and qualification of incomplete evidence. In the trace, verify the exact query ID targeted for cancellation, the final backend status when available, and whether any retry overlapped with the original call. Also exercise a completion racing with cancellation and a cancellation request denied by permissions.

A November 2026 preprint on simulated banking agents provides an example of why this distinction matters. The authors observed episodes where an agent’s message denied an action recorded in its tool trace. The result comes from a banking simulation. For analytics, the corresponding test is to compare the chat’s claim about a stopped query with the warehouse’s recorded outcome. Banking harness preprint

An acceptance checklist for the example is short.

  • Evidence. The final answer reports the four-point decline from complete weekly totals and leaves the drivers unresolved.
  • Coverage. The runtime records that the product result was truncated. The answer avoids a full-assortment ranking from those 50 rows.
  • Execution. A local timeout and a confirmed backend cancellation have distinct states. The trace can explain what happened when cancellation failed or the query finished first.
  • Recovery. Restarting a worker while the cost query is running triggers reconciliation before any new attempt.
  • Budget. The run stays within the configured dispatch limits even if the model suggests another drill-down.

With cancellation still unconfirmed, the answer might read: “Gross margin fell from 28% to 24% across the two closed weeks. The product breakdown was incomplete, so I couldn’t establish the main drivers. The supplier-cost query timed out, and cancellation has not yet been confirmed.”

That answer gives finance a number it can use and a clear account of the work still open. To build the first version of your harness, take one workflow your analysts already run. Define what counts as complete evidence, give every warehouse call a traceable identity, and test the path where the last query outlives the chat’s patience.
